He greeted them with salutation and then sat down and said: Ask forgiveness for Ma'iz b. Malik. They said: May Allah forgive Ma'iz b. Malik. Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: He (Ma'iz) has made such a repentance that if that were to be divided among a people, it would have been enough for all of them. He (the narrator) said: Then a woman of Ghamid, a branch of Azd, came to him and said: Messenger of of Allah, purify me, whereupon he said: Woe be upon you; go back and beg forgiveness from Allah and turn to Him in repentance. She said: I find that you intend to send me back as you sent back Ma'iz. b. Malik. He (the Holy, Prophet) said: What has happened to you? She said that she had become pregnant as a result of fornication. He (the Holy Prophet) said: Is it you (who has done that)? She said: Yes. He (the Holy Prophet) said to her: (You will not be punished) until you deliver what is there in your womb. One of the Ansar became responsible for her until she was delivered (of the child). He (that Ansari) came to Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) and said the woman of Ghamid has given birth to a child. He (the Holy Prophet) said: In that case we shall not stone her and so leave her infant with none to suckle him. One of the Ansar got up and said: Allah's Apostle, let the responsibility of his suckling be upon me. She was then stoned to death

muslim:4431.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad discouraged confessions of adultery by repeatedly turning Ma'iz b. Malik and the woman of Ghamid away to seek Allah's forgiveness privately, and that postponing the woman's execution until after childbirth demonstrates judicial mercy. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that once Ma'iz repeated his confession a fourth time (`الرَّابِعَةُ`) and was verified to be free of madness (`لَيْسَ بِمَجْنُونٍ`) or wine (`رِيحَ خَمْرٍ`), Muhammad ordered him stoned to death (`فَأَمَرَ بِهِ فَرُجِمَ`), with the companions defining his praised repentance (`تَوْبَةً`) by his plea, 'Kill me with stones' (`اقْتُلْنِي بِالْحِجَارَةِ`). Furthermore, rather than pardoning the repentant mother, Muhammad waited only until she gave birth (`حَتَّى وَضَعَتْ`) and an Ansari volunteered to take responsibility for nursing the infant (`إِلَىَّ رَضَاعُهُ`) before stoning her to death (`فَرَجَمَهَا`), permanently separating the young child (`وَلَدَهَا صَغِيرًا`) from his mother.

bukhari:6842.note: Swearing to judge by the Book of Allah (*bi-kitābi llāh*), Muhammad rejects a ransom of 100 sheep and a slave girl, sentences an unmarried laborer to 100 lashes and a one-year exile for committing adultery with his employer's wife, and orders Unays al-Aslami to stone the married woman to death if she confesses. After the woman confesses, she is stoned to death.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَجَلَدَ ابْنَهُ مِائَةً وَغَرَّبَهُ عَامًا، وَأَمَرَ أُنَيْسًا الأَسْلَمِيَّ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ امْرَأَةَ الآخَرِ، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ فَارْجُمْهَا، فَاعْتَرَفَتْ فَرَجَمَهَا‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) had the man's son flogged one hundred stripes and exiled for one year, and ordered Unais Al-Aslami to go to the wife of the other man, and if she confessed, stone her to death. She confessed and was stoned to death

bukhari:6842.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning to death (al-rajm) is absent from the Quran—which only prescribes a hundred lashes in Surah 24:2—or that the strict requirement of four eyewitnesses renders capital punishment a purely theoretical deterrent. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad swore an oath to judge by 'the Book of Allah' (lā-aqḍiyanna baynakumā bi-Kitābi Allāh) and immediately ordered a lone deputy, 'if she confesses, stone her; so she confessed and he stoned her' (fa-in i'tarafat fa-rjumhā, fa-'tarafat fa-rajamahā), executing the woman in the field without a single eyewitness. As Ibn Hajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī and Al-Nawawī in Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim confirm, this narration enforces the Quran's missing 'verse of stoning' (āyat al-rajm, cf. bukhari:6829)—whose text disappeared while its lethal ruling remained permanently binding—and proves that a single confession obtained by one investigator suffices for execution.

bukhari:1329.note: When the Jews brought a man and a woman from among them who had committed adultery, Muhammad ordered both of them to be stoned to death near the funeral prayer site beside the mosque. In fuller parallel narrations (bukhari:3635, bukhari:4556), he issued this execution order after inspecting the stoning prescription in their physical copy of the Torah.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ الْيَهُودَ، جَاءُوا إِلَى النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِرَجُلٍ مِنْهُمْ وَامْرَأَةٍ زَنَيَا، فَأَمَرَ بِهِمَا فَرُجِمَا قَرِيبًا مِنْ مَوْضِعِ الْجَنَائِزِ عِنْدَ الْمَسْجِدِ
problematic_excerpt.english: The Jew brought to the Prophet (ﷺ) a man and a woman from amongst them who had committed (adultery) illegal sexual intercourse. He ordered both of them to be stoned (to death), near the place of offering the funeral prayers beside the mosque

bukhari:1329.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and fuller parallel narrations (bukhari:3635, bukhari:4556)—that Muhammad was merely arbitrating for the Jewish community according to their own Mosaic Law in the Torah rather than initiating an Islamic punishment. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad personally issued the execution order (فَأَمَرَ بِهِمَا فَرُجِمَا, 'he ordered concerning them both, so they were stoned'), enforcing the exact same brutal ḥadd penalty that he mandated for Muslims and that Sunni jurisprudence maintains as permanent law.

bukhari:7157.note: Upon finding a man with Abu Musa who had embraced Islam and then reverted to Judaism, Mu'adh bin Jabal refuses to sit down until the man is killed, declaring his execution to be the verdict of Allah and His Messenger.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً، أَسْلَمَ ثُمَّ تَهَوَّدَ، فَأَتَى مُعَاذُ بْنُ جَبَلٍ وَهْوَ عِنْدَ أَبِي مُوسَى فَقَالَ مَا هَذَا قَالَ أَسْلَمَ ثُمَّ تَهَوَّدَ‏.‏ قَالَ لاَ أَجْلِسُ حَتَّى أَقْتُلَهُ، قَضَاءُ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم
problematic_excerpt.english: A man embraced Islam and then reverted back to Judaism. Mu`adh bin Jabal came and saw the man with Abu Musa. Mu`adh asked, "What is wrong with this (man)?" Abu Musa replied, "He embraced Islam and then reverted back to Judaism." Mu`adh said, "I will not sit down unless you kill him (as it is) the verdict of Allah and His Apostle

bukhari:7157.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the death penalty for apostasy in early Islam only applied to political high treason or armed rebellion against the state, often appealing to Quran 2:256 ('There is no compulsion in religion'). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the man's sole offense was religious conversion—"أَسْلَمَ ثُمَّ تَهَوَّدَ" ('he embraced Islam and then reverted to Judaism')—with zero mention of political treason or violence, yet Mu'adh bin Jabal immediately demands his execution as "قَضَاءُ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ" ('the verdict of Allah and His Messenger'). Furthermore, parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:6923, bukhari:3017) and Ibn Hajar's commentary in Fatḥ al-Bārī confirm that the fettered man had simply been asked to repent of his religious reversion before Mu'adh had him executed strictly under Muhammad's blanket command: "مَنْ بَدَّلَ دِينَهُ فَاقْتُلُوهُ" ('Whoever changes his religion, kill him').

muslim:4414.note: Declaring that Allah has ordained the promised 'way' for women that supersedes the interim confinement rule of [Quran 4:15](quran://4/15), Muhammad commands that unmarried offenders receive one hundred lashes and a year's banishment ([Quran 24:2](quran://24/2)), while married adulterers receive one hundred lashes and stoning to death (*al-rajm*).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ خُذُوا عَنِّي خُذُوا عَنِّي قَدْ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ لَهُنَّ سَبِيلاً الْبِكْرُ بِالْبِكْرِ جَلْدُ مِائَةٍ وَنَفْىُ سَنَةٍ وَالثَّيِّبُ بِالثَّيِّبِ جَلْدُ مِائَةٍ وَالرَّجْمُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Ubada b. as-Samit reported:Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying: Receive (teaching) from me, receive (teaching) from me. Allah has ordained a way for those (women). When an unmarried male commits adultery with an unmarried female (they should receive) one hundred lashes and banishment for one year. And in case of married male committing adultery with a married female, they shall receive one hundred lashes and be stoned to death

muslim:4414.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning to death is absent from the Quran because [Quran 24:2](quran://24/2) prescribes only one hundred lashes, or that the combined punishment in this report was a temporary ruling rather than permanent Islamic law. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad announced this command as the direct divine fulfillment of [Quran 4:15](quran://4/15)—declaring *"qad ja'ala Allāhu lahunna sabīlan"* ("Allah has ordained a way for those women")—and mandated that married adulterers (*al-thayyibu bi-al-thayyib*) receive one hundred lashes and stoning to death (*jaldu mi'atin wa-al-rajm*), while unmarried offenders (*al-bikru bi-al-bikr*) receive one hundred lashes and one year's banishment (*jaldu mi'atin wa-nafyu sanatin*). Parallel Sahih narrations (`muslim:4416`, `muslim:4417`, `bukhari:6831`) further confirm that stoning to death (*al-rajm*) remained the established prophetic punishment for married adulterers.

bukhari:6819.note: After consulting a physical Torah scroll brought by the Jews of Medina to verify the verse of stoning (ayat al-rajm), Muhammad orders a Jewish man and woman to be stoned to death for illicit sexual intercourse (bukhari:3635). Ibn Umar records witnessing their execution at the Balat, where the man bent over the woman to shield her from the stones, contrasting with Jesus Christ's refusal to stone the adulteress in.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَأَمَرَ بِهِمَا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَرُجِمَا‏.‏ قَالَ ابْنُ عُمَرَ فَرُجِمَا عِنْدَ الْبَلاَطِ، فَرَأَيْتُ الْيَهُودِيَّ أَجْنَأَ عَلَيْهَا
problematic_excerpt.english: So Allah's Apostle ordered that the two (sinners) be stoned to death, and so they were stoned. Ibn `Umar added: So both of them were stoned at the Balat and I saw the Jew sheltering the Jewess

bukhari:6819.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was merely acting as a neutral arbitrator applying Jewish Mosaic law at the community's own request rather than instituting an Islamic punishment, or that stoning has no basis in the Quran. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states فَأَمَرَ بِهِمَا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَرُجِمَا ('So Allah's Messenger ordered that the two be stoned, and so they were stoned'), and as Ibn Ḥajar (Fatḥ al-Bārī) and Al-Nawawī (Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ muslim:4437) confirm, Muhammad examined their scroll solely to expose the rabbis' concealment before enforcing الرَّجْمِ (stoning to death) as a binding, permanent mandate of Islamic Sharia—declaring in the parallel narration (Ṣaḥīḥ muslim:4437), 'O Allah, I am the first to revive Your command.' Furthermore, by testifying that the physical Torah (بِالتَّوْرَاةِ) present in 7th-century AD Medina still contained the authentic 'Divine Verse of Stoning' (آيَةِ الرَّجْمِ), this Hadith simultaneously collapses the modern Islamic claim that the Torah had been textually corrupted (taḥrīf).

bukhari:644.note: Muhammad swears by Allah that he intended (`هَمَمْتُ`) to order firewood to be gathered, appoint a man to lead the people in prayer, and go burn down the houses of men upon them (`فَأُحَرِّقَ عَلَيْهِمْ بُيُوتَهُمْ`) for failing to attend the congregational prayer. He swears again that if any of them knew he would find a fat meaty bone or two good pieces of rib meat, he would have attended the night (`'Isha'`) prayer.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ لَقَدْ هَمَمْتُ أَنْ آمُرَ بِحَطَبٍ فَيُحْطَبَ، ثُمَّ آمُرَ بِالصَّلاَةِ فَيُؤَذَّنَ لَهَا، ثُمَّ آمُرَ رَجُلاً فَيَؤُمَّ النَّاسَ، ثُمَّ أُخَالِفَ إِلَى رِجَالٍ فَأُحَرِّقَ عَلَيْهِمْ بُيُوتَهُمْ، وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ لَوْ يَعْلَمُ أَحَدُهُمْ أَنَّهُ يَجِدُ عَرْقًا سَمِينًا أَوْ مِرْمَاتَيْنِ حَسَنَتَيْنِ لَشَهِدَ الْعِشَاءَ
problematic_excerpt.english: "By Him in Whose Hand my soul is I was about to order for collecting firewood (fuel) and then order Someone to pronounce the Adhan for the prayer and then order someone to lead the prayer then I would go from behind and burn the houses of men who did not present themselves for the (compulsory congregational) prayer. By Him, in Whose Hands my soul is, if anyone of them had known that he would get a bone covered with good meat or two (small) pieces of meat present in between two ribs, he would have turned up for the `Isha' prayer

bukhari:644.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*—that this was merely an unexecuted rhetorical threat (*zajr*) directed at known hypocrites (*munāfiqūn*), and that Muhammad refrained out of concern for the innocent women and children inside those homes. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states under a solemn prophetic oath (*wa-lladhī nafsī bi-yadihi laqad hamamtu*) that he resolved to burn their houses down over them (*fa-uḥarriqa 'alayhim buyūtahum*) for missing the congregational prayer, leading classical jurists like Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal to cite this exact narration as binding legal proof that rulers may violently punish ordinary Muslim men who neglect congregation. Moreover, the excuse that he abstained only because of the women and children inside (*Musnad Aḥmad* 8796) confirms the threat was literal rather than hyperbolic, demonstrating that he viewed burning men alive for skipping a ritual prayer as a morally legitimate punishment deterred solely by collateral damage.

muslim:4433.note: When a pregnant woman from the tribe of Juhaina confesses to adultery and asks for the prescribed punishment, Muhammad instructs her guardian to treat her well until she gives birth and then bring her back to him. Upon her delivery, Muhammad orders her clothes bound around her and commands that she be stoned to death.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ امْرَأَةً، مِنْ جُهَيْنَةَ أَتَتْ نَبِيَّ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهِيَ حُبْلَى مِنَ الزِّنَى فَقَالَتْ يَا نَبِيَّ اللَّهِ أَصَبْتُ حَدًّا فَأَقِمْهُ عَلَىَّ فَدَعَا نَبِيُّ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَلِيَّهَا فَقَالَ ‏"‏ أَحْسِنْ إِلَيْهَا فَإِذَا وَضَعَتْ فَائْتِنِي بِهَا ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَفَعَلَ فَأَمَرَ بِهَا نَبِيُّ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَشُكَّتْ عَلَيْهَا ثِيَابُهَا ثُمَّ أَمَرَ بِهَا فَرُجِمَتْ
problematic_excerpt.english: Imran b. Husain reported that a woman from Juhaina came to Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) and she had become pregnant because of adultery. She said:Allah's Apostle, I have done something for which (prescribed punishment) must be imposed upon me, so impose that. Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) called her master and said: Treat her well, and when she delivers bring her to me. He did accordingly. Then Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) pronounced judgment about her and her clothes were tied around her and then he commanded and she was stoned to death.

muslim:4433.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that postponing the execution until after childbirth (فَإِذَا وَضَعَتْ) and instructing her guardian (وَلِيَّهَا) to treat her well (أَحْسِنْ إِلَيْهَا) demonstrate judicial mercy, or that sincere repentance averts the death penalty. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that once her guardian brought her back after delivery, Muhammad ordered her clothes tied around her and had her stoned to death (فَشُكَّتْ عَلَيْهَا ثِيَابُهَا ثُمَّ أَمَرَ بِهَا فَرُجِمَتْ). Rather than granting pardon upon confession, Muhammad declares to Umar that no repentance is better than surrendering her life (وَهَلْ وَجَدْتَ تَوْبَةً أَفْضَلَ مِنْ أَنْ جَادَتْ بِنَفْسِهَا لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى) to the prescribed punishment (حَدًّا).

bukhari:7332.note: Muhammad orders a Jewish man and woman who committed adultery to be stoned to death near the mosque.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ الْيَهُودَ، جَاءُوا إِلَى النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِرَجُلٍ وَامْرَأَةٍ زَنَيَا، فَأَمَرَ بِهِمَا فَرُجِمَا
problematic_excerpt.english: The Jews brought a man and a woman who had committed illegal sexual intercourse, to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered them to be stoned to death

bukhari:7332.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was merely arbitrating for the Jewish community according to their own Torah law (Leviticus 20:10), or claim that stoning is foreign to Islamic law since [Quran 24:2](quran://24/2) only prescribes one hundred lashes. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states فَأَمَرَ بِهِمَا فَرُجِمَا ('he ordered concerning them both, and they were stoned'), and in the parallel narration (bukhari:3635; cf. muslim:4440) Muhammad forces them to expose آيَة الرَّجْمِ ('the verse of stoning') and celebrates enforcing it as Allah's own revived command (أَوَّلُ مَنْ أَحْيَا أَمْرَكَ). Furthermore, Umar ibn al-Khattab testifies in bukhari:6829 that the Quran originally contained a verse of stoning and that Muhammad stoned married Muslims to death, establishing *rajm* as binding Sunni law (as affirmed by Ibn Hajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī*).

bukhari:6878.note: Muhammad declares that shedding a Muslim's blood is lawful in three cases: retaliation for murder, a married person who commits adultery, and one who abandons the religion and leaves the Muslim community. Classical commentators such as Ibn Hajar and al-Nawawi affirm this ruling as a foundational legal basis for capital punishment against married adulterers and apostates.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: لاَ يَحِلُّ دَمُ امْرِئٍ مُسْلِمٍ يَشْهَدُ أَنْ لاَ إِلَهَ إِلاَّ اللَّهُ وَأَنِّي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ إِلاَّ بِإِحْدَى ثَلاَثٍ النَّفْسُ بِالنَّفْسِ وَالثَّيِّبُ الزَّانِي، وَالْمَارِقُ مِنَ الدِّينِ التَّارِكُ الْجَمَاعَةَ
problematic_excerpt.english: The blood of a Muslim who confesses that none has the right to be worshipped but Allah and that I am His Apostle, cannot be shed except in three cases: In Qisas for murder, a married person who commits illegal sexual intercourse and the one who reverts from Islam (apostate) and leaves the Muslims

bukhari:6878.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the phrase al-tārik al-jamāʿah ('leaving the community') restricts capital punishment for apostasy to political treason or armed rebellion against the state rather than peaceful change of belief. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states al-māriq min al-dīn (الْمَارِقُ مِنَ الدِّينِ, 'the one who exits the religion'), and both Al-Nawawī (Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ muslim:4375) and Ibn Ḥajar (Fatḥ al-Bārī 6878) confirm that 'leaving the community' is merely an explanatory description of every apostate who severs himself from the Muslim body by abandoning Islam. This unconditional death penalty for religious conversion is confirmed by the parallel narration in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6922, where Muhammad commands without any political qualification: 'Whoever changes his religion, kill him' (man baddala dīnahu fa-qtulūhu).

bukhari:6899.note: Abu Qilaba states that Muhammad executed people in three situations: unjust murder, adultery committed by a married person, and fighting against Allah and His Messenger while apostatizing from Islam. Because this narration links apostasy with waging war in the context of the 'Ukl incident, it should be read alongside narrations prescribing execution for apostasy alone (bukhari:6878, bukhari:6922).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَوَاللَّهِ مَا قَتَلَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَطُّ، إِلاَّ فِي إِحْدَى ثَلاَثِ خِصَالٍ رَجُلٌ قَتَلَ بِجَرِيرَةِ نَفْسِهِ فَقُتِلَ، أَوْ رَجُلٌ زَنَى بَعْدَ إِحْصَانٍ، أَوْ رَجُلٌ حَارَبَ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَارْتَدَّ عَنِ الإِسْلاَمِ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: By Allah, Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) never killed anyone except in one of the following three situations: (1) A person who killed somebody unjustly, was killed (in Qisas,) (2) a married person who committed illegal sexual intercourse and (3) a man who fought against Allah and His Apostle and deserted Islam and became an apostate.

bukhari:6899.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue from Abū Qilābah's phrasing—"a man who fought against Allah and His Apostle and deserted Islam" (*ḥāraba llāha wa-rasūlahu wa-rtadda ʿani l-islām*)—that capital punishment applies only to violent armed treason (*ḥirābah*) rather than peaceful apostasy of conscience, while dismissing stoning as a rarely applied deterrent. However, the primary Arabic text of Muhammad's own direct legal formula in parallel Sahih narrations (`bukhari:6878` and `bukhari:3017`) explicitly mandates death for married adultery (*al-thayyibu l-zānī*) and for mere ideological defection: "the one who leaves his religion and separates from the community" (*al-tāriku li-dīnihi l-mufāriqu lil-jamāʿah*) and "whoever changes his religion, kill him" (*man baddala dīnahu fa-qtulūhu*). Consequently, Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī explains in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* on this very passage that open unbelief after Islam inherently constitutes waging war against Allah, cementing the unanimous consensus (*ijmāʿ*) of all four Sunni schools of jurisprudence that unrepentant peaceful apostates must be executed.

bukhari:6899.note: After the men of 'Ukl recover, kill Muhammad's shepherd, drive away the camels, and apostatize, Muhammad has them captured and orders their hands and feet cut off, their eyes branded with heated iron, and their bodies cast into the sun until they die.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَأَمَرَ بِهِمْ فَقُطِّعَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَأَرْجُلُهُمْ، وَسَمَرَ أَعْيُنَهُمْ، ثُمَّ نَبَذَهُمْ فِي الشَّمْسِ حَتَّى مَاتُوا‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: He then ordered to cut their hands and feet, and their eyes were branded with heated pieces of iron, and then he threw them in the sun till they died.

bukhari:6899.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue, citing Ibn Ḥajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, that branding the captives' eyes was strictly proportional retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*) because the tribesmen had allegedly blinded the shepherd first, or that such mutilation (*muthlah*) was later abrogated by the revelation of Quran 5:33. However, the primary Arabic text of this narration explicitly states only that they killed the shepherd (*fa-qatalū rāʿiya rasūli llāhi*) with zero mention of blinding him, before Muhammad ordered their hands and feet amputated (*fa-quṭṭiʿat aydīhim wa-arjuluhum*), their eyes pierced with heated iron (*wa-samara aʿyunahum*), and their bodies cast into the sun until they died (*ḥattā mātū*). Furthermore, parallel Sahih narrations (`bukhari:233`, `bukhari:6802`, `muslim:4353`) explicitly confirm that Quran 5:33 was revealed to divinely endorse—not abrogate—this torture, recording that the mutilated men were left biting the scorching stones of Al-Ḥarrah and begging for water, which Muhammad refused to let them be given until they perished.

bukhari:6899.note: When eight men from the tribe of 'Ukl fall ill in Medina, Muhammad instructs them to go out with his shepherd and drink the milk and urine of the camels to recover.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ ‏"‏ أَفَلاَ تَخْرُجُونَ مَعَ رَاعِينَا فِي إِبِلِهِ، فَتُصِيبُونَ مِنْ أَلْبَانِهَا وَأَبْوَالِهَا ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالُوا بَلَى، فَخَرَجُوا فَشَرِبُوا مِنْ أَلْبَانِهَا وَأَبْوَالِهَا
problematic_excerpt.english: He said (to them ), "Won't you go out with the shepherd of our camels and drink of the camels' milk and urine (as medicine)?" They said, "Yes." So they went out and drank the camels' milk and urine,

bukhari:6899.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad's prescription of camel urine was merely a non-binding local folk remedy rather than divine revelation, or they cite classical jurists who permitted it strictly out of extreme necessity (*ḍarūrah*) while claiming modern studies validate its medicinal properties. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad personally directed the sick men to drink both the camels' milk and urine (*fa-tuṣībūna min albānihā wa-abwālihā*), and Imām al-Bukhārī alongside Ibn Ḥajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* use this exact narration (and `bukhari:233` / `bukhari:5686`) to establish the permanent ritual purity (*ṭahārah*) and prophetic medical validity (*al-ṭibb al-nabawī*) of ingesting camel waste—a practice the World Health Organization warns against as a primary transmission vector for deadly MERS-CoV.

muslim:4440.note: When a Jewish adulterer who had been lashed and had his face blackened with coal passes by, Muhammad adjures a Jewish scholar to confirm that their Torah prescribes stoning rather than the substitute flogging they had adopted to spare their nobles ([Quran 5:41](quran://5/41), [Quran 5:44](quran://5/44)). Declaring himself the first to revive Allah's command, Muhammad orders the man stoned to death.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: مُرَّ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِيَهُودِيٍّ مُحَمَّمًا مَجْلُودًا فَدَعَاهُمْ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ ‏"‏ هَكَذَا تَجِدُونَ حَدَّ الزَّانِي فِي كِتَابِكُمْ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالُوا نَعَمْ ‏.‏ فَدَعَا رَجُلاً مِنْ عُلَمَائِهِمْ فَقَالَ ‏"‏ أَنْشُدُكَ بِاللَّهِ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ عَلَى مُوسَى أَهَكَذَا تَجِدُونَ حَدَّ الزَّانِي فِي كِتَابِكُمْ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ لاَ وَلَوْلاَ أَنَّكَ نَشَدْتَنِي بِهَذَا لَمْ أُخْبِرْكَ نَجِدُهُ الرَّجْمَ وَلَكِنَّهُ كَثُرَ فِي أَشْرَافِنَا فَكُنَّا إِذَا أَخَذْنَا الشَّرِيفَ تَرَكْنَاهُ وَإِذَا أَخَذْنَا الضَّعِيفَ أَقَمْنَا عَلَيْهِ الْحَدَّ قُلْنَا تَعَالَوْا فَلْنَجْتَمِعْ عَلَى شَىْءٍ نُقِيمُهُ عَلَى الشَّرِيفِ وَالْوَضِيعِ فَجَعَلْنَا التَّحْمِيمَ وَالْجَلْدَ مَكَانَ الرَّجْمِ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَوَّلُ مَنْ أَحْيَا أَمْرَكَ إِذْ أَمَاتُوهُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَأَمَرَ بِهِ فَرُجِمَ
problematic_excerpt.english: There happened to pass by Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) a Jew blackened and lashed. Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) called them (the Jews) and said: Is this the punishment that you find in your Book (Torah) as a prescribed punishment for adultery? They said: Yes. He (the Holy Prophet) called one of the scholars amongst them and said: I ask you in the name of Allah Who sent down the Torah on Moses if that is the prescribed punishment for adultery that you find in your Book. He said: No. Had you not asked me in the name of Allah, I would not have given you this information. We find stoning to death (as punishment prescribed in the Torah). But this (crime) became quite common amongst our aristocratic class. So when we caught hold of any rich person (indulging in this offence) we spared him, but when we caught hold of a helpless person we imposed the prescribed punishment upon him. We then said: Let us argree (on a punishment) which we can inflict both upon the rich and the poor. So We decided to blacken the face with coal and flog as a substitute punishment for stoning. Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: O Allah, I am the first to revive Thy command when they had made it dead. He then commanded and he (the offender) was stoned to death.

muslim:4440.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was merely arbitrating a dispute among the Jews according to their own law rather than enforcing an Islamic penalty, and that he was rectifying their unequal treatment of the aristocratic class (`الشَّرِيفَ`) and the weak (`الضَّعِيفَ`). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad claimed ownership of the stoning penalty as Allah's own decree—declaring, 'O Allah, I am the first to revive Thy command when they had made it dead' (`اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَوَّلُ مَنْ أَحْيَا أَمْرَكَ إِذْ أَمَاتُوهُ`)—before ordering the already-lashed man stoned to death (`فَأَمَرَ بِهِ فَرُجِمَ`). Furthermore, the narration links this execution directly to [Quran 5:44](quran://5/44), [Quran 5:45](quran://5/45), and [Quran 5:47](quran://5/47), which condemn those who do not judge by 'what Allah has revealed' (`بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ`), thereby affirming both the stoning mandate and the authoritative status of the Torah (`فِي كِتَابِكُمْ`) in the Jews' possession (`bukhari:3635`, `bukhari:6841`, `muslim:4437`).

bukhari:7260.note: Swearing to judge "according to Allah's Book," Muhammad sentences an unmarried man to 100 lashes and one year of exile for illicit sexual intercourse while commanding Unais to stone the married woman to death if she confesses, an execution carried out the following morning.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَأَمَّا أَنْتَ يَا أُنَيْسُ ـ لِرَجُلٍ مِنْ أَسْلَمَ ـ فَاغْدُ عَلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ فَارْجُمْهَا ‏"‏‏.‏ فَغَدَا عَلَيْهَا أُنَيْسٌ فَاعْتَرَفَتْ فَرَجَمَهَا
problematic_excerpt.english: You, O Unais!" addressing a man from Bani Aslam, "Go tomorrow morning to the wife of this (man) and if she confesses, then stone her to death." The next morning Unais went to the wife and she confessed, and he stoned her to death

bukhari:7260.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (*rajm*) is either absent from the Quran or restricted by an almost impossible evidentiary bar—requiring four eyewitnesses or four unprompted confessions that the judge actively tries to turn away—making the punishment a mere theoretical deterrent. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad proactively dispatched an agent to interrogate the accused wife (*faghdu ʿalā imraʾati hādhā, fa-in iʿtarafat fa-rjumhā*) and had her executed immediately upon a single confession (*fa-iʿtarafat fa-rajamahā*), which classical commentators like Ibn Hajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and Al-Nawawī cite as proof that a single confession suffices without encouraging retraction. Furthermore, Muhammad's oath to judge this case strictly by "the Book of Allah" (*la-aqḍiyanna baynakumā bi-kitābi Allāh*) directly refutes Quran-only deflections while exposing the textual crisis of the missing Quranic "verse of stoning" (*āyat al-rajm*, cf. `bukhari:6829`).

muslim:4406.note: Ibn Umar reports that Muhammad cut off the hand of a thief for stealing a shield valued at three dirhams ([Quran 5:38](quran://5/38); cf. bukhari:6795, muslim:4407). Although neighboring reports note that a shield was considered valuable at that time (muslim:4404, muslim:4405), this narration establishes the three-dirham threshold for hand amputation.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَطَعَ سَارِقًا فِي مِجَنٍّ قِيمَتُهُ ثَلاَثَةُ دَرَاهِمَ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Ibn 'Umar reported that Allah's Messenger (may peace upon him) cut off the hand of a thief (in case of the theft) of a shield the price of which was three dirhams

muslim:4406.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that amputation under [Quran 5:38](quran://5/38) is reserved only for high-value grand larceny and serves mainly as a theoretical deterrent subject to strict legal thresholds. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad cut off a thief's hand (*qaṭaʿa sāriqan*) for a shield worth only three dirhams (*fī mijannin qīmatuhu thalāthatu darāhima*), a ruling confirmed across `bukhari:6795`, `bukhari:6796`, and `muslim:4407`. Rather than severing a thief's hand over three dirhams, the New Testament commands that a thief stop stealing and work with his own hands to share with those in need ([Ephesians 4:28](bible://eph/4/28)).

muslim:2462.note: After Ali remarks that in matters between himself and his listeners 'war is deceit,' he narrates that Muhammad commanded Muslims to kill a young, foolish-minded group (identified by commentators as the Khawarij) who recite the Quran yet pass out of the religion like an arrow through game, promising a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection for whoever kills them ([Matthew 26:52](bible://mt/26/52), [2 Timothy 2:24](bible://2tm/2/24)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ عَلِيٌّ إِذَا حَدَّثْتُكُمْ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَلأَنْ أَخِرَّ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ أَحَبُّ إِلَىَّ مِنْ أَنْ أَقُولَ عَلَيْهِ مَا لَمْ يَقُلْ وَإِذَا حَدَّثْتُكُمْ فِيمَا بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكُمْ فَإِنَّ الْحَرْبَ خَدْعَةٌ ‏.‏ سَمِعْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ ‏ "‏ سَيَخْرُجُ فِي آخِرِ الزَّمَانِ قَوْمٌ أَحْدَاثُ الأَسْنَانِ سُفَهَاءُ الأَحْلاَمِ يَقُولُونَ مِنْ خَيْرِ قَوْلِ الْبَرِيَّةِ يَقْرَءُونَ الْقُرْآنَ لاَ يُجَاوِزُ حَنَاجِرَهُمْ يَمْرُقُونَ مِنَ الدِّينِ كَمَا يَمْرُقُ السَّهْمُ مِنَ الرَّمِيَّةِ فَإِذَا لَقِيتُمُوهُمْ فَاقْتُلُوهُمْ فَإِنَّ فِي قَتْلِهِمْ أَجْرًا لِمَنْ قَتَلَهُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Ali said:Whenever I narrate to you anything from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) believe it to be absolutely true as falling from the sky is dearer to me than that of attributing anything to him (the Holy Prophet) which he never said. When I talk to you of anything which is between me and you (there might creep some error in it) for battle is an outwitting. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as saying: There would arise at the end of the age a people who would be young in age and immature in thought, but they would talk (in such a manner) as if their words are the best among the creatures. They would recite the Qur'an, but it would not go beyond their throats, and they would pass through the religion as an arrow goes through the prey. So when you meet them, kill them, for in their killing you would get a reward with Allah on the Day of Judgement

muslim:2462.literal_translation: Ali said: 'When I narrate to you from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to fall from the sky is dearer to me than to attribute to him what he did not say; and when I speak to you regarding matters between me and you, indeed war is deceit.' I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'There will emerge at the end of time a people young in age and foolish of mind, speaking some of the best words of creation; they will recite the Quran, but it will not go past their throats, and they will pass through the religion as an arrow passes through the game. So when you meet them, kill them, for indeed in killing them there is a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection for whoever kills them.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: وَإِذَا حَدَّثْتُكُمْ فِيمَا بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكُمْ فَإِنَّ الْحَرْبَ خَدْعَةٌ
translation_issue.published_rendering: When I talk to you of anything which is between me and you (there might creep some error in it) for battle is an outwitting
translation_issue.literal_meaning: And when I speak to you regarding matters between me and you, indeed war is deceit
translation_issue.explanation: The translator inserts the apologetic parenthetical '(there might creep some error in it)' and softens 'khad'ah' ('deceit') to 'an outwitting' to disguise Ali's admission of intentional wartime deception as unintentional error.

muslim:2462.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this prophecy merely authorizes defensive state warfare against violent Kharijite rebels, and that Ali's opening remark only refers to benign military strategy rather than personal dishonesty. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that these youths are identified by superficially reciting the Quran (*lā yujāwizu ḥanājarahum*) and defecting from the religion (*yamruqūna mina d-dīn*), unconditionally commanding Muslims to slaughter them on sight (*fa-idhā laqītumūhum fa-qtulūhum*) for eternal reward. Furthermore, Al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*) records that classical authorities cited this exact narration to mandate executing such religious dissenters as apostates (*kuffār*), while Ali directly contrasts truthful prophetic transmission with his own interpersonal speech by invoking *al-ḥarbu khadʿah* ('war is deceit').

muslim:4398.note: Aisha reports that Muhammad cut off the hand of a thief for stealing a quarter of a dinar and upwards ([Quran 5:38](quran://5/38), bukhari:6789, muslim:4400).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَائِشَةَ، قَالَتْ كَانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقْطَعُ السَّارِقَ فِي رُبْعِ دِينَارٍ فَصَاعِدًا
problematic_excerpt.english: A'isha reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) cut off the hand of a thief for a quarter of a dinar rid upwards

muslim:4398.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that hand amputation under [Quran 5:38](quran://5/38) applies only to high-value theft or serves as a theoretical deterrent rather than an enforced practice. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad cut off the thief's hand (*kāna rasūlu llāhi ... yaqṭaʿu al-sāriqa*) for items worth a quarter of a dinar and upwards (*fī rubʿi dīnārin fa-ṣāʿidan*, `bukhari:6789`, `bukhari:6790`, `muslim:4400`). Rather than requiring proportional restitution ([Exodus 22:1](bible://ex/22/1)) or instructing the former thief to labor with his own hands to share with those in need ([Ephesians 4:28](bible://eph/4/28)), this practice imposes permanent amputation for a fraction of a single dinar.

bukhari:3611.note: Muhammad prophesied the emergence of young, foolish people who speak the best words yet pass out of Islam like an arrow through game, commanding his followers to kill them wherever they are met for a reward on the Day of Resurrection. While classical commentators primarily identify this group with the Khawarij sect, al-Bukhari also cites this narration in his Book of Apostates (bukhari:6930) regarding those who abandon the religion.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: سَمِعْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ ‏ "‏ يَأْتِي فِي آخِرِ الزَّمَانِ قَوْمٌ حُدَثَاءُ الأَسْنَانِ، سُفَهَاءُ الأَحْلاَمِ، يَقُولُونَ مِنْ خَيْرِ قَوْلِ الْبَرِيَّةِ، يَمْرُقُونَ مِنَ الإِسْلاَمِ كَمَا يَمْرُقُ السَّهْمُ مِنَ الرَّمِيَّةِ، لاَ يُجَاوِزُ إِيمَانُهُمْ حَنَاجِرَهُمْ، فَأَيْنَمَا لَقِيتُمُوهُمْ فَاقْتُلُوهُمْ، فَإِنَّ قَتْلَهُمْ أَجْرٌ لِمَنْ قَتَلَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: I heard Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) saying, "In the last days of this world there will appear some young foolish people who will use (in their claim) the best speech of all people (i.e. the Qur'an) and they will abandon Islam as an arrow going through the game. Their belief will not go beyond their throats (i.e. they will have practically no belief), so wherever you meet them, kill them, for he who kills them shall get a reward on the Day of Resurrection

bukhari:3611.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this prophecy applies exclusively to defensive warfare against the Khawārij (Kharijites) as armed political insurgents who rebelled against Caliph ʿAlī, rather than a mandate to execute ideological dissidents or apostates. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly defines their capital offense purely by their theological defect—that their faith does not pass their throats (lā yujāwizu īmānuhum ḥanājirahum) and that they exit the religion (yamruqūna mina al-Islām)—before issuing an unconditional bounty to slaughter them on sight (fa-aynamā laqītumūhum fa-qtulūhum, 'wherever you meet them, kill them') without any mention of armed rebellion. Furthermore, Imām al-Bukhārī himself codified the parallel narration (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6930) directly under the legal book of executing apostates (Kitāb Istitābat al-Murtaddīn wa-al-Muʿānidīn wa-Qitālihim), confirming that classical Sunni jurisprudence applied this command to religious defection.

bukhari:6812.note: Ali stones a woman on a Friday and declares that he stoned her in accordance with the Sunnah of Muhammad. Classical commentators such as Ibn Hajar identify the woman as Shurahah al-Hamdaniyyah and cite Ali's declaration as proof that capital stoning for adultery remained the binding prophetic practice after the revelation of [Quran 24:2](quran://24/2).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَلِيٍّ، رضى الله عنه حِينَ رَجَمَ الْمَرْأَةَ يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ وَقَالَ قَدْ رَجَمْتُهَا بِسُنَّةِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم
problematic_excerpt.english: `Ali when the latter stoned a lady to death on a Friday. `Ali said, "I have stoned her according to the tradition of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)

bukhari:6812.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning to death (rajm) is absent from the Quran—which prescribes only 100 lashes in Surah 24:2—or that it was an early carryover from Jewish law later abrogated by Quranic revelation. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Caliph Ali publicly stoned the woman to death (رَجَمَ الْمَرْأَةَ) long after Muhammad's death and declared, 'I have stoned her according to the tradition of Allah's Messenger' (قَدْ رَجَمْتُهَا بِسُنَّةِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ). Furthermore, as Ibn Hajar details in Fatḥ al-Bārī regarding this exact incident (the case of Shurāḥah al-Hamdāniyyah), Ali flogged her on Thursday 'according to the Book of Allah' and then stoned her to death on Friday 'according to the Sunnah of Allah's Messenger,' proving that lethal stoning remained a binding, post-Quranic prophetic mandate.

bukhari:1304.note: Pointing to his tongue, Muhammad declares that while Allah does not punish for tears or grief of the heart, a deceased person is punished for their family's vocal weeping over them, on account of which `Umar used to beat mourners with a stick, pelt them with stones, and throw dust. Although `A'isha rejected `Umar and Ibn `Umar's transmission of this ruling as contradicting [Quran 6:164](quran://6/164) (bukhari:1288), the unrestricted wording here is reinforced by `Umar's enforcement and Muhammad's command to throw dust into the mouths of wailing women (bukhari:1305).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ ‏"‏ أَلاَ تَسْمَعُونَ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لاَ يُعَذِّبُ بِدَمْعِ الْعَيْنِ، وَلاَ بِحُزْنِ الْقَلْبِ، وَلَكِنْ يُعَذِّبُ بِهَذَا ـ وَأَشَارَ إِلَى لِسَانِهِ ـ أَوْ يَرْحَمُ وَإِنَّ الْمَيِّتَ يُعَذَّبُ بِبُكَاءِ أَهْلِهِ عَلَيْهِ ‏"‏‏.‏ وَكَانَ عُمَرُ ـ رضى الله عنه ـ يَضْرِبُ فِيهِ بِالْعَصَا، وَيَرْمِي بِالْحِجَارَةِ وَيَحْثِي بِالتُّرَابِ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: He said, "Will you listen? Allah does not punish for shedding tears, nor for the grief of the heart but he punishes or bestows His Mercy because of this." He pointed to his tongue and added, "The deceased is punished for the wailing of his relatives over him." `Umar used to beat with a stick and throw stones and put dust over the faces (of those who used to wail over the dead)

bukhari:1304.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the verb `yu'adhdhabu` ('is punished') merely refers to the deceased feeling emotional distress or applies only if they instructed their family to wail before death, citing Aisha's appeal to Quran 6:164 ('no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another') in bukhari:1286 and Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī*. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states without qualification that 'the deceased is punished for the weeping of his relatives over him' (`wa-inna al-mayyita yu'adhdhabu bi-bukā'i ahlihi 'alayhi`), employing the exact same verb for divine torment (`yu'adhdhibu`) that Muhammad just used for Allah punishing sins of the tongue. Furthermore, both `Umar and his son `Abdullah upheld this literal vicarious punishment over Aisha's Quranic objection, directly motivating `Umar to beat grieving mourners with a stick (`yaḍribu fīhi bi-l-'aṣā`), pelt them with stones, and fling dirt into their faces.

muslim:4442.note: Jabir ibn Abdullah reports that Muhammad executed a man from the tribe of Aslam as well as a Jewish man and his wife by stoning them to death.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّهُ سَمِعَ جَابِرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ، يَقُولُ رَجَمَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم رَجُلاً مِنْ أَسْلَمَ وَرَجُلاً مِنَ الْيَهُودِ وَامْرَأَتَهُ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Jabir b. 'Abdullah reported that Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) stoned (to death) a person from Banu Aslam, and a Jew and his wife

muslim:4442.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning to death is absent from the Quran ([Quran 24:2](quran://24/2)), functioned only as an unenforceable legal deterrent, or was applied by Muhammad solely to Jewish litigants under their own law. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the Prophet stoned (رَجَمَ النَّبِيُّ) both a man from Banu Aslam (رَجُلاً مِنْ أَسْلَمَ) and a Jewish man and his wife (وَرَجُلاً مِنَ الْيَهُودِ وَامْرَأَتَهُ). Together with parallel reports (bukhari:6814, muslim:4424, muslim:4437), this confirms that Muhammad actively executed both Muslims and Jews by stoning.

bukhari:4344.note: Sent by Muhammad to Yemen with instructions to make things easy and not repulse people, Mu`adh bin Jabal visited Abu Musa, found a chained Jewish man who had embraced Islam and then apostatized, and swore to strike off his neck (cf. [Quran 4:89](quran://4/89)). While this abridged narration concludes with Mu`adh's oath, the fuller parallel transmissions (bukhari:4341, bukhari:4342, bukhari:6923) record that he had the man executed as the judgment of Allah and His Messenger.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَزَارَ مُعَاذٌ أَبَا مُوسَى، فَإِذَا رَجُلٌ مُوثَقٌ، فَقَالَ مَا هَذَا فَقَالَ أَبُو مُوسَى يَهُودِيٌّ أَسْلَمَ ثُمَّ ارْتَدَّ‏.‏ فَقَالَ مُعَاذٌ لأَضْرِبَنَّ عُنُقَهُ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Once Mu`adh paid a visit to Abu Musa and saw a chained man. Mu`adh asked, "What is this?" Abu Musa said, "(He was) a Jew who embraced Islam and has now turned apostate." Mu`adh said, "I will surely chop off his neck

bukhari:4344.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that apostasy in early Islam was only punishable by death when accompanied by political treason or armed rebellion (*ḥirābah*), or cite Muhammad's opening instruction in this hadith—"facilitate things and do not repulse people" (`يَسِّرَا وَلاَ تُعَسِّرَا، وَبَشِّرَا وَلاَ تُنَفِّرَا`)—as proof of religious tolerance. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the chained prisoner's sole offense was a change of religious conscience—`يَهُودِيٌّ أَسْلَمَ ثُمَّ ارْتَدَّ` ("a Jew who embraced Islam and then apostatized")—with zero mention of treason or violence, immediately prompting Mu`adh to swear, `لأَضْرِبَنَّ عُنُقَهُ` ("I will surely chop off his neck"). Furthermore, parallel Sahih narrations (`bukhari:4341`, `bukhari:6923`) and Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* confirm that after Abu Musa unsuccessfully pressured the man to reconvert, Mu`adh refused to even dismount until the man was executed on the spot (`فَأُمِرَ بِهِ فَقُتِلَ`), enforcing death for mere religious apostasy as `قَضَاءُ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ` ("the verdict of Allah and His Messenger").

bukhari:4345.note: Sent by the Prophet to Yemen alongside Abu Musa, Mu'adh visited Abu Musa, found a bound man identified as a Jew who had embraced Islam and then apostatized, and swore to strike off his neck (cf. bukhari:4341).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَزَارَ مُعَاذٌ أَبَا مُوسَى، فَإِذَا رَجُلٌ مُوثَقٌ، فَقَالَ مَا هَذَا فَقَالَ أَبُو مُوسَى يَهُودِيٌّ أَسْلَمَ ثُمَّ ارْتَدَّ‏.‏ فَقَالَ مُعَاذٌ لأَضْرِبَنَّ عُنُقَهُ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Once Mu`adh paid a visit to Abu Musa and saw a chained man. Mu`adh asked, "What is this?" Abu Musa said, "(He was) a Jew who embraced Islam and has now turned apostate." Mu`adh said, "I will surely chop off his neck

bukhari:4345.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that apostasy (riddah) was only punished by death when accompanied by armed political treason against the state, or point to the Prophet's opening instruction in this Hadith (يَسِّرَا وَلاَ تُعَسِّرَا, 'facilitate and do not make things difficult') and Ibn Hajar's discussion of istitābah (granting a grace period for repentance) in Fatḥ al-Bārī as evidence of Islamic leniency. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the chained prisoner's sole offense was religious reversion—يَهُودِيٌّ أَسْلَمَ ثُمَّ ارْتَدَّ ('a Jew who embraced Islam and then apostatized')—with zero mention of rebellion or warfare, which immediately prompted Mu'adh's emphatic oath, لأَضْرِبَنَّ عُنُقَهُ ('I will surely strike off his neck'). Furthermore, the parallel Sahih narrations in bukhari:4341–4342 and bukhari:6923 confirm that even after Abu Musa had already spent months urging the man to repent, Mu'adh refused to sit down until the apostate was beheaded on the spot, declaring his execution for mere change of belief to be قَضَاءُ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ ('the judgment of Allah and His Messenger').

bukhari:6815.note: After turning away until a married man confesses to adultery four times, Muhammad orders him stoned to death, and when the man flees from the stones, the Companions overtake him at al-Harra and stone him to death. In parallel narrations (e.g., muslim:4418), Muhammad later asks why they did not leave him alone when he fled, which jurists interpret as treating flight during stoning as a retraction of a self-confession.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ اذْهَبُوا بِهِ فَارْجُمُوهُ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ ابْنُ شِهَابٍ فَأَخْبَرَنِي مَنْ، سَمِعَ جَابِرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ، قَالَ فَكُنْتُ فِيمَنْ رَجَمَهُ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ بِالْمُصَلَّى، فَلَمَّا أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ هَرَبَ، فَأَدْرَكْنَاهُ بِالْحَرَّةِ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ
problematic_excerpt.english: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'Take him away and stone him to death." Jabir bin `Abdullah said: I was among the ones who participated in stoning him and we stoned him at the Musalla. When the stones troubled him, he fled, but we over took him at Al-Harra and stoned him to death

bukhari:6815.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic ḥudūd punishments are merciful deterrents rarely meant to be carried out, pointing out that Muhammad turned away four times (فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ) and in parallel reports wished the companions had let the man go when he fled. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad himself issued the lethal command, 'Take him away and stone him' (اذْهَبُوا بِهِ فَارْجُمُوهُ), directly enforcing stoning to death for married adulterers (أَحْصَنْتَ)—a mandate Umar confirmed in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6830 was originally an explicit Quranic verse (آيَةُ الرَّجْمِ). Furthermore, as Ibn Hajar notes in Fatḥ al-Bārī, after the companions chased the fleeing man down at Al-Harra and stoned him to death (فَأَدْرَكْنَاهُ بِالْحَرَّةِ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ), Muhammad demanded neither blood-money (diyah) nor expiation from the executioners, cementing brutal stoning as binding prophetic law.

bukhari:2315.note: Muhammad commanded his companion Unais to go to a married woman accused of adultery and stone her to death if she confessed. In the full accounts of this ruling (bukhari:2695, bukhari:6827), she confessed and was stoned to death while her unmarried partner received one hundred lashes and a year of exile.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ ‏ "‏ وَاغْدُ يَا أُنَيْسُ إِلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ فَارْجُمْهَا ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "O Unais! Go to the wife of this (man) and if she confesses (that she has committed illegal sexual intercourse), then stone her to death

bukhari:2315.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (rajm) in Islamic law is merely a theoretical deterrent requiring an almost impossible standard of four eyewitnesses or four repeated, unprompted court confessions that a judge must actively try to turn away. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad proactively dispatched a deputy to interrogate the accused woman and execute her upon a single admission (وَاغْدُ يَا أُنَيْسُ إِلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ فَارْجُمْهَا — 'Go in the morning, O Unais, to the wife of this man, and if she confesses, stone her'), which both Ibn Hajar (Fatḥ al-Bārī) and Al-Nawawī (Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim) cite to prove that a single confession without four witnesses suffices for capital execution. Furthermore, the complete parallel narrations (bukhari:2695, bukhari:6827) confirm this was no symbolic deterrent, recording that while her unmarried male partner received lashes and exile, 'Unais went to her in the morning, and she confessed, so he stoned her to death' (فَغَدَا عَلَيْهَا أُنَيْسٌ فَاعْتَرَفَتْ، فَرَجَمَهَا).

bukhari:2695.note: Declaring that he is judging by the 'Book of Allah,' Muhammad sentences an unmarried laborer to one hundred lashes and one year of exile for illicit sexual intercourse, and orders Unais to execute the married woman involved by stoning her to death. Parallel narrations (bukhari:2315, bukhari:2725) add that Unais was instructed to question her first and stoned her after she confessed.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ، أَمَّا الْوَلِيدَةُ وَالْغَنَمُ فَرَدٌّ عَلَيْكَ، وَعَلَى ابْنِكَ جَلْدُ مِائَةٍ وَتَغْرِيبُ عَامٍ، وَأَمَّا أَنْتَ يَا أُنَيْسُ ـ لِرَجُلٍ ـ فَاغْدُ عَلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا فَارْجُمْهَا ‏"‏‏.‏ فَغَدَا عَلَيْهَا أُنَيْسٌ فَرَجَمَهَا‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "No doubt I will judge between you according to Allah's Laws. The slave-girl and the sheep are to go back to you, and your son will get a hundred lashes and one year exile." He then addressed somebody, "O Unais! go to the wife of this (man) and stone her to death" So, Unais went and stoned her to death

bukhari:2695.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning for adultery in Islam is either non-Quranic (appealing to the 100 lashes of Surah 24:2) or a purely theoretical deterrent requiring four eyewitnesses, while citing Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and parallel narrations (`bukhari:2315`, `bukhari:2725`) to emphasize that the woman was only executed after confessing (`فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ`). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad swore to issue this verdict "by the Book of Allah" (`لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ`)—which Al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*) and Ibn Hajar explain refers to Allah's binding decree (*ḥukm Allāh*) and the abrogated Quranic stoning verse (*āyat al-rajm*)—before commanding Unais, "go to the wife of this man and stone her to death" (`فَاغْدُ عَلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا فَارْجُمْهَا`). Far from being an unenforceable legal hypothetical, the narration explicitly confirms that Unais went and stoned her to death on Muhammad's order (`فَغَدَا عَلَيْهَا أُنَيْسٌ فَرَجَمَهَا`), while the enslaved girl (`وَلِيدَةٍ`) offered as a bribe was simply returned as chattel property (`فَرَدٌّ عَلَيْكَ`).

bukhari:2696.note: Judging by the Book of Allah, Muhammad sentenced an unmarried laborer to one hundred lashes and one year of exile for adultery, and ordered Unais to stone the married woman involved to death. In fuller parallel narrations (bukhari:2315, muslim:4414), Muhammad instructed Unais to question the woman first and stone her if she confessed, which she did.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ، أَمَّا الْوَلِيدَةُ وَالْغَنَمُ فَرَدٌّ عَلَيْكَ، وَعَلَى ابْنِكَ جَلْدُ مِائَةٍ وَتَغْرِيبُ عَامٍ، وَأَمَّا أَنْتَ يَا أُنَيْسُ ـ لِرَجُلٍ ـ فَاغْدُ عَلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا فَارْجُمْهَا ‏"‏‏.‏ فَغَدَا عَلَيْهَا أُنَيْسٌ فَرَجَمَهَا‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "No doubt I will judge between you according to Allah's Laws. The slave-girl and the sheep are to go back to you, and your son will get a hundred lashes and one year exile." He then addressed somebody, "O Unais! go to the wife of this (man) and stone her to death" So, Unais went and stoned her to death

bukhari:2696.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (rajm) is absent from the Quran (which prescribes only a hundred lashes in Surah 24:2) or serves merely as an unenforceable theoretical deterrent requiring four eyewitnesses, while classical commentators like Ibn Hajar (Fatḥ al-Bārī) and Al-Nawawī (Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim) stress from parallel narrations (bukhari:2315) that Unais only stoned the woman after she confessed. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad swore to judge "by the Book of Allah" (bi-kitābi llāhi — بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ) when sentencing the unmarried laborer to lashes and exile while ordering Unais, "Go to the wife of this man and stone her" (fa-ghdu ʿalā imraʾati hādhā fa-rjumhā — فَاغْدُ عَلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا فَارْجُمْهَا), ending in her actual execution (fa-rajamahā — فَرَجَمَهَا). This leaves apologists trapped between admitting that Muhammad enforced a brutal death penalty on a single interrogated confession without four witnesses, and conceding the classical Sunni doctrine that the "Book of Allah" originally contained a stoning verse (āyat al-rajm, bukhari:6830) whose text vanished from the extant Quran while its lethal ruling remained binding Law.

bukhari:2724.note: Swearing to judge by the Book of Allah (*Kitāb Allāh*), Muhammad ordered the return of a ransom of one hundred sheep and a slave girl, sentenced an unmarried laborer to one hundred lashes and one year of exile for fornication, and commanded Unais to question the employer's wife, who was subsequently stoned to death (*rajm*) upon confessing to adultery.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ، الْوَلِيدَةُ وَالْغَنَمُ رَدٌّ، وَعَلَى ابْنِكَ جَلْدُ مِائَةٍ وَتَغْرِيبُ عَامٍ، اغْدُ يَا أُنَيْسُ إِلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ فَارْجُمْهَا ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ فَغَدَا عَلَيْهَا فَاعْتَرَفَتْ، فَأَمَرَ بِهَا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَرُجِمَتْ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, "By Him in Whose Hands my soul is, I will judge between you according to Allah's Laws. The slave-girl and the sheep are to be returned to you, your son is to receive a hundred lashes and be exiled for one year. You, Unais, go to the wife of this (man) and if she confesses her guilt, stone her to death." Unais went to that woman next morning and she confessed. Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) ordered that she be stoned to death

bukhari:2724.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (al-rajm) has no basis in the Quran—which prescribes only a hundred lashes in Surah 24:2—or that Islamic law renders the penalty a purely theoretical deterrent by requiring four eyewitnesses or four separate, unprompted confessions before a judge. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad swore to judge between them 'by the Book of Allah' (لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ) when issuing the death sentence, which Ibn Hajar and Al-Nawawī explain refers to Allah's binding ordinance (farḍ Allāh) and the abrogated-in-recitation stoning verse (āyat al-rajm). Furthermore, rather than requiring four witnesses or turning away a confessor, Muhammad proactively dispatched a single agent (Unais) to interrogate the woman with the summary command, 'if she confesses, stone her' (فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ فَارْجُمْهَا), and upon her single confession she was executed (فَرُجِمَتْ).

bukhari:6633.note: Swearing to judge by the Book of Allah (*Kitāb Allāh*), Muhammad returned a private ransom of one hundred sheep and a slave girl, had an unmarried laborer flogged one hundred times and exiled for a year, and ordered Unays al-Aslamī to stone the employer's wife to death upon her confession of adultery.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ أَمَا وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ، أَمَّا غَنَمُكَ وَجَارِيَتُكَ فَرَدٌّ عَلَيْكَ ‏"‏‏.‏ وَجَلَدَ ابْنَهُ مِائَةً وَغَرَّبَهُ عَامًا، وَأُمِرَ أُنَيْسٌ الأَسْلَمِيُّ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ امْرَأَةَ الآخَرِ، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ رَجَمَهَا، فَاعْتَرَفَتْ فَرَجَمَهَا‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, "Indeed, by Him in Whose Hand my soul is, I will judge between you according to Allah's Laws: As for your sheep and slave girl, they are to be returned to you." Then he scourged his son one hundred lashes and exiled him for one year. Then Unais Al- Aslami was ordered to go to the wife of the second man, and if she confessed (the crime), then stone her to death. She did confess, so he stoned her to death

bukhari:6633.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (*rajm*) is absent from the Quran—which prescribes only lashing in Surah 24:2—or claim that Islamic law treats capital punishment as an unenforceable deterrent by requiring four eyewitnesses and discouraging investigation. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad swore an oath to judge "by the Book of Allah" (*bi-kitābi Allāh*, بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ) and proactively dispatched Unais al-Aslamī to interrogate the accused wife and stone her to death upon her confession (*fa-in iʿtarafat rajamahā, fa-iʿtarafat fa-rajamahā*, فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ رَجَمَهَا، فَاعْتَرَفَتْ فَرَجَمَهَا) without four witnesses. Furthermore, classical commentators like Ibn Hajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and al-Nawawī in *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* concede that judging by the "Book of Allah" here relies either on an abrogated Quranic stoning verse whose text vanished from the written Quran (*mansūkh al-tilāwah*) while its lethal ruling remained binding (*bukhari:6829*), or requires redefining *Kitāb Allāh* to mean non-Quranic decrees.

bukhari:6634.note: Swearing to judge according to the "Book of Allah" (kitab Allah), Muhammad returned the father's ransom of a hundred sheep and a slave girl, flogged the unmarried hired laborer ('asif) one hundred lashes with a year's exile, and ordered Unais al-Aslami to stone the employer's wife to death upon her confession.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ أَمَا وَالَّذِي نَفْسِي بِيَدِهِ لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ، أَمَّا غَنَمُكَ وَجَارِيَتُكَ فَرَدٌّ عَلَيْكَ ‏"‏‏.‏ وَجَلَدَ ابْنَهُ مِائَةً وَغَرَّبَهُ عَامًا، وَأُمِرَ أُنَيْسٌ الأَسْلَمِيُّ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ امْرَأَةَ الآخَرِ، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ رَجَمَهَا، فَاعْتَرَفَتْ فَرَجَمَهَا‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, "Indeed, by Him in Whose Hand my soul is, I will judge between you according to Allah's Laws: As for your sheep and slave girl, they are to be returned to you." Then he scourged his son one hundred lashes and exiled him for one year. Then Unais Al- Aslami was ordered to go to the wife of the second man, and if she confessed (the crime), then stone her to death. She did confess, so he stoned her to death

bukhari:6634.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (`al-rajm`) is absent from the Quran and that Muhammad never proactively investigated adultery accusations, claiming he only reluctantly enforced capital punishment when repentant sinners repeatedly insisted on confessing in person. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad swore to judge "according to the Book of Allah" (`لأَقْضِيَنَّ بَيْنَكُمَا بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ`)—which classical commentators like Ibn Hajar and Al-Nawawī link to Allah's binding decree and the abrogated Quranic stoning verse—and proactively dispatched Unais to interrogate the accused wife and stone her to death upon a single confession (`وَأُمِرَ أُنَيْسٌ الأَسْلَمِيُّ أَنْ يَأْتِيَ امْرَأَةَ الآخَرِ، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ رَجَمَهَا، فَاعْتَرَفَتْ فَرَجَمَهَا`).

bukhari:6825.note: After confirming that a man who confessed four times to adultery is sane and married, Muhammad orders his companions to stone him to death, and when the sharp pain of the stones causes the man to flee, they overtake him at Al-Harra and finish stoning him. Although parallel reports (abudawud:4419; tirmidhi:1428) record Muhammad later asking why they did not let the man go when he fled—treating flight as a retracted self-confession—his command to execute married adulterers by stoning remains binding hadd law.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ ‏"‏ اذْهَبُوا فَارْجُمُوهُ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ ابْنُ شِهَابٍ أَخْبَرَنِي مَنْ، سَمِعَ جَابِرًا، قَالَ فَكُنْتُ فِيمَنْ رَجَمَهُ، فَرَجَمْنَاهُ بِالْمُصَلَّى، فَلَمَّا أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ جَمَزَ حَتَّى أَدْرَكْنَاهُ بِالْحَرَّةِ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: The Prophet (ﷺ) said (to the people), "Take him away and stone him to death." Ibn Shihab added, "I was told by one who heard Jabir, that Jabir said, 'I was among those who stoned the man, and we stoned him at the Musalla (`Id praying Place), and when the stones troubled him, he jumped quickly and ran away, but we overtook him at Al-Harra and stoned him to death (there)

bukhari:6825.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing parallel narrations (`bukhari:6824`, `muslim:4418`) and Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī*—that Muhammad repeatedly turned away to avoid enforcing the *ḥadd* punishment and later wished the companions had let the man escape when he fled, treating his flight as a legal retraction of his confession (*rujūʿ*). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad himself issued the lethal command, *"idhhabū farjumūhu"* ("Go and stone him"), causing the companions to pelt him until *"adhlaqathu al-ḥijārah"* (the stones inflicted sharp, unbearable agony—deceptively softened in English to "troubled him") before chasing him down to finish the execution. Furthermore, as Al-Nawawī and Ibn Hajar confirm, Muhammad imposed no blood-money (*diyah*) or penalty on those who hunted him down, and whenever a confession is maintained or adultery is proven (as in `muslim:4431`), Sunni jurisprudence unequivocally mandates stoning the person to death.

bukhari:6816.note: After a married man confesses four times to committing adultery, Muhammad orders him taken away and stoned to death, and when the stones cause the man to flee, his companions overtake him at Al-Harra and stone him to death. In related reports (such as bukhari:6820), Muhammad later asks why they did not leave him alone when he fled, which classical jurists interpret as treating flight during execution as a retraction of a self-confession.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ اذْهَبُوا بِهِ فَارْجُمُوهُ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ ابْنُ شِهَابٍ فَأَخْبَرَنِي مَنْ، سَمِعَ جَابِرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ، قَالَ فَكُنْتُ فِيمَنْ رَجَمَهُ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ بِالْمُصَلَّى، فَلَمَّا أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ هَرَبَ، فَأَدْرَكْنَاهُ بِالْحَرَّةِ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ
problematic_excerpt.english: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'Take him away and stone him to death." Jabir bin `Abdullah said: I was among the ones who participated in stoning him and we stoned him at the Musalla. When the stones troubled him, he fled, but we over took him at Al-Harra and stoned him to death

bukhari:6816.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic law makes stoning virtually impossible to enforce by turning away voluntary confessors, and cite parallel narrations where Muhammad asked his companions, 'Why did you not leave him alone?' to claim the man's flight legally revoked his confession. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad himself issued the direct execution order—'Take him away and stone him' (idhhabū bihi farjumūhu)—leading his companions to chase the fleeing man down to Al-Harra and stone him to death (fa-adraknāhu bil-Ḥarrati fa-rajamnāhu). Furthermore, as Ibn Hajar notes in Fatḥ al-Bārī, Muhammad required neither blood money (diyah) nor legal penalty from the executioners afterward, cementing the binding Sunni consensus that stoning to death is a divinely mandated hadd punishment.

bukhari:6814.note: After a man from the tribe of Banu Aslam testifies against himself four times to committing unlawful sexual intercourse, Muhammad orders him stoned to death because he had been married (uhsina). Classical commentary identifies the man as Ma'iz ibn Malik and affirms his execution as a foundational legal precedent for the mandatory stoning (rajm) of married adulterers.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَأَمَرَ بِهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَرُجِمَ، وَكَانَ قَدْ أُحْصِنَ
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) ordered him to be stoned to death as he was a married Person

bukhari:6814.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (rajm) is either non-Quranic or a purely theoretical deterrent with an impossible evidentiary threshold, claiming Muhammad only sought to encourage private repentance rather than actual execution. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that once the man testified against himself four times (fashahida 'alā nafsihi arba'a shahādātin), Muhammad directly ordered his execution and he was stoned to death because he had been married (fa-amara bihi Rasūlu Allāhi... fa-rujima, wa-kāna qad uḥṣina). Furthermore, the immediately following narration (bukhari:6815) records that when the agony of the stones struck the man, he tried to flee for his life (haraba) but was chased down and pelted until he died (ḥattā māta), while Umar confirms in bukhari:6829 that stoning married adulterers is an unalterable, divinely revealed mandate in Sunni law.

bukhari:6820.note: After confirming the sanity and marital status of a man who confessed to adultery four times, Muhammad orders him stoned to death; when the impact of the stones causes the man to flee, he is caught and stoned until he dies. Parallel accounts (such as muslim:4418) add that Muhammad subsequently asked his companions why they had not let the man go when he fled.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَأَمَرَ بِهِ فَرُجِمَ بِالْمُصَلَّى، فَلَمَّا أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ فَرَّ، فَأُدْرِكَ فَرُجِمَ حَتَّى مَاتَ
problematic_excerpt.english: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that he be stoned to death, and he was stoned to death at the Musalla. When the stones troubled him, he fled, but he was caught and was stoned till he died.

bukhari:6820.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that stoning (rajm) is functionally a non-enforceable deterrent because Islamic law prioritizes concealing private sins, pointing to Muhammad initially turning away from the confessor and parallel narrations (bukhari:6824, muslim:4418) where he asked his companions why they did not let the man escape when he fled. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad himself issued the execution order (فَأَمَرَ بِهِ فَرُجِمَ — 'so he ordered regarding him, and he was stoned'), and when the piercing agony of the stones (أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ) drove the man to run, he was hunted down and stoned until dead (فَأُدْرِكَ فَرُجِمَ حَتَّى مَاتَ). Furthermore, as Ibn Hajar confirms in Fatḥ al-Bārī, Muhammad neither penalized the companions nor required blood-money (diyah) for killing the fleeing man, cementing death by stoning as a valid, permanent ḥadd punishment in Sunni law.

bukhari:5271.note: After a married man from Banu Aslam confessed to adultery four times—despite Muhammad turning his face away three times—and confirmed he was not insane, Muhammad ordered his companions to stone him to death. When the sharp edges of the stones struck the man, he fled, and the companions caught him at al-Harrah and stoned him until he died, though in parallel reports (bukhari:5270; muslim:4428) Muhammad later remarked that they should have let him go when he fled.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَتَى رَجُلٌ مِنْ أَسْلَمَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهْوَ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ فَنَادَاهُ فَقَالَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إِنَّ الأَخِرَ قَدْ زَنَى ـ يَعْنِي نَفْسَهُ ـ فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ فَتَنَحَّى لِشِقِّ وَجْهِهِ الَّذِي أَعْرَضَ قِبَلَهُ فَقَالَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إِنَّ الأَخِرَ قَدْ زَنَى فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ فَتَنَحَّى لِشِقِّ وَجْهِهِ الَّذِي أَعْرَضَ قِبَلَهُ فَقَالَ لَهُ ذَلِكَ فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ فَتَنَحَّى لَهُ الرَّابِعَةَ، فَلَمَّا شَهِدَ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ أَرْبَعَ شَهَادَاتٍ دَعَاهُ فَقَالَ ‏"‏ هَلْ بِكَ جُنُونٌ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ لاَ‏.‏ فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ اذْهَبُوا بِهِ فَارْجُمُوهُ ‏"‏‏.‏ وَكَانَ قَدْ أُحْصِنَ‏.‏ وَعَنِ الزُّهْرِيِّ، قَالَ أَخْبَرَنِي مَنْ، سَمِعَ جَابِرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ الأَنْصَارِيَّ، قَالَ كُنْتُ فِيمَنْ رَجَمَهُ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ بِالْمُصَلَّى بِالْمَدِينَةِ، فَلَمَّا أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ جَمَزَ حَتَّى أَدْرَكْنَاهُ بِالْحَرَّةِ، فَرَجَمْنَاهُ حَتَّى مَاتَ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: A man from Bani Aslam came to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) while he was in the mosque and called (the Prophet (ﷺ) ) saying, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! I have committed illegal sexual intercourse." On that the Prophet (ﷺ) turned his face from him to the other side, whereupon the man moved to the side towards which the Prophet (ﷺ) had turned his face, and said, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! I have committed illegal sexual intercourse." The Prophet turned his face (from him) to the other side whereupon the man moved to the side towards which the Prophet (ﷺ) had turned his face, and repeated his statement. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned his face (from him) to the other side again. The man moved again (and repeated his statement) for the fourth time. So when the man had given witness four times against himself, the Prophet (ﷺ) called him and said, "Are you insane?" He replied, "No." The Prophet (ﷺ) then said (to his companions), "Go and stone him to death." The man was a married one. Jabir bin `Abdullah Al-Ansari said: I was one of those who stoned him. We stoned him at the Musalla (`Id praying place) in Medina. When the stones hit him with their sharp edges, he fled, but we caught him at Al-Harra and stoned him till he died

bukhari:5271.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad's repeated turning away (*fa-aʿraḍa ʿanhu*) and his subsequent remark in parallel narrations (bukhari:5270, muslim:4428) asking why the companions did not let the fleeing man go prove that Islamic law seeks to avoid stoning and treats flight as a valid retraction of confession. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that once the man confirmed he was sane, Muhammad himself issued the unconditional execution command (*idhhabū bihi farjumūhu* — 'Go with him and stone him') without ever instructing his executioners that fleeing suspends the *ḥadd* penalty. Moreover, as Ibn Ḥajar (*Fatḥ al-Bārī*) and Al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*) note, Muhammad neither held the companions liable for unlawful killing or blood-money (*diyah*) after they hunted the agonized man down at al-Ḥarrah and stoned him to death (*farajamnāhu ḥattā māta*), nor did he abrogate the mandate of stoning married adulterers.

bukhari:5272.note: After a married man from Banu Aslam confessed to adultery four times—despite Muhammad turning away from him three times and asking whether he was insane—Muhammad ordered his companions to stone him to death. When the sharp edges of the stones struck the man at the prayer ground in Medina, he fled, and the companions caught him at al-Harrah and stoned him until he died.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَتَى رَجُلٌ مِنْ أَسْلَمَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهْوَ فِي الْمَسْجِدِ فَنَادَاهُ فَقَالَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إِنَّ الأَخِرَ قَدْ زَنَى ـ يَعْنِي نَفْسَهُ ـ فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ فَتَنَحَّى لِشِقِّ وَجْهِهِ الَّذِي أَعْرَضَ قِبَلَهُ فَقَالَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إِنَّ الأَخِرَ قَدْ زَنَى فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ فَتَنَحَّى لِشِقِّ وَجْهِهِ الَّذِي أَعْرَضَ قِبَلَهُ فَقَالَ لَهُ ذَلِكَ فَأَعْرَضَ عَنْهُ فَتَنَحَّى لَهُ الرَّابِعَةَ، فَلَمَّا شَهِدَ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ أَرْبَعَ شَهَادَاتٍ دَعَاهُ فَقَالَ ‏"‏ هَلْ بِكَ جُنُونٌ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَ لاَ‏.‏ فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ اذْهَبُوا بِهِ فَارْجُمُوهُ ‏"‏‏.‏ وَكَانَ قَدْ أُحْصِنَ‏.‏ وَعَنِ الزُّهْرِيِّ، قَالَ أَخْبَرَنِي مَنْ، سَمِعَ جَابِرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ الأَنْصَارِيَّ، قَالَ كُنْتُ فِيمَنْ رَجَمَهُ فَرَجَمْنَاهُ بِالْمُصَلَّى بِالْمَدِينَةِ، فَلَمَّا أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ جَمَزَ حَتَّى أَدْرَكْنَاهُ بِالْحَرَّةِ، فَرَجَمْنَاهُ حَتَّى مَاتَ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: A man from Bani Aslam came to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) while he was in the mosque and called (the Prophet (ﷺ) ) saying, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! I have committed illegal sexual intercourse." On that the Prophet (ﷺ) turned his face from him to the other side, whereupon the man moved to the side towards which the Prophet (ﷺ) had turned his face, and said, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! I have committed illegal sexual intercourse." The Prophet turned his face (from him) to the other side whereupon the man moved to the side towards which the Prophet (ﷺ) had turned his face, and repeated his statement. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned his face (from him) to the other side again. The man moved again (and repeated his statement) for the fourth time. So when the man had given witness four times against himself, the Prophet (ﷺ) called him and said, "Are you insane?" He replied, "No." The Prophet (ﷺ) then said (to his companions), "Go and stone him to death." The man was a married one. Jabir bin `Abdullah Al-Ansari said: I was one of those who stoned him. We stoned him at the Musalla (`Id praying place) in Medina. When the stones hit him with their sharp edges, he fled, but we caught him at Al-Harra and stoned him till he died

bukhari:5272.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic law prioritizes mercy and the concealment of sins (*satr*), noting that Muhammad turned away four times to discourage Ma'iz's confession and, as cited by Ibn Hajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* via parallel narrations (*Sahih al-Bukhari* 6820; *Sahih Muslim* 1691), later chided his companions for not letting the man go when he fled as a tacit retraction (*rujūʿ*) of his testimony. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that once Muhammad verified the man was sane (`هَلْ بِكَ جُنُونٌ`) and married (`وَكَانَ قَدْ أُحْصِنَ`), he personally issued the lethal command, "Go with him and stone him" (`اذْهَبُوا بِهِ فَارْجُمُوهُ`), causing the man to be hunted down as he fled the sharp stones (`فَلَمَّا أَذْلَقَتْهُ الْحِجَارَةُ جَمَزَ`) and bludgeoned to death (`فَرَجَمْنَاهُ حَتَّى مَاتَ`). Far from extending forgiveness to a contrite sinner upon confession, Muhammad enforced *rajm* as a mandatory statute—rooted in the lost Quranic 'verse of stoning' (*āyat al-rajm* in *Sahih al-Bukhari* 6830)—and required neither blood-money (*diyah*) nor penance from the companions who killed the fleeing man.

bukhari:6859.note: Swearing to judge by the "Book of Allah" (kitab Allah), Muhammad sentences an unmarried laborer to one hundred lashes and a year's exile for adultery, while ordering Unais to question the married woman involved and stone her to death (rajm) if she confesses. Upon her confession, she is stoned to death—a ruling classical Sunni jurisprudence upholds as the binding capital penalty for married adulterers, even though stoning does not appear in the extant Quran.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَيَا أُنَيْسُ اغْدُ عَلَى امْرَأَةِ هَذَا فَسَلْهَا، فَإِنِ اعْتَرَفَتْ فَارْجُمْهَا ‏"‏‏.‏ فَاعْتَرَفَتْ فَرَجَمَهَا
problematic_excerpt.english: And O Unais! Go in the morning to the wife of this man and ask her, and if she confesses, stone her to death." She confessed and he stoned her to death

bukhari:6859.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic capital punishments are nearly impossible to enforce because the Prophet forbade investigating private sins, actively discouraged confessions, and required four eyewitnesses or four unprompted judicial confessions, while modern reformists claim stoning (*rajm*) contradicts the Quran (Surah 24:2).
