muslim:3531.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this ruling is a protective deterrent designed to stop men from recklessly pronouncing triple divorce, insisting that pre-arranged temporary marriages (*nikāḥ al-taḥlīl*) are prohibited. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that reconciliation is forbidden *'until the last one tastes of her little honey what the first tasted'* (*ḥattā yadhūqa al-ākhiru min ʿusaylatihā mā dhāqa al-awwalu*), which Imām al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*) confirms is a legal mandate for actual vaginal penetration (*māghīb al-ḥashafah fī al-farj*). Rather than penalizing the reckless husband directly, this law uses the woman's body as the instrument of punishment by requiring her to be sexually penetrated by another man before she can return home—a prerequisite Muhammad enforced in parallel narrations (bukhari:5260, muslim:3526) even when the woman was being physically beaten by her second husband.

muslim:3529.note: Muhammad rules that a divorced woman who marries another man and is divorced before sexual intercourse remains unlawful to her first husband until the second husband has sexually consummated the marriage ('tasted her sweetness'; [Quran 2:230](quran://2/230), cf. [Deuteronomy 24:1](bible://dt/24/1)). Classical commentators including Al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar affirm that this report establishes actual vaginal penetration (*jima'*) with the intervening husband as a binding legal prerequisite before an irrevocably divorced woman may remarry her first husband.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم سُئِلَ عَنِ الْمَرْأَةِ يَتَزَوَّجُهَا الرَّجُلُ فَيُطَلِّقُهَا فَتَتَزَوَّجُ رَجُلاً فَيُطَلِّقُهَا قَبْلَ أَنْ يَدْخُلَ بِهَا أَتَحِلُّ لِزَوْجِهَا الأَوَّلِ قَالَ ‏ "‏ لاَ حَتَّى يَذُوقَ عُسَيْلَتَهَا ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) was asked about a woman whom a man married and then divorced her, and then she married (another) person, and she was divorced before sexual intercourse with her, whether it was lawful for her first husband (to marry her in this state). He (the Holy Prophet) said:No, until he has tasted her sweetness

muslim:3529.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this ruling on Quran 2:230 was designed to protect women by deterring men from pronouncing reckless triple-divorces, adding that pre-arranged sham marriages (nikāḥ al-taḥlīl) are cursed in other traditions. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states "lā, ḥattā yadhūqa ʿusaylatahā" ("No, until he has tasted her sweetness")—defined in Al-Nawawī's Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim as actual penile penetration (ghaybūbat al-ḥashafah)—meaning Islamic law penalizes the woman for her first husband's rashness by requiring her to be sexually penetrated by another man before reconciliation is permitted. As the parallel narration (Ṣaḥīḥ muslim:3526; Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5260) confirms, even when Rifāʿah's divorced wife pleaded that her second husband was impotent, Muhammad forbade her from returning to her first husband until the second man consummated the marriage, directly inverting the moral law of Deuteronomy 24:1–4.

muslim:5804.note: Muhammad unconditionally declares in the Arabic text that evil omen (*al-shu'm*) resides in the house, the woman, and the horse, grouping women alongside residential property and livestock as carriers of bad luck. Although the English translation interpolates a conditional 'If there be' absent from this Arabic narration, neighboring reports confirm that even after denying general ill omen, Muhammad explicitly restricts evil omen to these three things (muslim:5805, bukhari:2858, bukhari:5093).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عُمَرَ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ الشُّؤْمُ فِي الدَّارِ وَالْمَرْأَةِ وَالْفَرَسِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Abdullah b. 'Umar reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:If there be bad luck, it is in the house, and the wife, and the horse

muslim:5804.literal_translation: Abdullah b. 'Umar reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'Evil omen (bad luck) is in the house, the woman, and the horse.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: الشُّؤْمُ فِي الدَّارِ وَالْمَرْأَةِ وَالْفَرَسِ
translation_issue.published_rendering: If there be bad luck, it is in the house, and the wife, and the horse
translation_issue.literal_meaning: Evil omen (bad luck) is in the house, the woman, and the horse
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates the unbracketed conditional clause 'If there be' into an unconditional Arabic nominal sentence that contains no conditional particle.

muslim:5804.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was speaking hypothetically—relying on the English rendering 'If there be bad luck'—or that the statement merely describes practical incompatibility with a home, a wife, or a mount. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states an unconditional nominal declaration, 'Al-shu'm fī al-dār wa-al-mar'ah wa-al-faras' ('Evil omen is in the house, the woman, and the horse'), with no conditional particle present in the original wording. Even with the translator's interpolated 'If there be' to soften the declaration, the narration still classifies women alongside real estate and livestock as vessels of bad luck (bukhari:2858, bukhari:5093, muslim:5805).

muslim:5805.note: Muhammad declares with the restrictive particle *innamā* that evil omen (*al-shu'm*) exists only in three things: the woman, the horse, and the house. Although an adjacent narration (muslim:5807) frames this statement conditionally, this report and muslim:5804 state it categorically.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عُمَرَ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ لاَ عَدْوَى وَلاَ طِيَرَةَ وَإِنَّمَا الشُّؤْمُ فِي ثَلاَثَةٍ الْمَرْأَةِ وَالْفَرَسِ وَالدَّارِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Abdullah b. 'Umar reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:There is no transitive disease, no ill omen, and bad luck is lound in the house, or wife or horse. Note: The majority of scholars interpret this to mean that these things in and of themselves do not transmit or cause harm through supernatural or hidden means but that Allah is ultimately in control and any fearful superstition around these is false

muslim:5805.literal_translation: Abdullah b. 'Umar reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'There is no contagion and no evil omen, and evil omen (bad luck) is only in three things: the woman, the horse, and the house.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: وَإِنَّمَا الشُّؤْمُ فِي ثَلاَثَةٍ الْمَرْأَةِ وَالْفَرَسِ وَالدَّارِ
translation_issue.published_rendering: and bad luck is lound in the house, or wife or horse. Note: The majority of scholars interpret this to mean that these things in and of themselves do not transmit or cause harm through supernatural or hidden means but that Allah is ultimately in control and any fearful superstition around these is false
translation_issue.literal_meaning: and evil omen (bad luck) is only in three things: the woman, the horse, and the house
translation_issue.explanation: The English rendering omits the restrictive phrase 'only in three' (innamā ... fī thalāthatin), narrows 'the woman' (al-mar'ah) to 'wife' while moving it from first position in the Arabic list, and appends an editorial note absent from the Arabic matn.

muslim:5805.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that these words merely reject fearful superstition under Allah's control or refer figuratively to practical incompatibility rather than attributing actual bad luck to women, as the English translator's appended note claims. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *wa-innamā al-shu'mu fī thalāthatin: al-mar'ati wa-al-farasi wa-al-dār* ('and evil omen is only in three things: the woman, the horse, and the house'), using the restrictive particle *innamā* to carve out a literal exception to the preceding denial of ill omens (*lā ṭiyarah*). By listing 'the woman' (*al-mar'ah*) first among these three exceptions, the narration directly classifies women alongside horses and houses as carriers of *al-shu'm* (`bukhari:5093`, `muslim:5804`).

muslim:5805.note: Muhammad declares that there is no transitive disease (*lā ʿadwā*) and no general ill omen (*lā ṭiyarah*), yet immediately restricts evil omen (*innamā al-shu'm*) to the woman, the horse, and the house (bukhari:5753, muslim:5804). Although the English translation appends an editorial note claiming these things merely lack independent causation apart from Allah, the Arabic text negates contagious disease in the same sentence that it affirms evil omen in those three things.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عُمَرَ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ لاَ عَدْوَى وَلاَ طِيَرَةَ وَإِنَّمَا الشُّؤْمُ فِي ثَلاَثَةٍ الْمَرْأَةِ وَالْفَرَسِ وَالدَّارِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Abdullah b. 'Umar reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:There is no transitive disease, no ill omen, and bad luck is lound in the house, or wife or horse. Note: The majority of scholars interpret this to mean that these things in and of themselves do not transmit or cause harm through supernatural or hidden means but that Allah is ultimately in control and any fearful superstition around these is false

muslim:5805.literal_translation: Abdullah b. 'Umar reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'There is no contagion and no evil omen, and evil omen (bad luck) is only in three things: the woman, the horse, and the house.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: وَإِنَّمَا الشُّؤْمُ فِي ثَلاَثَةٍ الْمَرْأَةِ وَالْفَرَسِ وَالدَّارِ
translation_issue.published_rendering: and bad luck is lound in the house, or wife or horse. Note: The majority of scholars interpret this to mean that these things in and of themselves do not transmit or cause harm through supernatural or hidden means but that Allah is ultimately in control and any fearful superstition around these is false
translation_issue.literal_meaning: and evil omen (bad luck) is only in three things: the woman, the horse, and the house
translation_issue.explanation: The English rendering omits the restrictive phrase 'only in three' (innamā ... fī thalāthatin) and appends an editorial note absent from the Arabic matn to qualify the statement on contagion and bad omens.

muslim:5805.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the denial of contagion (*lā ʿadwā*) only means diseases do not transmit independently of Allah's control, as the translator's interpolated note asserts to reconcile the text with medical reality. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *lā ʿadwā wa-lā ṭiyarah wa-innamā al-shu'mu fī thalāthatin* ('there is no contagion and no evil omen, and evil omen is only in three things'), pairing the categorical negation of disease transmission directly with the negation of omens while restricting actual bad luck (*al-shu'm*) to the woman, the horse, and the house (`bukhari:5753`, `muslim:5804`). Supplying an unstated 'in and of themselves' into *lā ʿadwā* cannot undo the text's direct contrast, which denies biological contagion while affirming supernatural bad luck in three physical things (`bukhari:5772`).

muslim:6942.note: Muhammad declares via Imran bin Husain that women constitute the fewest of the inhabitants of Paradise (*inna aqalla sākinī al-jannati al-nisā'*). In the Arabic text—though omitted from the published English translation—Mutarrif bin Abdullah cites this pronouncement to one of his two wives when she remarks that he has just come from being with her co-wife.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: كَانَ لِمُطَرِّفِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ امْرَأَتَانِ فَجَاءَ مِنْ عِنْدِ إِحْدَاهُمَا فَقَالَتِ الأُخْرَى جِئْتَ مِنْ عِنْدِ فُلاَنَةَ فَقَالَ جِئْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِ عِمْرَانَ بْنِ حُصَيْنٍ فَحَدَّثَنَا أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ إِنَّ أَقَلَّ سَاكِنِي الْجَنَّةِ النِّسَاءُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Imran b. Husain reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said:Amongst the inmates of Paradise the women would form a minority

muslim:6942.literal_translation: Mutarrif b. Abdullah had two wives. He came from being with one of them, and the other said: 'You have come from being with so-and-so!' He replied: 'I have come from Imran b. Husain, and he narrated to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the fewest of the inhabitants of Paradise are women."'

translation_issue.arabic_term: كَانَ لِمُطَرِّفِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ امْرَأَتَانِ فَجَاءَ مِنْ عِنْدِ إِحْدَاهُمَا فَقَالَتِ الأُخْرَى جِئْتَ مِنْ عِنْدِ فُلاَنَةَ
translation_issue.published_rendering: [omitted]
translation_issue.literal_meaning: Mutarrif b. Abdullah had two wives; he came from being with one of them, and the other said: 'You have come from being with so-and-so!'
translation_issue.explanation: The published translation completely excises the opening narrative showing Mutarrif silencing his jealous co-wife by citing Muhammad's declaration that women are the smallest minority in Paradise.

muslim:6942.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad's statement is merely a neutral demographic observation rather than a moral indictment used to police wives' behavior toward their husbands. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states—in a framing omitted from the published English translation—that Mutarrif bin Abdullah had two wives (*imra'atāni*) and cited Muhammad's decree that women are the fewest inhabitants of Paradise (*inna aqalla sākinī al-jannati al-nisā'*) to rebuke one wife when she complained, 'You have come from being with so-and-so!' (*ji'ta min 'indi fulānata*). This direct link between a wife's complaint against her husband and female exclusion from Paradise aligns with parallel narrations (bukhari:304, bukhari:3241).

bukhari:5198.note: Muhammad declares that upon looking into Paradise he saw that the majority of its inhabitants were the poor, and upon looking into the Hellfire he saw that the majority of its inhabitants were women. Classical commentators such as Ibn Hajar and Al-Nawawi affirm the literal meaning of this report, rationalizing it through demographic theories or parallel traditions citing women's alleged ungratefulness toward their husbands.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَاطَّلَعْتُ فِي النَّارِ، فَرَأَيْتُ أَكْثَرَ أَهْلِهَا النِّسَاءَ
problematic_excerpt.english: and I looked at the (Hell) Fire and saw that the majority of its residents were women

bukhari:5198.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī—that women comprise the majority of Hell's inhabitants simply because females outnumber males in the overall human population, or that Muhammad's words were merely a rhetorical exhortation to charity rather than an ontological condemnation of women. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states فَرَأَيْتُ أَكْثَرَ أَهْلِهَا النِّسَاءَ ('I saw that the majority of its residents were women'), and parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:29, bukhari:304) directly attribute women's mass damnation to their ungratefulness toward their husbands (يَكْفُرْنَ الْعَشِيرَ) and their inherent 'deficiency in intelligence and religion' (نَاقِصَاتِ عَقْلٍ وَدِينٍ). Furthermore, the demographic excuse collapses against bukhari:3245, which states that every man in Paradise has two wives (لِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ زَوْجَتَانِ), proving that Islamic eschatology places women in Hell due to their alleged moral and spiritual inferiority rather than population ratios.

bukhari:5196.note: Muhammad declares via Usama ibn Zayd that while standing at the gate of Paradise he saw the poor forming the majority of its entrants, whereas standing at the gate of Hell revealed that the majority of those entering the Fire were women. In the immediately following report (bukhari:5197), this disparity is attributed to women being ungrateful toward their husbands and denying their favors.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَقُمْتُ عَلَى باب النَّارِ فَإِذَا عَامَّةُ مَنْ دَخَلَهَا النِّسَاءُ
problematic_excerpt.english: Then I stood at the gate of the Fire and saw that the majority of those who entered it were women

bukhari:5196.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that women only form the majority in Hell because females statistically outnumber males in the overall human population, or that this vision is merely a rhetorical warning against specific moral failings rather than an inherent disparagement of women. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that 'the vast majority of those who entered it were women' (فَإِذَا عَامَّةُ مَنْ دَخَلَهَا النِّسَاءُ), and parallel Ṣaḥīḥ narrations directly refute the demographic excuse by recording Muhammad's declaration that women are the smallest minority in Paradise (إِنَّ أَقَلَّ سَاكِنِي الْجَنَّةِ النِّسَاءُ, Ṣaḥīḥ muslim:6942). Furthermore, in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 304, Muhammad explicitly grounds women's predominance in the Fire in their alleged 'deficiency in intelligence and religion' (نَاقِصَاتِ عَقْلٍ وَدِينٍ) and their ungratefulness toward their husbands (يَكْفُرْنَ الْعَشِيرَ).

muslim:4573.note: During a raid against Banu Fazara commanded by Abu Bakr, Salama captured women and children and was awarded a Fazari woman's daughter as a war prize. Salama states that he had not yet disrobed her when Muhammad twice asked him to hand her over, after which Muhammad sent her to Mecca as ransom for Muslim prisoners.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَجِئْتُ بِهِمْ أَسُوقُهُمْ وَفِيهِمُ امْرَأَةٌ مِنْ بَنِي فَزَارَةَ عَلَيْهَا قِشْعٌ مِنْ أَدَمٍ - قَالَ الْقِشْعُ النِّطَعُ - مَعَهَا ابْنَةٌ لَهَا مِنْ أَحْسَنِ الْعَرَبِ فَسُقْتُهُمْ حَتَّى أَتَيْتُ بِهِمْ أَبَا بَكْرٍ فَنَفَّلَنِي أَبُو بَكْرٍ ابْنَتَهَا فَقَدِمْنَا الْمَدِينَةَ وَمَا كَشَفْتُ لَهَا ثَوْبًا فَلَقِيَنِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فِي السُّوقِ فَقَالَ ‏"‏ يَا سَلَمَةُ هَبْ لِي الْمَرْأَةَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقُلْتُ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ أَعْجَبَتْنِي وَمَا كَشَفْتُ لَهَا ثَوْبًا
problematic_excerpt.english: So I brought them, driving them along. Among them was a woman from Banu Fazara. She was wearing a leather coat. With her was her daughter who was one of the prettiest girls in Arabia. I drove them along until I brought them to Abu Bakr who bestowed that girl upon me as a prize. So we arrived in Medina. I had not yet disrobed her when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met me in the street and said: Give me that girl, O Salama. I said: Messenger of Allah, she has fascinated me. I had not yet disrobed her.

muslim:4573.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this narration demonstrates humanitarian restraint toward captives because Salama ibn al-Akwa' never consummated his ownership of the Fazari woman and Muhammad ultimately used her in a prisoner exchange. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that after women and children (al-dharārī) were captured (sabā) and driven along (fasuqtuhum), Abu Bakr awarded the daughter to Salama as personal war booty (fanaffalanī Abū Bakr ibnatahā), and Salama's repeated clarification that he 'had not yet disrobed her' (wa-mā kashaftu lahā thawban) confirms that sexual access to a female captive was the captor's recognized right. Furthermore, Muhammad did not revoke her status as chattel or return her to her captured Banu Fazara mother, but asked Salama to gift the woman to him (hab lī al-mar'ata) and sent her to the people of Mecca as payment to ransom Muslim prisoners (fafadā bihā nāsan min al-muslimīna).

bukhari:4138.note: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that during the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq, Muhammad's companions took Arab captives and, because celibacy had become hard on them and they desired women, asked Muhammad about practicing coitus interruptus (*'azl*) with them (which parallel report bukhari:2542 states was to preserve their ransom value). Muhammad raised no objection to their sexual relations with the captives ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24)), replying only that they need not practice *'azl* because every soul predestined to exist until the Day of Resurrection will come into being.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: خَرَجْنَا مَعَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فِي غَزْوَةِ بَنِي الْمُصْطَلِقِ، فَأَصَبْنَا سَبْيًا مِنْ سَبْىِ الْعَرَبِ، فَاشْتَهَيْنَا النِّسَاءَ وَاشْتَدَّتْ عَلَيْنَا الْعُزْبَةُ، وَأَحْبَبْنَا الْعَزْلَ، فَأَرَدْنَا أَنْ نَعْزِلَ، وَقُلْنَا نَعْزِلُ وَرَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم بَيْنَ أَظْهُرِنَا قَبْلَ أَنْ نَسْأَلَهُ فَسَأَلْنَاهُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ مَا عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ لاَ تَفْعَلُوا، مَا مِنْ نَسَمَةٍ كَائِنَةٍ إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ إِلاَّ وَهْىَ كَائِنَةٌ ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: We went out with Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) for the Ghazwa of Banu Al-Mustaliq and we received captives from among the Arab captives and we desired women and celibacy became hard on us and we loved to do coitus interruptus. So when we intended to do coitus interruptus, we said, 'How can we do coitus interruptus before asking Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) who is present among us?" We asked (him) about it and he said, 'It is better for you not to do so, for if any soul (till the Day of Resurrection) is predestined to exist, it will exist

bukhari:4138.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that sexual relations with female war captives required marriage or mutual consent, or cite Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* to claim that Muhammad's reply (*mā 'alaykum an lā taf'alū*) discouraged coitus interruptus (*'azl*) to protect the women's status before the Banu al-Mustaliq captives were eventually freed. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the soldiers seized Arab women as war booty (*fa-aṣabnā sabyan min sabyi al-'arab*) to satisfy their sexual cravings (*fa-shtahaynā al-nisā'*), and parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:2229, bukhari:2542) confirm they practiced withdrawal specifically so they could still sell the women or collect their ransom (*al-fidā'*) without pregnancy voiding their market value. Rather than condemning the immediate sexual exploitation of newly captured women for financial gain, Muhammad permitted the intercourse and dismissed their contraceptive precautions on purely fatalistic grounds (*mā min nasamatin kā'inatin ilā yawmi al-qiyāmati illā wa-hiya kā'inatun*).

muslim:4445.note: Muhammad commands a slave owner whose female slave commits fornication to personally flog her with the prescribed punishment without reproaching her on the first two offenses, and on the third offense to sell her even for a rope of hair.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: سَمِعْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ ‏ "‏ إِذَا زَنَتْ أَمَةُ أَحَدِكُمْ فَتَبَيَّنَ زِنَاهَا فَلْيَجْلِدْهَا الْحَدَّ وَلاَ يُثَرِّبْ عَلَيْهَا ثُمَّ إِنْ زَنَتْ فَلْيَجْلِدْهَا الْحَدَّ وَلاَ يُثَرِّبْ عَلَيْهَا ثُمَّ إِنْ زَنَتِ الثَّالِثَةَ فَتَبَيَّنَ زِنَاهَا فَلْيَبِعْهَا وَلَوْ بِحَبْلٍ مِنْ شَعَرٍ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: When the slave-woman of any of you commits adultery and this (offence of hers) becomes clear, she should be flogged (as the prescribed) punishment, but hurl no reproach at her. If she commits adultery again, she should (again be punished) by flogging, but hurl no reproach upon her. If she commits fornication for the third time and it becomes clear, then he should sell her, even if only for a rope of hair

muslim:4445.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam humanized slavery by forbidding verbal reproach (وَلاَ يُثَرِّبْ عَلَيْهَا, 'do not reproach her') and regulating discipline under legal standards rather than arbitrary abuse. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states فَلْيَجْلِدْهَا الْحَدَّ ('let him flog her the prescribed punishment') and فَلْيَبِعْهَا وَلَوْ بِحَبْلٍ مِنْ شَعَرٍ ('let him sell her, even for a rope of hair'), addressing the individual master (أَحَدِكُمْ, 'one of you') in the active voice. Rather than granting the woman freedom or independent judicial protection, the command authorizes private owners to personally whip their female slaves on two occasions and then sell them off as property for the price of a rope of hair (bukhari:2152, bukhari:6837, muslim:4447).

muslim:3556.note: When a man tells Muhammad that he has sexual intercourse with his female slave (`jariyah`)—who works as his household servant and water-carrier (`khadimuna wa saniyatuna`)—but dislikes for her to conceive, Muhammad permits him to practice coitus interruptus (`'azl`) while declaring that whatever is decreed for her will still occur ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24), [Quran 23:6](quran://23/6)). After the slave woman later becomes pregnant despite withdrawal, Muhammad reiterates that her conception was predestined, a report classical jurists cite to affirm a master's right to use his female domestic servant for sexual intercourse and practice `'azl` without her consent.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً، أَتَى رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ إِنَّ لِي جَارِيَةً هِيَ خَادِمُنَا وَسَانِيَتُنَا وَأَنَا أَطُوفُ عَلَيْهَا وَأَنَا أَكْرَهُ أَنْ تَحْمِلَ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ ‏"‏ اعْزِلْ عَنْهَا إِنْ شِئْتَ فَإِنَّهُ سَيَأْتِيهَا مَا قُدِّرَ لَهَا ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَلَبِثَ الرَّجُلُ ثُمَّ أَتَاهُ فَقَالَ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ قَدْ حَبِلَتْ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ ‏"‏ قَدْ أَخْبَرْتُكَ أَنَّهُ سَيَأْتِيهَا مَا قُدِّرَ لَهَا ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: a man came to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and said:I have a slave-girl who is our servant and she carries water for us and I have intercourse with her, but I do not want her to conceive. He said: Practise 'azl, if you so like, but what is decreed for her will come to her. The person stayed back (for some time) and then came and said: The girl has become pregnant, whereupon he said: I told you what was decreed for her would come to her

muslim:3556.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic concubinage was a compassionate institution designed to integrate captive women into the family with marriage-like rights and elevate them to emancipation through motherhood (*umm walad*). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the master used his slave-girl simultaneously as a manual laborer and water-carrier (*khādimunā wa-sāniyatunā*) and for regular sexual intercourse (*wa-anā aṭūfu 'alayhā*), while actively seeking to prevent her from conceiving (*wa-anā akrahu an taḥmila*) so her labor and property value would not be compromised. Rather than condemning this dual exploitation or asking for the woman's consent, Muhammad grants the master unilateral permission to practice withdrawal at will (*i'zil 'anhā in shi'ta*), which Imām al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*) cites to establish that—unlike a free wife—a female slave has no right to consent regarding coitus interruptus.

muslim:4338.note: When an Ansari man with no other property declared his Coptic slave free after his death, Muhammad sold the slave to Nu'aym ibn al-Nahham for eight hundred dirhams and handed the proceeds to the master, leaving the man enslaved until he died in the first year of the caliphate of Abdullah ibn al-Zubair.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً، مِنَ الأَنْصَارِ أَعْتَقَ غُلاَمًا لَهُ عَنْ دُبُرٍ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ مَالٌ غَيْرُهُ فَبَلَغَ ذَلِكَ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ مَنْ يَشْتَرِيهِ مِنِّي ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَاشْتَرَاهُ نُعَيْمُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بِثَمَانِمِائَةِ دِرْهَمٍ فَدَفَعَهَا إِلَيْهِ ‏.‏ قَالَ عَمْرٌو سَمِعْتُ جَابِرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ يَقُولُ عَبْدًا قِبْطِيًّا مَاتَ عَامَ أَوَّلَ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Jabir b. 'Abdullah said that a person among the Ansar declared his slave free after his death, as he had no other property. This news reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and he said:Who will buy him from me? And Nu'aim b. al-Nahham bought him for eight hundred dirhams and he handed them over to him, 'Amr (one of the narrators) said: I heard Jabir b. 'Abdullah as saying: He was a Coptic slave, and he died in the first year (of the Caliphate of 'Abdullah b. Zubair)

muslim:4338.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam systematically promoted the emancipation of slaves and that Muhammad only intervened here out of financial prudence because the Ansari owner had no other property (لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ مَالٌ غَيْرُهُ). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that after the owner declared his slave free upon his death (أَعْتَقَ غُلاَمًا لَهُ عَنْ دُبُرٍ), Muhammad asked, "Who will buy him from me?" (مَنْ يَشْتَرِيهِ مِنِّي), sold him to Nu'aim b. al-Nahham for eight hundred dirhams (فَاشْتَرَاهُ نُعَيْمُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بِثَمَانِمِائَةِ دِرْهَمٍ), and handed the money over to the owner (فَدَفَعَهَا إِلَيْهِ). As Jabir b. 'Abdullah records, the man remained a Coptic slave until he died in the first year of the Caliphate of 'Abdullah b. Zubair (عَبْدًا قِبْطِيًّا مَاتَ عَامَ أَوَّلَ), demonstrating that the master's financial liquidity took precedence over the slave's promised manumission (bukhari:2141, muslim:4339).

bukhari:2542.note: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri recounts that after capturing Arab women during the raid on Banu al-Mustaliq, the companions desired them because separation from their wives weighed heavily on them and asked Muhammad about practicing coitus interruptus (*'azl*) with the captives—a measure parallel reports (bukhari:2229, bukhari:4138) state was taken to preserve their ransom or sale value ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24)). Without prohibiting sexual intercourse with the newly acquired captives, Muhammad replied only that refraining from withdrawal brings no harm because every soul destined to exist until the Day of Resurrection will inevitably come into being.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَأَصَبْنَا سَبْيًا مِنْ سَبْىِ الْعَرَبِ، فَاشْتَهَيْنَا النِّسَاءَ فَاشْتَدَّتْ عَلَيْنَا الْعُزْبَةُ وَأَحْبَبْنَا الْعَزْلَ، فَسَأَلْنَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ مَا عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ لاَ تَفْعَلُوا، مَا مِنْ نَسَمَةٍ كَائِنَةٍ إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ إِلاَّ وَهْىَ كَائِنَةٌ ‏"‏
problematic_excerpt.english: we captured some of the 'Arabs as captives, and the long separation from our wives was pressing us hard and we wanted to practice coitus interruptus. We asked Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) (whether it was permissible). He said, "It is better for you not to do so. No soul, (that which Allah has) destined to exist, up to the Day of Resurrection, but will definitely come, into existence

translation_issue.arabic_term: فَاشْتَهَيْنَا النِّسَاءَ
translation_issue.published_rendering: [omitted]
translation_issue.literal_meaning: so we desired / lusted after the women
translation_issue.explanation: The published Darussalam/Muhsin Khan translation completely omits the clause fa-shtahaynā al-nisā'a ('so we desired/lusted after the women') and renders sabyan (female captives) generically as 'some of the Arabs as captives,' obscuring the explicit statement that the soldiers' sexual desire for the newly captured women prompted their inquiry about coitus interruptus.

bukhari:2542.literal_translation: So we acquired female captives from the captives of the Arabs, and we desired the women, as celibacy had become hard upon us, and we wanted to practice coitus interruptus ('azl). So we asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'There is no harm upon you if you do not do so; there is no soul that is to come into being up to the Day of Resurrection except that it will come into being.'
bukhari:2542.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that relations with female war captives (*milk al-yamīn*) functioned as a benevolent, consensual institution designed to shelter and integrate displaced women into Muslim households rather than exploit them. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the soldiers were driven by immediate sexual lust after capturing the women (*fa-shtahaynā al-nisā'a fa-shtaddat 'alaynā al-'uzbah*), and parallel Sahih narrations (`bukhari:2229`, `bukhari:4138`) confirm they practiced coitus interruptus (*'azl*) specifically so the captives would not conceive and forfeit their market resale or ransom value. Rather than condemning the sexual use of traumatized prisoners on the battlefield prior to selling them, Muhammad explicitly sanctioned the act by replying, *'mā 'alaykum an lā taf'alū'* ('There is no harm upon you if you do not do so').

bukhari:2229.note: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī informs Muhammad that the companions acquire female war captives (*saby*) and desire their sale prices (*al-athmān*), asking his ruling on practicing coitus interruptus (*ʿazl*) with them so pregnancy does not reduce their value. Without objecting to having sexual intercourse with the captives while intending to sell them, Muhammad states they need not practice withdrawal (*lā ʿalaykum an lā tafʿalū dhālikum*) because every soul Allah has decreed to exist will inevitably be born ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: بَيْنَمَا هُوَ جَالِسٌ عِنْدَ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إِنَّا نُصِيبُ سَبْيًا، فَنُحِبُّ الأَثْمَانَ، فَكَيْفَ تَرَى فِي الْعَزْلِ فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ أَوَإِنَّكُمْ تَفْعَلُونَ ذَلِكَ لاَ عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ لاَ تَفْعَلُوا ذَلِكُمْ، فَإِنَّهَا لَيْسَتْ نَسَمَةٌ كَتَبَ اللَّهُ أَنْ تَخْرُجَ إِلاَّ هِيَ خَارِجَةٌ ‏"‏
problematic_excerpt.english: while he was sitting with Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) he said, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! We get female captives as our share of booty, and we are interested in their prices, what is your opinion about coitus interruptus?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Do you really do that? It is better for you not to do it. No soul that which Allah has destined to exist, but will surely come into existence

bukhari:2229.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic war captivity was strictly humanitarian and required marriage before sexual relations, or claim from English translations that Muhammad discouraged exploiting captives by saying, 'It is better for you not to do it.' However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the companions were having sex with female war captives (*sabyan*) while coveting their sale prices (*fa-nuḥibbu al-athmān*), practicing withdrawal (*'azl*) solely so pregnancy would not lower their market value or legally block their sale. Moreover, as Ibn Hajar (*Fatḥ al-Bārī*) and Al-Nawawī explain, Muhammad's reply (*lā 'alaykum an lā taf'alū dhālikum*, 'there is no harm upon you if you do not do that') merely noted that withdrawal cannot thwart divine predestination, completely validating their right to sexually use and then sell captive women for cash.

muslim:3608.note: After Muslim soldiers captured women at Awtas during the Battle of Hunayn (AD 630) and felt reluctant (taḥarrajū) to have sexual intercourse with them because of their polytheist husbands, [Quran 4:24](quran://4/24) was revealed declaring married female captives (mā malakat aymānukum) sexually lawful for their captors once their waiting period ('iddah) expired (cf. muslim:3609; [Exodus 20:14](bible://ex/20/14)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَوْمَ حُنَيْنٍ بَعَثَ جَيْشًا إِلَى أَوْطَاسٍ فَلَقُوا عَدُوًّا فَقَاتَلُوهُمْ فَظَهَرُوا عَلَيْهِمْ وَأَصَابُوا لَهُمْ سَبَايَا فَكَأَنَّ نَاسًا مِنْ أَصْحَابِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم تَحَرَّجُوا مِنْ غِشْيَانِهِنَّ مِنْ أَجْلِ أَزْوَاجِهِنَّ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ فَأَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ فِي ذَلِكَ ‏{‏ وَالْمُحْصَنَاتُ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ إِلاَّ مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ‏}‏ أَىْ فَهُنَّ لَكُمْ حَلاَلٌ إِذَا انْقَضَتْ عِدَّتُهُنَّ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: at the Battle of Hanain Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) sent an army to Autas and encountered the enemy and fought with them. Having overcome them and taken them captives, the Companions of Allah's Messenger (may peace te upon him) seemed to refrain from having intercourse with captive women because of their husbands being polytheists. Then Allah, Most High, sent down regarding that:" And women already married, except those whom your right hands possess (iv. 24)" (i. e. they were lawful for them when their 'Idda period came to an end)

muslim:3608.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Quran 4:24 required formal marriage and mutual consent with female captives, or that the classical ruling cited by Al-Nawawī—that enslavement automatically annuls a polytheist woman's marriage (*infisākh al-nikāḥ bil-saby*) following a waiting period—was a humane legal regulation. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the Companions only hesitated to have sexual intercourse with the captives (*taḥarrajū min ghishyānihinna*) because their polytheist husbands were still alive (*min ajli azwājihinna min al-mushrikīn*), prompting the revelation of *illā mā malakat aymānukum* ("except those whom your right hands possess") to declare married war captives directly lawful for sexual use (*fahunna lakum ḥalāl*) by mere chattel ownership—without a marriage contract or the woman's consent—as soon as a brief menstrual clearance (*inqaḍat 'iddatuhunna*) verified non-pregnancy.

bukhari:5210.note: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that Muhammad's companions took female war captives (*saby*) and practiced coitus interruptus (*'azl*) with them. When asked about the practice, Muhammad does not prohibit sexual intercourse with the captives ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24)), declaring only that every soul destined to exist until the Day of Resurrection will inevitably come into being.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَصَبْنَا سَبْيًا فَكُنَّا نَعْزِلُ فَسَأَلْنَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ أَوَإِنَّكُمْ لَتَفْعَلُونَ قَالَهَا ثَلاَثًا مَا مِنْ نَسَمَةٍ كَائِنَةٍ إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ إِلاَّ هِيَ كَائِنَةٌ ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: We got female captives in the war booty and we used to do coitus interruptus with them. So we asked Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) about it and he said, "Do you really do that?" repeating the question thrice, "There is no soul that is destined to exist but will come into existence, till the Day of Resurrection

bukhari:5210.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that sexual relations with female war captives were consensual, protective arrangements meant to integrate displaced women into society, or that Muhammad discouraged coitus interruptus (*'azl*) so captives would bear children and gain the emancipated legal status of *umm walad* (mother of her master's child). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the companions acquired these women as war booty (*أَصَبْنَا سَبْيًا فَكُنَّا نَعْزِلُ*), and parallel Sahih narrations of this exact incident (`bukhari:2229`, `bukhari:4138`) confirm they practiced withdrawal specifically because they intended to sell the women for profit and did not want pregnancy to prevent their sale. Rather than condemning the non-consensual sexual use and commercial trafficking of prisoners of war, Muhammad tacitly approved the practice and remarked only on the theological inevitability of predestined souls (*مَا مِنْ نَسَمَةٍ كَائِنَةٍ إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ إِلَّا هِيَ كَائِنَةٌ*).

muslim:3546.note: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that Muhammad's companions took female war captives (sabāyā) and were practicing coitus interruptus ('azl) with them (fa-kunnā naʿzilu), though the English translation softens this ongoing practice into mere intention ("we wanted to do 'azl"). When they asked Muhammad about it, he did not prohibit their sexual use of the captives, instead asking thrice whether they were indeed doing so and declaring that every soul decreed to exist until the Day of Resurrection will inevitably come into being ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24), [Quran 23:5-6](quran://23/5-6); bukhari:4138, bukhari:5210).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَصَبْنَا سَبَايَا فَكُنَّا نَعْزِلُ ثُمَّ سَأَلْنَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم عَنْ ذَلِكَ فَقَالَ لَنَا ‏ "‏ وَإِنَّكُمْ لَتَفْعَلُونَ وَإِنَّكُمْ لَتَفْعَلُونَ وَإِنَّكُمْ لَتَفْعَلُونَ مَا مِنْ نَسَمَةٍ كَائِنَةٍ إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ إِلاَّ هِيَ كَائِنَةٌ ‏"
problematic_excerpt.english: We took women captives, and we wanted to do 'azl with them. We then asked Allah's Messen- ger (ﷺ) about it, and he said to us: Verily you do it, verily you do it, verily you do it, but the soul which has to be born until the Day of judg- ment must be born

muslim:3546.literal_translation: We captured female captives, and we were practicing coitus interruptus ('azl) [with them]. We then asked Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) about that, and he said to us: 'And do you indeed do that? And do you indeed do that? And do you indeed do that? There is no soul that is to exist until the Day of Resurrection except that it will exist.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: أَصَبْنَا سَبَايَا فَكُنَّا نَعْزِلُ
translation_issue.published_rendering: We took women captives, and we wanted to do 'azl with them
translation_issue.literal_meaning: We captured female captives, and we were practicing coitus interruptus (withdrawal during intercourse)
translation_issue.explanation: The translator alters the past continuous verb 'fa-kunnā naʿzilu' ('so we were practicing coitus interruptus') into mere intention ('we wanted to do') and leaves ''azl' untranslated to obscure that Muhammad's troops were already sexually using the female captives before asking him.

muslim:3546.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that concubinage in early Islam was a benign, marriage-like institution for integrating captives, or cite Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* to claim Muhammad's repeated questioning (*wa-innakum la-tafʿalūna*) discouraged coitus interruptus out of concern for the women. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *aṣabnā sabāyā fa-kunnā naʿzilu* ('we captured female captives, and we were practicing coitus interruptus'), and parallel Sahih accounts of this exact raid (bukhari:4138) admit the troops used withdrawal solely so they could sexually gratify themselves while still selling the women for ransom without impregnating them. Rather than condemning the immediate sexual use of newly seized prisoners of war, Muhammad permitted the intercourse and merely remarked that withdrawal cannot thwart predestined conception.

bukhari:2534.note: When a man pledged to free his slave after his own death (*mudabbar*), Muhammad summoned the slave and sold him, and the slave died that same year. Parallel reports clarify that because the owner had no other property and was in financial need, Muhammad overrode the manumission pledge and auctioned the slave for 800 dirhams (bukhari:2141, bukhari:2403).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَعْتَقَ رَجُلٌ مِنَّا عَبْدًا لَهُ عَنْ دُبُرٍ، فَدَعَا النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِهِ فَبَاعَهُ‏.‏ قَالَ جَابِرٌ مَاتَ الْغُلاَمُ عَامَ أَوَّلَ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: A man amongst us declared that his slave would be freed after his death. The Prophet (ﷺ) called for that slave and sold him. The slave died the same year

bukhari:2534.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam sought to phase out slavery by encouraging manumission, claiming (via Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and parallel narrations like bukhari:2141 and bukhari:2403) that Muhammad only intervened here because the master was impoverished and in debt with no other assets. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that after the master voluntarily pledged to free his slave upon death (aʿtaqa ... ʿabdan lahu ʿan duburin), Muhammad personally summoned the slave and auctioned him off as commercial property (fa-daʿā al-nabiyyu ... bihi fa-bāʿahu) to the highest bidder for 800 dirhams (bukhari:2141). Rather than relieving the master's poverty from communal funds to preserve the man's promised liberty, Muhammad revoked the emancipation and liquidated a human being as chattel—who then died within his first year of renewed bondage (māta al-ghulāmu ʿāma awwala).

bukhari:2141.note: After a man pledged to free his slave upon his death (*mudabbar*) and subsequently fell into financial need, Muhammad took the slave, asked who would buy him, and sold him to Nu'aim ibn 'Abdullah—an action classical commentators cite as legal proof that a *mudabbar* slave's post-mortem manumission pledge can be revoked through sale.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً أَعْتَقَ غُلاَمًا لَهُ عَنْ دُبُرٍ، فَاحْتَاجَ فَأَخَذَهُ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ مَنْ يَشْتَرِيهِ مِنِّي ‏"‏ فَاشْتَرَاهُ نُعَيْمُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بِكَذَا وَكَذَا، فَدَفَعَهُ إِلَيْهِ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: A man decided that a slave of his would be manumitted after his death and later on he was in need of money, so the Prophet (ﷺ) took the slave and said, "Who will buy this slave from me?" Nu'aim bin `Abdullah bought him for such and such price and the Prophet (ﷺ) gave him the slave

bukhari:2141.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam systematically promoted manumission and that, as discussed in Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī*, Muhammad either merely leased the slave's temporary labor (*manfa'ah*) or prioritized relieving the destitute owner's crushing debts. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that after the master pledged to free the boy upon his death (*a'taqa ghulāman lahu 'an duburin*), Muhammad personally seized the slave and auctioned his person on the spot, asking, "Who will buy him from me?" (*man yashtarīhi minnī*). Parallel Sahih narrations (`bukhari:2403`, `muslim:4338`) confirm that Muhammad revoked the emancipation entirely by selling him as permanent chattel for 800 dirhams—under which he died in bondage that very first year—explicitly ruling that a master's personal financial welfare supersedes a slave's freedom.

bukhari:6603.note: A man from the Ansar tells Muhammad that the companions acquire female war captives (*sabyan*) and, because they love property (*al-mal*)—seeking to preserve the women's sale or ransom value by avoiding pregnancy (cf. bukhari:2229, bukhari:4138)—asks about practicing coitus interruptus (*'azl*) with them. Treating sexual relations with female captives as lawful ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24)), Muhammad replies only that there is no harm in refraining from withdrawal because every soul Allah has ordained to exist will inevitably come into being.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: بَيْنَمَا هُوَ جَالِسٌ عِنْدَ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم جَاءَ رَجُلٌ مِنِ الأَنْصَارِ فَقَالَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إِنَّا نُصِيبُ سَبْيًا وَنُحِبُّ الْمَالَ، كَيْفَ تَرَى فِي الْعَزْلِ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ أَوَإِنَّكُمْ تَفْعَلُونَ ذَلِكَ، لاَ عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ لاَ تَفْعَلُوا، فَإِنَّهُ لَيْسَتْ نَسَمَةٌ كَتَبَ اللَّهُ أَنْ تَخْرُجَ إِلاَّ هِيَ كَائِنَةٌ
problematic_excerpt.english: while he was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ) a man from the Ansar came and said, "O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ)! We get slave girls from the war captives and we love property; what do you think about coitus interruptus?" Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, "Do you do that? It is better for you not to do it, for there is no soul which Allah has ordained to come into existence but will be created

bukhari:6603.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic concubinage functioned as a humane wartime welfare system requiring marriage-like protections, and that Muhammad discouraged coitus interruptus (*al-'azl*) to secure captive women the protected legal status of *umm al-walad* (mothers of children who cannot be sold). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the companions had sex with female war captives (*nuṣību sabyan*) while practicing withdrawal specifically because "we love wealth" (*wa-nuḥibbu al-māl*)—which parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:2229, bukhari:4138) and Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* confirm meant avoiding pregnancy so the women could still be sold as chattel or ransomed for profit. Far from requiring consent or forbidding the sexual commodification of newly captured women ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24)), Muhammad raised zero moral objection to using captives for sex before selling them, reducing the entire issue to fatalistic predestination (*qadar*).

bukhari:2403.note: When a man pledged to manumit his slave after his death (*'an dubur*), Muhammad intervened by asking who would buy the slave from him, sold the slave to Nu'aim bin 'Abdullah, and gave the purchase price to the owner. Parallel narrations (bukhari:2141, bukhari:2415) specify that the owner was in need and had no other property, prompting Muhammad to override the promised posthumous manumission to liquidate the slave for the master's financial relief.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَعْتَقَ رَجُلٌ غُلاَمًا لَهُ عَنْ دُبُرٍ فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ مَنْ يَشْتَرِيهِ مِنِّي ‏"‏‏.‏ فَاشْتَرَاهُ نُعَيْمُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ، فَأَخَذَ ثَمَنَهُ، فَدَفَعَهُ إِلَيْهِ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: A man pledged that his slave would be manumitted after his death. The Prophet (ﷺ) asked, "Who will buy the slave from me?" Nu'aim bin `Abdullah bought the slave and the Prophet (ﷺ) took its price and gave it to the owner

bukhari:2403.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam systematically worked to abolish slavery by encouraging manumission, citing Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and parallel narrations (`bukhari:2141`, `bukhari:2230`) to claim Muhammad only intervened here because the slave's owner was impoverished and in debt. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that after the owner pledged to free his slave upon death (*a'taqa rajulun ghulāman lahu 'an duburin*), Muhammad personally nullified that emancipation and auctioned the man off by calling out, "Who will buy him from me?" (*man yashtarīhi minnī*). Rather than settling the owner's modest debt through the public treasury or charity to preserve the slave's promised liberty, Muhammad prioritized a debtor's financial liquidity over human freedom by acting as a slave broker himself.

muslim:3544.note: During the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq, Muhammad's companions captured noble Arab women and intended to have sexual intercourse with them while practicing coitus interruptus (*'azl*) so they could still collect ransom for them. When consulted, Muhammad permitted the act and stated there was no harm in not practicing withdrawal, declaring that every soul decreed by Allah to be created until the Day of Resurrection will inevitably be born ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24), [Deuteronomy 21:10](bible://dt/21/10)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: غَزَوْنَا مَعَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم غَزْوَةَ بَلْمُصْطَلِقِ فَسَبَيْنَا كَرَائِمَ الْعَرَبِ فَطَالَتْ عَلَيْنَا الْعُزْبَةُ وَرَغِبْنَا فِي الْفِدَاءِ فَأَرَدْنَا أَنْ نَسْتَمْتِعَ وَنَعْزِلَ فَقُلْنَا نَفْعَلُ وَرَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم بَيْنَ أَظْهُرِنَا لاَ نَسْأَلُهُ ‏.‏ فَسَأَلْنَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ لاَ عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ لاَ تَفْعَلُوا مَا كَتَبَ اللَّهُ خَلْقَ نَسَمَةٍ هِيَ كَائِنَةٌ إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ إِلاَّ سَتَكُونُ ‏"
problematic_excerpt.english: We went out with Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) on the expedition to the Bi'l-Mustaliq and took captive some excellent Arab women; and we desired them, for we were suffering from the absence of our wives, (but at the same time) we also desired ransom for them. So we decided to have sexual intercourse with them but by observing 'azl (Withdrawing the male sexual organ before emission of semen to avoid-conception). But we said: We are doing an act whereas Allah's Messenger is amongst us; why not ask him? So we asked Allah's Mes- senger (ﷺ), and he said: It does not matter if you do not do it, for every soul that is to be born up to the Day of Resurrection will be born

muslim:3544.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that sexual relations with war captives required mutual consent or marriage and served to humanely integrate displaced women into households rather than exploit them. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the soldiers captured noble Arab women (*sabaynā karā'ima al-'arab*) and decided to 'enjoy them sexually and practice withdrawal' (*nastamti'a wa-na'zila*) specifically because they 'desired the ransom' (*raghibnā fī al-fidā'*)—treating the captives as temporary sexual commodities to be used before being sold back to their families. Furthermore, as Imām al-Nawawī confirms in *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, a captive slave woman's consent is never required for intercourse or withdrawal, and Muhammad directly endorsed their unrestricted sexual use by replying, 'It is no sin upon you if you do not withdraw' (*lā 'alaykum an lā taf'alū*).

bukhari:7409.note: During the expedition against Banu al-Mustaliq, Muslim fighters took female war captives and sought to have sexual relations with them without impregnating them. When asked about practicing coitus interruptus ('azl) with these captives, Muhammad raised no objection to the intercourse itself, advising only that withdrawal cannot prevent the creation of any soul Allah has decreed.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّهُمْ أَصَابُوا سَبَايَا فَأَرَادُوا أَنْ يَسْتَمْتِعُوا بِهِنَّ وَلاَ يَحْمِلْنَ فَسَأَلُوا النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم عَنِ الْعَزْلِ فَقَالَ ‏"‏ مَا عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ لاَ تَفْعَلُوا
problematic_excerpt.english: they (Muslims) captured some females and intended to have sexual relation with them without impregnating them. So they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about coitus interruptus. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "It is better that you should not do it

bukhari:7409.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic concubinage was a humane institution requiring mutual consent, and claim (citing Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and Al-Nawawī) that Muhammad discouraged coitus interruptus ('azl) so captive women would bear children and gain protected legal status as umm al-walad (mother of the master's child). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the soldiers sought strictly unilateral sexual gratification from freshly seized war captives—'to enjoy them without them becoming pregnant' (أَنْ يَسْتَمْتِعُوا بِهِنَّ وَلاَ يَحْمِلْنَ, an yastamti'ū bihinna wa-lā yaḥmilna)—without any mention or requirement of the women's consent. Furthermore, the parallel narration in bukhari:4138 reveals that the soldiers practiced 'azl specifically because they 'desired ransom' (أَحْبَبْنَا الْفِدَاءَ) and intended to sell the captives back for profit after using them sexually, a practice Muhammad implicitly endorsed by addressing only divine predestination rather than forbidding the abuse.

bukhari:2415.note: When a man with no other property manumitted his slave—described in fuller parallel reports (bukhari:2141, bukhari:2534) as a post-mortem emancipation (mudabbar) granted by an impoverished or indebted owner—Muhammad revoked the manumission and sold the slave to Nu'aim bin al-Nahham.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً، أَعْتَقَ عَبْدًا لَهُ، لَيْسَ لَهُ مَالٌ غَيْرُهُ، فَرَدَّهُ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم، فَابْتَاعَهُ مِنْهُ نُعَيْمُ بْنُ النَّحَّامِ
problematic_excerpt.english: A man manumitted a slave and he had no other property than that, so the Prophet (ﷺ) canceled the manumission (and sold the slave for him). Nu'aim bin Al-Nahham bought the slave from him

bukhari:2415.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam sought to phase out slavery at every opportunity, citing Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and parallel narrations (bukhari:2141, muslim:4338) to claim the destitute owner had merely pledged post-mortem emancipation (tadbīr), requiring his sole asset to be liquidated to support himself and his creditors. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the owner manumitted his slave (أَعْتَقَ عَبْدًا لَهُ) and the Prophet directly revoked the emancipation (فَرَدَّهُ النَّبِيُّ) so the man could be bought as chattel property (مَالٌ) by Nu'aim bin al-Nahham (فَابْتَاعَهُ مِنْهُ). Even across the parallel mudabbar accounts, Muhammad prioritized an owner's financial solvency over human liberty by personally auctioning the man on the spot for eight hundred dirhams rather than relieving the master's poverty from the public treasury (bayt al-māl) to preserve the slave's freedom.

bukhari:2592.note: After Maymuna bint al-Harith informs Muhammad that she emancipated her slave-girl without first seeking his permission, he tells her that she would have earned a greater reward had she given the slave-girl to her maternal uncles instead of freeing her.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّهَا، أَعْتَقَتْ وَلِيدَةً وَلَمْ تَسْتَأْذِنِ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم، فَلَمَّا كَانَ يَوْمُهَا الَّذِي يَدُورُ عَلَيْهَا فِيهِ قَالَتْ أَشَعَرْتَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أَنِّي أَعْتَقْتُ وَلِيدَتِي قَالَ ‏"‏ أَوَفَعَلْتِ ‏"‏‏.‏ قَالَتْ نَعَمْ‏.‏ قَالَ ‏"‏ أَمَا إِنَّكِ لَوْ أَعْطَيْتِيهَا أَخْوَالَكِ كَانَ أَعْظَمَ لأَجْرِكِ ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: she manumitted a slave-girl without taking the permission of the Prophet. On the day when it was her turn to be with the Prophet, she said, "Do you know, O Allah's Messenger (ﷺ), that I have manumitted my slave-girl?" He said, "Have you really?" She replied in the affirmative. He said, "You would have got more reward if you had given her (i.e. the slave-girl) to one of your maternal uncles

bukhari:2592.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam sought the gradual abolition of slavery by making emancipation the highest spiritual virtue, or cite Ibn Ḥajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* to claim Maymūnah's maternal uncles were in desperate financial need of a servant (*ṣilat al-raḥim*). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that transferring the slave-girl (*walīdah*) as chattel property to her relatives was spiritually superior to freeing her (*law aʿṭaytīhā akhwālaki kāna aʿẓama li-ajriki*—'had you given her to your maternal uncles, it would have been greater for your reward'). This directly collapses the modern abolitionist narrative by proving that Muhammad himself criticized an already-completed act of manumission (*iʿtāq*) and assigned higher divine reward to keeping a human being in lifelong servitude.

bukhari:4213.note: While returning from Khaybar, Muhammad stayed for three nights to consummate his union (*yubnā 'alayhi*) with the war captive Safiyya (taken after her husband was killed at Khaybar, bukhari:4211) and held a banquet. Even after the consummation, the Muslims debated whether she was one of his wives ('Mothers of the Believers') or a slave concubine ('what his right hand possesses,' *mā malakat yamīnuhu*), determining that she was a wife only when he extended the veil over her upon departure.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَقَامَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم بَيْنَ خَيْبَرَ وَالْمَدِينَةِ ثَلاَثَ لَيَالٍ يُبْنَى عَلَيْهِ بِصَفِيَّةَ، فَدَعَوْتُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ إِلَى وَلِيمَتِهِ، وَمَا كَانَ فِيهَا مِنْ خُبْزٍ وَلاَ لَحْمٍ، وَمَا كَانَ فِيهَا إِلاَّ أَنْ أَمَرَ بِلاَلاً بِالأَنْطَاعِ فَبُسِطَتْ، فَأَلْقَى عَلَيْهَا التَّمْرَ وَالأَقِطَ وَالسَّمْنَ، فَقَالَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ إِحْدَى أُمَّهَاتِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ، أَوْ مَا مَلَكَتْ يَمِينُهُ قَالُوا إِنْ حَجَبَهَا فَهْىَ إِحْدَى أُمَّهَاتِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ، وَإِنْ لَمْ يَحْجُبْهَا فَهْىَ مِمَّا مَلَكَتْ يَمِينُهُ‏.‏ فَلَمَّا ارْتَحَلَ وَطَّأَ لَهَا خَلْفَهُ، وَمَدَّ الْحِجَابَ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: The Prophet (ﷺ) stayed for three nights between Khaibar and Medina and was married to Safiya. I invited the Muslim to his marriage banquet and there waa neither meat nor bread in that banquet but the Prophet ordered Bilal to spread the leather mats on which dates, dried yogurt and butter were put. The Muslims said amongst themselves, "Will she (i.e. Safiya) be one of the mothers of the believers, (i.e. one of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) ) or just (a lady captive) of what his right-hand possesses" Some of them said, "If the Prophet (ﷺ) makes her observe the veil, then she will be one of the mothers of the believers (i.e. one of the Prophet's wives), and if he does not make her observe the veil, then she will be his lady slave." So when he departed, he made a place for her behind him (on his camel and made her observe the veil)

bukhari:4213.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad nobly emancipated Safiyya and married her as an honored 'Mother of the Believers' (citing Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī) to elevate her status after the Battle of Khaybar rather than keeping her in bondage. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that while Muhammad was consummating his union with her over three nights (ثَلاَثَ لَيَالٍ يُبْنَى عَلَيْهِ بِصَفِيَّةَ), his own companions casually debated whether she was a wife or merely a captive concubine ('what his right hand possesses,' مَا مَلَكَتْ يَمِينُهُ), a status they could only determine upon departure by whether he imposed the veil (إِنْ حَجَبَهَا). This exchange—alongside parallel narrations (bukhari:4211, bukhari:5085) recording that she was taken immediately after her husband and kinsmen were killed and that her release from slavery was simply counted as her 'dowry'—proves that sexually using newly seized war captives was completely routine for Muhammad and that female slaves were systematically denied the veil and protections of free women.

bukhari:6363.note: Returning from the conquest of Khaybar (AD 628), Muhammad brought Safiyya bint Huyayy after acquiring her as war booty (*qad ḥāzahā*) and consummated his marriage to her (*bināʾuhu bihā*) on the journey back to Medina at al-Sahba' after preparing a banquet of *ḥays* (with parallel reports such as bukhari:371 and bukhari:5085 noting that her manumission served as her dowry).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَلَمْ أَزَلْ أَخْدُمُهُ حَتَّى أَقْبَلْنَا مِنْ خَيْبَرَ، وَأَقْبَلَ بِصَفِيَّةَ بِنْتِ حُيَىٍّ قَدْ حَازَهَا، فَكُنْتُ أَرَاهُ يُحَوِّي وَرَاءَهُ بِعَبَاءَةٍ أَوْ كِسَاءٍ ثُمَّ يُرْدِفُهَا وَرَاءَهُ حَتَّى إِذَا كُنَّا بِالصَّهْبَاءِ صَنَعَ حَيْسًا فِي نِطَعٍ، ثُمَّ أَرْسَلَنِي فَدَعَوْتُ رِجَالاً فَأَكَلُوا، وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ بِنَاءَهُ بِهَا
problematic_excerpt.english: I kept on serving him till he returned from (the battle of) Khaibar. He then brought Safiya, the daughter of Huyay whom he had got (from the booty). I saw him making a kind of cushion with a cloak or a garment for her. He then let her ride behind him. When we reached a place called As-Sahba', he prepared (a special meal called) Hais, and asked me to invite the men who (came and) ate, and that was the marriage banquet given on the consummation of his marriage to her.

bukhari:6363.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad honored Safiyya bint Huyayy by emancipating her and marrying her with her consent as a free noblewoman rather than keeping her as a slave, citing Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī that her manumission graciously served as her bridal dowry (mahr). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad first seized her as his personal war booty (قَدْ حَازَهَا, qad ḥāzahā) and consummated the union (بِنَاءَهُ بِهَا, bināʾahu bihā) at al-Sahba' on the immediate return march from the AD 628 Battle of Khaybar in which her family and husband were killed. Furthermore, parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:371, bukhari:2235, bukhari:5085) confirm she was initially allotted as chattel to Dihya al-Kalbi before Muhammad claimed her in exchange for other captives, and that his own companions could not tell whether she was a wife or a slave concubine (أَمْ أُمُّ وَلَدٍ) until they saw whether he veiled her.

muslim:3550.note: When asked by Muhammad why they practice coitus interruptus (*'azl*), his companions state that a man has sexual intercourse with his nursing wife or with his female slave (*al-amah*) while disliking that she conceive from him (though the English translation adds an explanatory gloss about *umm walad* status absent from the Arabic text). Muhammad raises no objection to sexual intercourse with female slaves ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24), [Quran 23:5](quran://23/5)), stating only that there is no harm in refraining from withdrawal because conception is determined by predestination (*al-qadar*).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: ذُكِرَ الْعَزْلُ عِنْدَ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ ‏"‏ وَمَا ذَاكُمْ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالُوا الرَّجُلُ تَكُونُ لَهُ الْمَرْأَةُ تُرْضِعُ فَيُصِيبُ مِنْهَا وَيَكْرَهُ أَنْ تَحْمِلَ مِنْهُ وَالرَّجُلُ تَكُونُ لَهُ الأَمَةُ فَيُصِيبُ مِنْهَا وَيَكْرَهُ أَنْ تَحْمِلَ مِنْهُ ‏.‏ قَالَ ‏"‏ فَلاَ عَلَيْكُمْ أَنْ لاَ تَفْعَلُوا ذَاكُمْ فَإِنَّمَا هُوَ الْقَدَرُ ‏"
problematic_excerpt.english: mention was made of 'azl in the presence of Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) whereupon he said:Why do you practise it? They said: There is a man whose wife has to suckle the child, and if that person has a sexual intercourse with her (she may conceive) which he does not like, and there is another person who has a slave-girl and he has a sexual intercourse with her, but he does not like her to have conception so that she may not become Umm Walad, whereupon he (the Holy Prophet) said: There is no harm if you do not do that, for that (the birth of the child) is something pre- ordained.

muslim:3550.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic concubinage was a benevolent institution meant to integrate female captives into the family, claiming that Muhammad's discouragement of withdrawal (*'azl*) protected slave women by allowing them to conceive and gain elevated status as the mothers of their masters' children (*umm walad*). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that men routinely used their female slaves sexually (`تَكُونُ لَهُ الأَمَةُ فَيُصِيبُ مِنْهَا`) while actively seeking to prevent pregnancy (`وَيَكْرَهُ أَنْ تَحْمِلَ مِنْهُ`), and parallel narrations (`bukhari:4138`, `muslim:3546`) confirm the companions did this specifically so they could still sell or ransom the captive women for profit after using them sexually. Furthermore, as Al-Nawawī explains in *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, Islamic law requires a free wife's permission for *'azl* but grants a female slave (*al-amah*) zero consent over either sexual intercourse or withdrawal because she is her master's chattel, and Muhammad raised no moral objection to her sexual exploitation—merely remarking that conception is governed by predestination (`فَإِنَّمَا هُوَ الْقَدَرُ`).

muslim:3557.note: When a man informs Muhammad that he has a female slave (jariyah) with whom he practices coitus interruptus ('azl) and later reports that she conceived anyway, Muhammad raises no objection to the sexual use of the enslaved woman, stating only that withdrawal cannot prevent what Allah has decreed ([Quran 4:24](quran://4/24), [Quran 23:6](quran://23/6)). In the immediately preceding parallel report (muslim:3556), where the master specifies that the slave-girl is their domestic servant and water-carrier whom he has intercourse with but dislikes to impregnate, Muhammad explicitly permits him to practice 'azl if he wishes.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: سَأَلَ رَجُلٌ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَقَالَ إِنَّ عِنْدِي جَارِيَةً لِي وَأَنَا أَعْزِلُ عَنْهَا ‏.‏ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ إِنَّ ذَلِكَ لَنْ يَمْنَعَ شَيْئًا أَرَادَهُ اللَّهُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ فَجَاءَ الرَّجُلُ فَقَالَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ الَّتِي كُنْتُ ذَكَرْتُهَا لَكَ حَمَلَتْ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ أَنَا عَبْدُ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولُهُ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: a person asked Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) saying:I have a slave-girl and I practise 'azl with her, whereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: This cannot prevent that which Allah has decreed. The person then came (after some time) and said: Messenger of Allah, the slave-girl about whom I talked to you has conceived, whereupon Allah's Messeuger (ﷺ) said: I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger

muslim:3557.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islamic concubinage was a benevolent system of social integration and that this narration merely affirms divine decree (*qadar*) while elevating the pregnant bondwoman to the protected status of *umm al-walad* (mother of the master's child). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the man held her as personal chattel (`إِنَّ عِنْدِي جَارِيَةً لِي`, 'I have a slave-girl of mine') and practiced withdrawal (`أَعْزِلُ عَنْهَا`) to use her sexually while avoiding the financial loss of pregnancy—a motive confirmed in the immediately preceding narration (`muslim:3556`), where he admits exploiting her for both manual labor and sex while hating for her to conceive (`وَأَنَا أَطُوفُ عَلَيْهَا وَأَنَا أَكْرَهُ أَنْ تَحْمِلَ`). Furthermore, as Al-Nawawī explains in *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, Sunni jurists cite Muhammad's tacit approval (*taqrīr*) here to rule that unlike a free wife, a female slave has no right to consent regarding sexual relations or *'azl* because her master owns her person and labor.

muslim:229.note: Muhammad declares that any slave who runs away from his master forfeits the covenant of protection (*bari'at minhu al-dhimmah*), contrasting with the Biblical command to shelter escaped slaves ([Deuteronomy 23:15](bible://dt/23/15)). Even where commentators interpret this forfeiture as severe deterrence (*taghliz*) rather than literal apostasy, classical consensus affirms that a slave fleeing bondage (*ibaq*) is a major sin.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ جَرِيرٍ، قَالَ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ أَيُّمَا عَبْدٍ أَبَقَ فَقَدْ بَرِئَتْ مِنْهُ الذِّمَّةُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: It is narrated on the authority of Jarir that the Messenger of Allah (may peace and blessings be upon him) observed:The slave who fled from his master, responsibility with regard to him was absolved

muslim:229.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that, as explained in Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, this warning either applies only to a slave who defects to enemy polytheist territory (*dār al-ḥarb*) or functions as rhetorical hyperbole (*taghlīẓ*) to deter breaching a social contract. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states the unconditional universal rule *ayyumā 'abdin abaqa faqad bari'at minhu al-dhimmah* ('whichever slave flees, the covenant of protection is withdrawn from him'), containing no geographic or political restriction whatsoever. Furthermore, the immediate parallel narrations (muslim:228, muslim:230) confirm that merely running away from one's masters—even independently of defecting to polytheists—invalidates the slave's prayers (*lam tuqbal lahu ṣalātun*) and brands him with disbelief (*faqad kafara*) until he returns to bondage.

muslim:230.note: Muhammad declares via Jarir ibn Abdullah that when an enslaved person flees from his master, his prayer is not accepted (cf. muslim:228, muslim:229; contrast [Deuteronomy 23:15](bible://dt/23/15), [Galatians 3:28](bible://gal/3/28)). In *Sharh Sahih Muslim*, al-Nawawi explains that by scholarly consensus (*ijma'*), a slave's flight is a major sin and this ruling means the spiritual reward (*thawab*) of his prayers is voided until he returns to his master.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: كَانَ جَرِيرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ يُحَدِّثُ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ إِذَا أَبَقَ الْعَبْدُ لَمْ تُقْبَلْ لَهُ صَلاَةٌ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Jarir b. Abdullah reported it from the Holy Prophet:When the slave runs away from his master, his prayer is not accepted

muslim:230.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam sought to gradually abolish slavery and, citing Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, claim this warning either applies only to captives defecting to enemy territory or merely denotes a loss of extra reward (*thawāb*) rather than divine rejection. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states an unconditional condemnation of any runaway slave (*idhā abaqa al-ʿabdu lam tuqbal lahu ṣalātun*), while the adjacent narration (muslim:228) declares that a fleeing slave commits disbelief until he returns to his masters (*faqad kafara ḥattā yarjiʿa ilayhim*). Even in Al-Nawawī's own commentary, Sunni scholarly consensus classifies escaping human bondage as a major sin (*kabīrah*) that strips the enslaved person of all spiritual reward for prayer until they submit back to their owner.

bukhari:97.note: Muhammad declares a double reward for an enslaved person who fulfills his duties to both Allah and his masters, and for a man who has sexual intercourse with his female slave (*yaṭaʾuhā*), disciplines and educates her well, and subsequently manumits and marries her ([Quran 4:3](quran://4/3), [Quran 23:6](quran://23/6)). Although the standard English translation omits *yaṭaʾuhā* (preserved in al-Kashmihani's recension), classical commentators like Ibn Hajar in *Fath al-Bari* confirm that it denotes the master having sexual relations with his bondwoman by right of ownership prior to freeing and marrying her (bukhari:2547, bukhari:5083).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: ثَلاَثَةٌ لَهُمْ أَجْرَانِ رَجُلٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ آمَنَ بِنَبِيِّهِ، وَآمَنَ بِمُحَمَّدٍ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَالْعَبْدُ الْمَمْلُوكُ إِذَا أَدَّى حَقَّ اللَّهِ وَحَقَّ مَوَالِيهِ، وَرَجُلٌ كَانَتْ عِنْدَهُ أَمَةٌ ‏{‏يَطَؤُهَا‏}‏ فَأَدَّبَهَا، فَأَحْسَنَ تَأْدِيبَهَا، وَعَلَّمَهَا فَأَحْسَنَ تَعْلِيمَهَا، ثُمَّ أَعْتَقَهَا فَتَزَوَّجَهَا، فَلَهُ أَجْرَانِ
problematic_excerpt.english: Three persons will have a double reward: 1. A Person from the people of the scriptures who believed in his prophet (Jesus or Moses) and then believed in the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) (i.e. has embraced Islam). 2. A slave who discharges his duties to Allah and his master. 3. A master of a woman-slave who teaches her good manners and educates her in the best possible way (the religion) and manumits her and then marries her

bukhari:97.literal_translation: Three persons will have a double reward: a man from the People of the Scripture who believed in his prophet and believed in Muhammad (ﷺ); an owned slave when he fulfills the right of Allah and the right of his masters; and a man who had a female slave with whom he has sexual intercourse (yaṭaʾuhā), and he disciplined her and excelled in her discipline, and taught her and excelled in her teaching, then manumitted her and married her—he will have a double reward.

translation_issue.arabic_term: يَطَؤُهَا
translation_issue.published_rendering: [omitted]
translation_issue.literal_meaning: with whom he has sexual intercourse
translation_issue.explanation: The translator completely omits the Arabic verb 'yaṭaʾuhā' (from waṭiʾa, 'to tread upon' / idiomatically 'to have sexual intercourse with'), which is attested in the majority of Bukhari's manuscript recensions (as noted by Ibn Hajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī) and printed in the accompanying Arabic text, thereby concealing that the master was using the enslaved woman as a sexual concubine prior to freeing and marrying her.

bukhari:97.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this Hadith demonstrates Islam's humanitarian reform of slavery by encouraging masters to educate, emancipate, and elevate enslaved women to the honorable status of legal wives. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the master already uses the enslaved woman for sexual intercourse (يَطَؤُهَا, yaṭaʾuhā—a clause deliberately omitted from the standard English translation) by right of ownership ([Quran 23:6](quran://23/6)) prior to any emancipation or marriage. Furthermore, as Ibn Hajar confirms in Fatḥ al-Bārī, freeing and marrying a concubine remains strictly optional rather than mandatory, while the Hadith simultaneously reinforces chattel bondage by tying an enslaved person's salvation to obeying their earthly masters (حَقَّ مَوَالِيهِ).

muslim:4113.note: When a slave pledged allegiance to Muhammad for migration without his knowledge and the man's master came to demand him back, Muhammad asked the master to sell the man to him, bought him in exchange for two black slaves, and thereafter did not accept anyone's pledge until he asked whether he was a slave.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: جَاءَ عَبْدٌ فَبَايَعَ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم عَلَى الْهِجْرَةِ وَلَمْ يَشْعُرْ أَنَّهُ عَبْدٌ فَجَاءَ سَيِّدُهُ يُرِيدُهُ فَقَالَ لَهُ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ بِعْنِيهِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَاشْتَرَاهُ بِعَبْدَيْنِ أَسْوَدَيْنِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يُبَايِعْ أَحَدًا بَعْدُ حَتَّى يَسْأَلَهُ ‏"‏ أَعَبْدٌ هُوَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: There came a slave and pledg- ed allegiance to Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) on migration; he (the Holy Prophet) did not know that he was a slave. Then there came his master and demanded him back, whereupon Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) said: Sell him to me. And he bought him for two black slaves, and he did not afterwards take allegiance from anyone until he had asked him whether he was a slave (or a free man)

muslim:4113.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad worked to abolish slavery and intervened here to rescue the migrating slave from his master. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad bought him in exchange for two black slaves (fa-shtarāhu bi-ʿabdayni aswadayni), trading two enslaved people into the master's ownership to acquire one man. Furthermore, rather than invalidating the master's property claim, Muhammad thereafter refused to accept a pledge of allegiance from anyone until he first asked whether he was a slave (a-ʿabdun huwa).

bukhari:2154.note: When asked about an unmarried female slave who commits fornication, Muhammad instructed that she be flogged for the first two offenses and sold upon the third (or fourth) offense, even for the price of a braided rope.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم سُئِلَ عَنِ الأَمَةِ إِذَا زَنَتْ وَلَمْ تُحْصِنْ قَالَ ‏ "‏ إِنْ زَنَتْ فَاجْلِدُوهَا، ثُمَّ إِنْ زَنَتْ فَاجْلِدُوهَا، ثُمَّ إِنْ زَنَتْ فَبِيعُوهَا وَلَوْ بِضَفِيرٍ
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) was asked about the slave-girl, if she was a virgin and committed illegal sexual intercourse. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "If she committed illegal sexual intercourse, lash her, and if she did it a second time, then lash her again, and if she repeated the third time, then sell her even for a hair rope."

bukhari:2154.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Islam showed mercy to enslaved women by halving their prescribed punishment compared to free women (Quran 4:25), and that selling her after repeated offenses was a compassionate measure to place her in a better environment. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly commands her owner to repeatedly flog her (فَاجْلِدُوهَا) and then liquidate her as degraded chattel (فَبِيعُوهَا وَلَوْ بِضَفِيرٍ—'sell her even for a braided hair rope'). Rather than emancipating a vulnerable woman, this ruling empowers slaveholders to inflict corporal punishment and discard her onto the market for a pittance, transferring her to a new buyer who immediately acquires legal sexual access to her.

muslim:4335.note: Imran ibn Husayn reported that when a dying man who owned no other property emancipated his six slaves, Muhammad summoned them, divided them into three sections, cast lots among them to free two while keeping four in slavery, and spoke severely of the owner.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً، أَعْتَقَ سِتَّةَ مَمْلُوكِينَ لَهُ عِنْدَ مَوْتِهِ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ مَالٌ غَيْرُهُمْ فَدَعَا بِهِمْ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَجَزَّأَهُمْ أَثْلاَثًا ثُمَّ أَقْرَعَ بَيْنَهُمْ فَأَعْتَقَ اثْنَيْنِ وَأَرَقَّ أَرْبَعَةً وَقَالَ لَهُ قَوْلاً شَدِيدًا ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Imran b. Husain reported that a person who had no other property emancipated six slaves of his at the time of his death.
