problematic_excerpt.arabic: أُتِيتُ بِالْبُرَاقِ - وَهُوَ دَابَّةٌ أَبْيَضُ طَوِيلٌ فَوْقَ الْحِمَارِ وَدُونَ الْبَغْلِ يَضَعُ حَافِرَهُ عِنْدَ مُنْتَهَى طَرْفِهِ - قَالَ فَرَكِبْتُهُ حَتَّى أَتَيْتُ بَيْتَ الْمَقْدِسِ - قَالَ - فَرَبَطْتُهُ بِالْحَلْقَةِ الَّتِي يَرْبِطُ بِهِ الأَنْبِيَاءُ - قَالَ - ثُمَّ دَخَلْتُ الْمَسْجِدَ فَصَلَّيْتُ فِيهِ رَكْعَتَيْنِ
problematic_excerpt.english: I was brought al-Buraq Who is an animal white and long, larger than a donkey but smaller than a mule, who would place his hoof a distance equal to the range of version. I mounted it and came to the Temple (Bait Maqdis in Jerusalem), then tethered it to the ring used by the prophets. I entered the mosque and prayed two rak'ahs in it

muslim:411.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the Arabic word *masjid* merely denotes an open 'place of prostration' referring to the bare Temple Mount esplanade rather than an actual building, or claim that the Night Journey (*Isrāʾ*) was a purely spiritual vision. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad physically tethered his beast to an exterior ring (`فَرَبَطْتُهُ بِالْحَلْقَةِ`), 'entered the mosque' (`ثُمَّ دَخَلْتُ الْمَسْجِدَ`), and 'then came out' (`ثُمَّ خَرَجْتُ`), while parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:3886, muslim:415) show the Quraysh demanding he describe the Temple's physical architecture and doors (`صِفْ لَنَا بَيْتَ الْمَقْدِسِ`)—proving the narrative anachronistically assumes a standing structure on a site destroyed in AD 70.

muslim:454.note: Echoing [Quran 9:30](quran://9/30), Muhammad states that when the Jews and Christians are summoned on the Day of Resurrection, the Jews will collectively declare, 'We used to worship Uzair (Ezra), the son of Allah,' and both groups will be told they lied because 'Allah never took a female spouse (*ṣāḥibah*) or a son.' Because this profession is attributed to the Jewish nation as a whole on Judgment Day rather than a localized sect, it directly conflicts with historical Jewish monotheism ([Deuteronomy 6:4](bible://dt/6/4)) and Christian doctrine regarding the Virgin Birth ([Luke 1:34-35](bible://lk/1/34-35)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَيُدْعَى الْيَهُودُ فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ قَالُوا كُنَّا نَعْبُدُ عُزَيْرَ ابْنَ اللَّهِ ‏.‏ فَيُقَالُ كَذَبْتُمْ مَا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ مِنْ صَاحِبَةٍ وَلاَ وَلَدٍ فَمَاذَا تَبْغُونَ قَالُوا عَطِشْنَا يَا رَبَّنَا فَاسْقِنَا ‏.‏ فَيُشَارُ إِلَيْهِمْ أَلاَ تَرِدُونَ فَيُحْشَرُونَ إِلَى النَّارِ كَأَنَّهَا سَرَابٌ يَحْطِمُ بَعْضُهَا بَعْضًا فَيَتَسَاقَطُونَ فِي النَّارِ ‏.‏ ثُمَّ يُدْعَى النَّصَارَى فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ قَالُوا كُنَّا نَعْبُدُ الْمَسِيحَ ابْنَ اللَّهِ ‏.‏ فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ كَذَبْتُمْ ‏.‏ مَا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ مِنْ صَاحِبَةٍ وَلاَ وَلَدٍ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Then the Jews would be summoned, and it would be said to them: What did you worship? They will say: We worshipped 'Uzair, son of Allah. It would be said to them: You tell a lie; Allah had never had a spouse or a son. What do you want now? They would say: We feel thirsty, O our Lord! Quench our thirst. They would be directed (to a certain direction) and asked: Why don't you go there to drink water? Then they would be pushed towards the Fire (and they would find to their great dismay that) it was but a mirage (and the raging flames of fire) would be consuming one another, and they would fall into the Fire. Then the Christians would be summoned and it would be said to them: What did you worship? They would say: We worshipped Jesus, son of Allah. It would be said to them: You tell a lie; Allah did not take for Himself either a spouse or a son.

muslim:454.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue, citing Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr on Quran 9:30, that the charge of worshipping ʿUzayr (Ezra) as the 'son of Allah' only applied to a small, extinct sect of Arabian Jews in Medina, and that denying a 'spouse' (*ṣāḥibah*) is merely a general rhetorical negation of physical procreation. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly indicts the entire Jewish nation on Judgment Day—stating unconditionally that 'the Jews (*al-Yahūd*) will be summoned' and will collectively confess, 'We used to worship ʿUzayr, the son of Allah (*kunnā naʿbudu ʿUzayra bna Allāh*),' parallel to the collective Christians (*al-Naṣārā*). Moreover, by answering both communities with the identical rebuttal that 'Allah never took a female consort (*ṣāḥibah*) or a son,' the Hadith directly attributes Ezra-worship to normative Judaism and physical consort-begetting to normative Christianity, contradicting all historical and textual evidence.

muslim:454.note: Muhammad states that on the Day of Resurrection Allah will come to the believers in a form (*ṣūrah*) other than the one in which they first saw Him—prompting them to seek refuge from Him two or three times—until a shin is uncovered (*yukshafu ʿan sāqin*, [Quran 68:42](quran://68/42)) as a recognition sign and He transforms (*taḥawwala*) into the form in which they saw Him the first time (cf. [John 4:24](bible://jn/4/24)). Although the English translation renders the initial appearance as 'in a form recognisable to them' and the uncovering of the shin as 'the things would be laid bare,' the Arabic text explicitly states that Allah comes in a lower form (*adnā ṣūrah*), uncovers a shin, and transforms back into His initial form (cf. bukhari:7439).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَتَاهُمْ رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى فِي أَدْنَى صُورَةٍ مِنَ الَّتِي رَأَوْهُ فِيهَا ‏.‏ قَالَ فَمَا تَنْتَظِرُونَ تَتْبَعُ كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ مَا كَانَتْ تَعْبُدُ ‏.‏ قَالُوا يَا رَبَّنَا فَارَقْنَا النَّاسَ فِي الدُّنْيَا أَفْقَرَ مَا كُنَّا إِلَيْهِمْ وَلَمْ نُصَاحِبْهُمْ ‏.‏ فَيَقُولُ أَنَا رَبُّكُمْ ‏.‏ فَيَقُولُونَ نَعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنْكَ لاَ نُشْرِكُ بِاللَّهِ شَيْئًا - مَرَّتَيْنِ أَوْ ثَلاَثًا - حَتَّى إِنَّ بَعْضَهُمْ لَيَكَادُ أَنْ يَنْقَلِبَ ‏.‏ فَيَقُولُ هَلْ بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَهُ آيَةٌ فَتَعْرِفُونَهُ بِهَا فَيَقُولُونَ نَعَمْ ‏.‏ فَيُكْشَفُ عَنْ سَاقٍ فَلاَ يَبْقَى مَنْ كَانَ يَسْجُدُ لِلَّهِ مِنْ تِلْقَاءِ نَفْسِهِ إِلاَّ أَذِنَ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِالسُّجُودِ وَلاَ يَبْقَى مَنْ كَانَ يَسْجُدُ اتِّقَاءً وَرِيَاءً إِلاَّ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ ظَهْرَهُ طَبَقَةً وَاحِدَةً كُلَّمَا أَرَادَ أَنْ يَسْجُدَ خَرَّ عَلَى قَفَاهُ ‏.‏ ثُمَّ يَرْفَعُونَ رُءُوسَهُمْ وَقَدْ تَحَوَّلَ فِي صُورَتِهِ الَّتِي رَأَوْهُ فِيهَا أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ فَقَالَ أَنَا رَبُّكُمْ ‏.‏ فَيَقُولُونَ أَنْتَ رَبُّنَا ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: The Lord of the Universe, Glorified and Exalted, would come to them in a form recognisable to them and say; What are you looking for? Every people follow that which they worshipped. They would say: Our Lord, we kept ourselves separate from the people in the world, though we felt great need of them; we, however, did not associate ourselves with them. He would say: I am your Lord. They would say: We take refuge with Allah from thee and do not associate anything with Allah. They would repeat it twice or thrice, till some of them would be about to return. It would be said: Is there any sign between you and Him by which you will recognise Him? They would say: Yes. and the things would be laid bare. Those who used to prostrate themselves before God of their own accord would be permitted by God to prostrate themselves. But there would remain none who used to prostrate out of fear (of people) and ostentation but Allah would make his back as one piece, and whenever he would attempt to prostrate he would fall on his back. Then they would raise their heads and He would assume the Form in which they had seen Him the first time and would say: I am your Lord. They would say: Thou art our Lord.

muslim:454.literal_translation: The Lord of the Worlds, Glorified and Exalted, will come to them in a lower form than the one in which they had seen Him, and say: 'What are you waiting for? Every nation follows what it used to worship.' They will say: 'O our Lord, we separated ourselves from the people in the world when we were most in need of them, and we did not keep their company.' He will say: 'I am your Lord.' They will say: 'We take refuge with Allah from you; we do not associate anything with Allah'—twice or three times—until some of them are about to turn back. He will say: 'Is there any sign between you and Him by which you will recognize Him?' They will say: 'Yes.' Then a shin will be uncovered, and there will remain no one who used to prostrate to Allah of his own accord but that Allah will permit him to prostrate, and there will remain no one who used to prostrate out of fear and ostentation but that Allah will make his back a single rigid plate; whenever he tries to prostrate, he will fall on the back of his neck. Then they will raise their heads, and He will have transformed into His form in which they saw Him the first time, and He will say: 'I am your Lord.' They will say: 'You are our Lord.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: فَيُكْشَفُ عَنْ سَاقٍ
translation_issue.published_rendering: and the things would be laid bare.
translation_issue.literal_meaning: Then a shin [of Allah] will be uncovered/bared.
translation_issue.explanation: While 'kashf ʿan sāq' can function elsewhere as an idiom for a severe affair being laid bare, here it is explicitly presented as the visual recognition sign ('āyah') by which believers identify their Lord (explicitly 'fa-yakshifu ʿan sāqihi'—'so He uncovers His shin'—in the parallel narration of the same chain in Bukhari 4919 and 7439). The translator renders it abstractly as 'and the things would be laid bare,' turns 'fa-yaqūlu' ('He says') into the passive 'It would be said,' and alters 'fī adnā ṣūratin min allatī raʾawhu fīhā' ('in a lower form than the one in which they had seen Him') to 'in a form recognisable to them' to obscure Allah changing forms and baring His shin.

muslim:454.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* and Ibn Ḥajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī*—that 'uncovering a shin' (*yukshafu ʿan sāqin*) is merely a classical Arabic idiom for severe terror (*shiddat al-amr*), and that the unrecognized 'form' (*ṣūrah*) belongs to a created angel rather than Allah Himself. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that 'the Lord of the Worlds (*Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn*) will come to them in a lower form (*fī adnā ṣūratin*)' and later 'transformed into His form (*taḥawwala fī ṣūratihi*) in which they saw Him the first time.' Furthermore, parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:4919, 7439) explicitly use the personal possessive pronoun *yakshifu ʿan sāqihi* ('He uncovers His shin') as the physical sign (*āyah*) by which believers visually recognize their Lord, refuting any metaphorical deflection.

muslim:454.subcategory: Divine Immanence, Entering Creation & Visible Form (Incarnation Precedents)
muslim:454.note: Muhammad states that on the Day of Resurrection the Lord of the Worlds will come to the believers in a visible form (*ṣūrah*), uncover His shin (*yukshafu ʿan sāqin*) as an identifying sign ([Quran 68:42](quran://68/42), [Ibn Kathir 68:42](ibnkathir://68/42)), and transform (*taḥawwala*) into the form in which they first saw Him (cf. bukhari:806, bukhari:7439). Despite later Ash'ari metaphorical reinterpretations (*taʾwīl*), the primary Arabic text explicitly affirms that God can manifest to humanity in a visible, recognizable form ([John 1:14](bible://jn/1/14), [Colossians 1:15](bible://col/1/15)).

muslim:454.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Allah's appearance on the Day of Resurrection occurs 'without modality' (*bilā kayf*) or merely reflects a change in human perception in the Hereafter, which they claim is categorically different from God assuming a visible nature in the Christian Incarnation. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that 'the Lord of the Worlds (*Rabb al-ʿĀlamīn*) will come to them in a lower form (*fī adnā ṣūratin*)' and subsequently 'transformed into His form (*taḥawwala fī ṣūratihi*) in which they saw Him the first time,' while parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:7439, muslim:451) affirm He comes 'in a form other than His form (*fī ṣūratin ghayri ṣūratihi*).' By conceding that Allah can assume, alter, and manifest Himself in distinct visible forms (*ṣuwar*) to converse with creation without compromising His deity, Sunni orthodoxy collapses its own philosophical objection against the Incarnation.

bukhari:7439.note: Muhammad states that on the Day of Resurrection, "the Jews" (*al-Yahūd*) collectively will confess to having worshipped Ezra (*'Uzayr*) as the son of Allah, paralleling the Christians' confession of worshipping the Messiah ([Quran 9:30](quran://9/30)). Neither Jewish scripture nor historical records contain any evidence of Jews worshipping Ezra as the Son of God.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَيُقَالُ لِلْيَهُودِ مَا كُنْتُمْ تَعْبُدُونَ قَالُوا كُنَّا نَعْبُدُ عُزَيْرَ ابْنَ اللَّهِ
problematic_excerpt.english: Then it will be said to the Jews, "What did you use to worship?' They will reply, 'We used to worship Ezra, the son of Allah.'

bukhari:7439.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the charge of worshipping Ezra ('Uzayr) in Quran 9:30 only applied to a small, extinct heretical sect of Medinan Jews rather than mainstream Judaism. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the collective nation of the Jews (lil-Yahūd) on the Day of Judgment confesses literal worship of Ezra as the ontological Son of God (kunnā na'budu 'Uzayra ibna Allāh), prompting the rebuttal that Allah has neither a consort nor a son (ṣāḥibatun wa-lā walad). Furthermore, there is zero historical, rabbinic, or archaeological evidence prior to or during the 7th century AD that any Jewish sect ever worshipped Ezra or regarded him as the divine Son of God.

bukhari:7439.category: Christian Doctrines Muslims Attack That Are Conceded in Hadith
bukhari:7439.subcategory: Divine Immanence, Entering Creation & Visible Form (Incarnation Precedents)
bukhari:7439.note: Muhammad states that the Almighty (*al-Jabbār*) will come to the believers on the Day of Resurrection and uncover His shin (*sāq*) as the visible sign (*āyah*) by which they recognize Him ([Quran 68:42](quran://68/42), [Ibn Kathir 68:42](ibnkathir://68/42); cf. [John 1:14](bible://jn/1/14), [Colossians 1:15](bible://col/1/15)). While the English translation interpolates the clause about Allah appearing in an unfamiliar form (*ṣūrah*) from parallel narrations (bukhari:806, bukhari:6573), the Arabic text of this report directly affirms that Allah manifests visibly to creation and is identified by uncovering His shin.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَيَقُولُ هَلْ بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَهُ آيَةٌ تَعْرِفُونَهُ فَيَقُولُونَ السَّاقُ‏.‏ فَيَكْشِفُ عَنْ سَاقِهِ
problematic_excerpt.english: and then it will be said to them, 'Do you know any sign by which you can recognize Him?' They will say. 'The Shin,' and so Allah will then uncover His Shin

bukhari:7439.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue, citing Ash'ari commentaries in Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and al-Nawawī's Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, that 'uncovering the shin' is merely an Arabic idiom for severe calamity and that the visible form (ṣūrah) is a created manifestation rather than Allah Himself. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Allah uncovers His own Shin (fa-yakshifu 'an sāqihi) as a visible, recognizable sign (āyatun ta'rifūnahu), while parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:6573, muslim:451) confirm that Allah Himself appears in an unfamiliar form (ṣūrah) declaring 'I am your Lord' (anā Rabbukum) before transforming into the form they recognize. If Allah can assume distinct, visible forms to reveal Himself to humanity without ceasing to be God, Muslim philosophical objections against the Christian Incarnation collapse into a double standard.

bukhari:3636.note: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud reports that during Muhammad's lifetime the moon split into two parts (`شِقَّتَيْنِ`), upon which Muhammad commanded his companions to bear witness ([Quran 54:1](quran://54/1)). This eyewitness account establishes the splitting of the moon as a literal physical event during Muhammad's ministry rather than a future eschatological sign, and alongside `bukhari:3637`—which states it was shown in response to Meccan demands—contrasts with the Quran's statements that no sensory miracles were sent to the Meccans ([Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), [Quran 29:50-51](quran://29/50-51)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: انْشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم شِقَّتَيْنِ فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ اشْهَدُوا ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: During the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ) the moon was split into two parts and on that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Bear witness (to this)

bukhari:3636.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the splitting of the moon in Quran 54:1 either refers to a future eschatological sign on the Day of Judgment, or—citing Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and modern claims about NASA's *Rima Ariadaeus* lunar trench—that it was a brief physical miracle missed by the rest of the world due to time zones and sleep. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the moon split into two physical halves during Muhammad's own lifetime (`انْشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ... شِقَّتَيْنِ`) as an eyewitness sign (`اشْهَدُوا`), and parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:4864) specify that one half was seen above the mountain and the other below it (`فِرْقَةٌ فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ وَفِرْقَةٌ دُونَهُ`), completely ruling out any future-tense metaphor or lunar eclipse. Furthermore, NASA scientists have explicitly debunked the *Rima Ariadaeus* myth as a routine 300-km tectonic fault line rather than a bisected sphere, and not a single 7th-century AD astronomer in Byzantium, Persia, India, or China—who shared the exact same night sky—ever recorded the moon breaking in two.

bukhari:3637.note: Anas ibn Malik reports that when the people of Mecca asked Muhammad to show them a sign, he showed them the splitting of the moon ([Quran 54:1](quran://54/1)). This anchors the event as a literal past celestial miracle in Mecca rather than a future Day of Judgment sign, despite the absence of corroborating historical or astronomical records and Quranic verses stating that Allah declined to send physical signs on demand ([Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), [Quran 29:50-51](quran://29/50-51)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ أَهْلَ مَكَّةَ سَأَلُوا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم أَنْ يُرِيَهُمْ آيَةً، فَأَرَاهُمُ انْشِقَاقَ الْقَمَرِ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: That the Meccan people requested Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) to show them a miracle, and so he showed them the splitting of the moon

bukhari:3637.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the splitting of the moon in Quran 54:1 refers merely to a future eschatological sign on the Day of Judgment, or cite Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* to claim that 7th-century AD civilizations failed to record this cosmic event due to cloud cover or differing time zones. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *fa-arāhum inshiqāq al-qamar* (فَأَرَاهُمُ انْشِقَاقَ الْقَمَرِ — 'so he showed them the splitting of the moon') as a completed historical sign granted to the Meccans, with parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:3636, 3868) specifying that the moon physically parted into two distinct pieces (*firqatayn*) on either side of Mount Hira. This locks Sunni orthodoxy into defending an objective astronomical cataclysm that left zero geological trace on the lunar surface or historical record among contemporary observers across the hemisphere, while directly contradicting the Quran's own admission (Quran 17:59) that Allah refused to send sensory miracles (*āyāt*) to the Meccans.

bukhari:3868.note: Anas bin Malik reports that when the people of Mecca asked Muhammad for a sign, he showed them the moon split into two halves until they saw Mount Hira between them ([Quran 54:1](quran://54/1)). Classical commentators affirm by consensus that this was a literal, physical division of the moon during Muhammad's lifetime, despite the absence of contemporary astronomical records and Quranic passages stating that Allah declined Meccan demands for physical miracles ([Quran 13:7](quran://13/7), [Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), [Quran 29:50-51](quran://29/50-51)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ أَهْلَ، مَكَّةَ سَأَلُوا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم أَنْ يُرِيَهُمْ آيَةً، فَأَرَاهُمُ الْقَمَرَ شِقَّتَيْنِ، حَتَّى رَأَوْا حِرَاءً بَيْنَهُمَا‏
problematic_excerpt.english: The people of Mecca asked Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) to show them a miracle. So he showed them the moon split in two halves between which they saw the Hira' mountain

bukhari:3868.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Quran 54:1 refers only to a future eschatological sign on the Day of Judgment, or—citing Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* to explain the total absence of 7th-century AD astronomical records—claim the split was a brief, localized nighttime event missed by the rest of the world due to sleep or time zones. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad showed the Meccans an immediate, physical sign (*āyah*) on demand by splitting the moon into two distinct halves (*shiqqatayn*) so far apart that eyewitnesses saw Mount Hira directly between them (*ḥattā ra'aw ḥirā'an baynahumā*), with `bukhari:3636` specifying that one piece stood above the mountain and the other beyond it. Such a massive physical bifurcation of a celestial body would have been visible across the entire lunar hemisphere and left permanent planetary scarring, collapsing both the future-prophecy deflection and Ibn Hajar's excuse for why not a single 7th-century AD astronomer in China, Byzantium, or Persia ever recorded it.

bukhari:3869.note: ʿAbd Allāh (ibn Masʿūd) reports that the moon split while they were with Muhammad in Mina (or Mecca in an appended transmission), with one piece moving toward the mountain as Muhammad commanded them to bear witness (cf. [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1); contrast [Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), [Quran 29:50-51](quran://29/50-51)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: انْشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ وَنَحْنُ مَعَ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِمِنًى فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ اشْهَدُوا ‏"‏‏.‏ وَذَهَبَتْ فِرْقَةٌ نَحْوَ الْجَبَلِ
problematic_excerpt.english: The moon was split ( into two pieces ) while we were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in Mina. He said, "Be witnesses." Then a Piece of the moon went towards the mountain

bukhari:3869.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the splitting of the moon in Quran 54:1 was either a future eschatological sign or a brief miracle unseen by 7th-century AD global astronomers due to time zones and cloud cover (as Ibn Hajar argues in *Fatḥ al-Bārī*), while modern polemicists cite lunar fault lines like Rima Ariadaeus as physical proof. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the moon physically split during Muhammad's lifetime at Mina (`انْشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ وَنَحْنُ مَعَ النَّبِيِّ... بِمِنًى`) and that one severed piece traveled toward the local mountain (`وَذَهَبَتْ فِرْقَةٌ نَحْوَ الْجَبَلِ`), with parallel narrations (`bukhari:3636`, `bukhari:4864`) describing one half positioned above the mountain and the other below it (`فِرْقَةٌ فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ وَفِرْقَةٌ دُونَهُ`). This eyewitness command (`اشْهَدُوا`, 'Be witnesses') refutes any future-tense reinterpretation and exposes a 7th-century AD cosmology that treats the moon as a small, local object maneuvering around Meccan hills rather than a massive celestial body visible across an entire hemisphere.

bukhari:3870.note: Ibn Abbas states that the moon split during the lifetime of Muhammad. Surrounding reports (bukhari:3868, bukhari:3869) specify that it divided into two pieces seen around Mount Hira, anchoring [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1) as a literal event during Muhammad's mission rather than solely a future eschatological sign.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ الْقَمَرَ، انْشَقَّ عَلَى زَمَانِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم‏
problematic_excerpt.english: During the lifetime of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) the moon was split (into two pieces)

bukhari:3870.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the splitting of the moon in Quran 54:1 uses the Arabic past tense prophetically to describe a future Day of Judgment event, or claim—following Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī—that it was a literal miracle missed by the rest of the world due to night-sky time zones and cloud cover. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states أَنَّ الْقَمَرَ انْشَقَّ عَلَى زَمَانِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ('that the moon was split during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah'), and parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:3638, bukhari:4867) specify that it physically parted into two distinct halves (فِرْقَتَيْنِ) around Mount Hira, completely ruling out a future eschatological metaphor. Because the moon is simultaneously visible across an entire hemisphere for hours, a literal lunar bisection in 7th-century AD Arabia could not have gone completely unrecorded by the meticulous astronomers of the contemporary Byzantine, Persian, Indian, and Chinese empires.

bukhari:4864.note: Recorded in the Book of Prophetic Commentary (*Tafsir*) on [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1), Ibn Masud reports that during Muhammad's lifetime the moon split into two parts—one part above the mountain and the other before it—whereupon Muhammad commanded, "Bear witness." This report anchors [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1) as a literal event during Muhammad's ministry rather than solely a future eschatological sign, contrasting with Quranic declarations that Allah refrained from sending physical miracles to the Meccans ([Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), [Quran 29:50-51](quran://29/50-51)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: انْشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فِرْقَتَيْنِ، فِرْقَةً فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ وَفِرْقَةً دُونَهُ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ اشْهَدُوا ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: During the lifetime of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) the moon was split into two parts; one part remained over the mountain, and the other part went beyond the mountain. On that, Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, "Witness this miracle

bukhari:4864.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the splitting of the moon in Quran 54:1 refers to a future eschatological sign on the Day of Judgment, a localized optical phenomenon, or a brief physical split that went unrecorded globally because other nations were asleep or obscured by clouds (as Ibn Hajar argues in *Fatḥ al-Bārī*). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the moon physically split during Muhammad's lifetime into two distinct pieces (`انْشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ... فِرْقَتَيْنِ`), with one half above the mountain and the other half below or before it (`فِرْقَةً فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ وَفِرْقَةً دُونَهُ`), while parallel Sahih narrations (`bukhari:3869`) state that observers saw Mount Hira literally standing between the two halves (`حَتَّى رَأَوْا حِرَاءً بَيْنَهُمَا`). This locks Sunni orthodoxy into defending a literal 7th-century AD cataclysm in which the moon parted around a local Meccan mountain—an astronomical impossibility completely unrecorded by any contemporary Byzantine, Persian, Chinese, or Indian astronomers.

bukhari:4867.note: Recorded in Bukhari's commentary on [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1), Anas ibn Malik reports that when the people of Mecca asked Muhammad to show them a miraculous sign, he showed them the cleaving of the moon. This narration anchors [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1) as a literal event during Muhammad's lifetime in Mecca rather than solely a future eschatological sign, while standing in tension with Meccan passages stating that Allah refrained from sending requested signs ([Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), [Quran 29:50](quran://29/50)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: سَأَلَ أَهْلُ مَكَّةَ أَنْ يُرِيَهُمْ آيَةً فَأَرَاهُمُ انْشِقَاقَ الْقَمَرِ
problematic_excerpt.english: The people of Mecca asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to show them a sign (miracle). So he showed them (the miracle) of the cleaving of the moon

bukhari:4867.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Quran 54:1 merely describes a future eschatological event on the Day of Judgment, or follow Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī in claiming the rest of the world missed the event due to time zones while citing lunar trenches like Rima Ariadaeus as scientific proof. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states fa-arāhumu nshiqāqa l-qamar ('so he showed them the cleaving of the moon') as an immediate physical sign to the Meccans, and parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:3637, bukhari:3868) specify it split into two distinct halves (firqatayn) until they saw Mount Ḥirāʾ between them. This locks Sunni orthodoxy into a literal 7th-century AD astronomical cataclysm that left zero geological evidence of a global split and went completely unrecorded by every contemporary civilization across the same hemisphere.

muslim:1006.note: Ibn Abbas reports that during Muhammad's mission, devils (*al-shayatin*) were blocked from intercepting heavenly news by having shooting stars or meteors (*al-shuhub*, rendered generically in the published English translation as "flames") hurled at them ([Quran 72:8-9](quran://72/8-9), [Quran 67:5](quran://67/5); cf. bukhari:4921).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَقَدْ حِيلَ بَيْنَ الشَّيَاطِينِ وَبَيْنَ خَبَرِ السَّمَاءِ وَأُرْسِلَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الشُّهُبُ فَرَجَعَتِ الشَّيَاطِينُ إِلَى قَوْمِهِمْ فَقَالُوا مَا لَكُمْ قَالُوا حِيلَ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَ خَبَرِ السَّمَاءِ وَأُرْسِلَتْ عَلَيْنَا الشُّهُبُ ‏.‏ قَالُوا مَا ذَاكَ إِلاَّ مِنْ شَىْءٍ حَدَثَ
problematic_excerpt.english: And there had been (at that time) obstructions between satans and the news from the Heaven, and there were flung flames upon them. So satan went back to their people and they said: What has happened to you? They said: There have been created obstructions between us and the news from the Heaven. And there have been flung upon us flames. They said: It cannot happen but for some (important) event.

muslim:1006.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that *al-shuhub* refers to unseen, metaphysical flames in the spiritual realm (*al-ghayb*) rather than physical meteors, while classical commentators like Al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*) and Ibn Ḥajar (*Fatḥ al-Bārī*) contend that shooting stars existed prior to Islam but merely intensified when Muhammad's mission began. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that *al-shuhub* (literally 'shooting stars' or 'meteors') were hurled at the devils (*ursilat 'alayhim al-shuhub*), prompting them to declare that this phenomenon could only be caused by a newly occurring earthly event (*mā dhāka illā min shay'in ḥadatha*). Furthermore, [Quran 67:5](quran://67/5) and parallel Sahih narrations explicitly identify these projectiles with the visible lamps (*al-maṣābīḥ*) adorning the lowest physical sky, confirming that Islamic cosmology treats ordinary astronomical meteors as literal missiles thrown at eavesdropping demons.

bukhari:773.note: Ibn Abbas reports that shooting stars (*al-shuhub*) were hurled at the devils (*al-shayatin*) to bar them from the news of heaven (*khabar al-sama'*), prompting them to search the earth until they heard Muhammad reciting the Quran at Nakhla and identified it as the cause ([Quran 72:1-9](quran://72/1-9)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَقَدْ حِيلَ بَيْنَ الشَّيَاطِينِ وَبَيْنَ خَبَرِ السَّمَاءِ، وَأُرْسِلَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الشُّهُبُ، فَرَجَعَتِ الشَّيَاطِينُ إِلَى قَوْمِهِمْ‏.‏ فَقَالُوا مَا لَكُمْ فَقَالُوا حِيلَ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَ خَبَرِ السَّمَاءِ، وَأُرْسِلَتْ عَلَيْنَا الشُّهُبُ‏.‏ قَالُوا مَا حَالَ بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَ خَبَرِ السَّمَاءِ إِلاَّ شَىْءٌ حَدَثَ
problematic_excerpt.english: At the same time, a barrier was put between the devils and the news of heaven. Fire commenced to be thrown at them. The Devils went to their people, who asked them, "What is wrong with you?" They said, "A barrier has been placed between us and the news of heaven. And fire has been thrown at us." They said, "The thing which has put a barrier between you and the news of heaven must be something which has happened recently.

bukhari:773.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that *al-shuhub* refers to unseen spiritual phenomena in the realm of *al-ghayb* rather than physical meteoroids, or cite Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* to claim that meteors existed prior to the 7th century AD but were merely intensified against eavesdropping jinn during Muhammad's mission. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states (*wa-ursilat 'alayhimu al-shuhub*) that these fiery projectiles were newly unleashed at the devils because of "something that has happened recently" (*illā shay'un ḥadatha*), treating the phenomenon as a sudden cosmic novelty. Furthermore, parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:4921, muslim:5819) and [Quran 67:5](quran://67/5) confirm that these missiles are the exact physical stars and meteors visibly witnessed streaking across the night sky by human observers.

muslim:6359.note: Abu Dharr reports that he stayed in Mecca for thirty days and nights consuming nothing but Zamzam water, feeling no hunger and growing so fat that folds formed on his stomach. Muhammad affirms this account by declaring that Zamzam water is blessed and serves as nourishing food.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: ثُمَّ رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ ثُمَّ قَالَ ‏"‏ مَتَى كُنْتَ هَا هُنَا ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ قُلْتُ قَدْ كُنْتُ هَا هُنَا مُنْذُ ثَلاَثِينَ بَيْنَ لَيْلَةٍ وَيَوْمٍ قَالَ ‏"‏ فَمَنْ كَانَ يُطْعِمُكَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ قُلْتُ مَا كَانَ لِي طَعَامٌ إِلاَّ مَاءُ زَمْزَمَ ‏.‏ فَسَمِنْتُ حَتَّى تَكَسَّرَتْ عُكَنُ بَطْنِي وَمَا أَجِدُ عَلَى كَبِدِي سُخْفَةَ جُوعٍ قَالَ ‏"‏ إِنَّهَا مُبَارَكَةٌ إِنَّهَا طَعَامُ طُعْمٍ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: He then lifted his head and said: Since how long have you been here? I said: I have been here for the last thirty nights or days. He said: Who has been feeding you? I said: There has been no food for me but the water of Zamzam. I have grown so bulky that there appear wrinkles upon my stomach and I do not feel any hunger. He said: It is blessed (water) and it also serves as food.

muslim:6359.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Abu Dharr's weight gain on water alone was either a unique supernatural miracle or figurative hyperbole for feeling satiated by the natural minerals in Zamzam. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states فَسَمِنْتُ حَتَّى تَكَسَّرَتْ عُكَنُ بَطْنِي ('I have grown so bulky that there appear wrinkles upon my stomach') over thirty nights and days (ثَلاَثِينَ بَيْنَ لَيْلَةٍ وَيَوْمٍ) while consuming nothing but Zamzam water (مَا كَانَ لِي طَعَامٌ إِلاَّ مَاءُ زَمْزَمَ), describing literal folds of belly fat forming with zero caloric intake. Furthermore, Muhammad does not attribute this to an isolated miracle for Abu Dharr, but instead declares it an intrinsic property of the water itself by stating إِنَّهَا مُبَارَكَةٌ إِنَّهَا طَعَامُ طُعْمٍ ('It is blessed, and it also serves as food'), as confirmed in muslim:6361.

bukhari:3207.note: Muhammad states that in the seventh heaven he saw four rivers at the root of Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary)—two hidden and two apparent—and that Gabriel identified the two apparent rivers as the Nile and the Euphrates.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: وَرُفِعَتْ لِي سِدْرَةُ الْمُنْتَهَى فَإِذَا نَبِقُهَا كَأَنَّهُ قِلاَلُ هَجَرٍ، وَوَرَقُهَا كَأَنَّهُ آذَانُ الْفُيُولِ، فِي أَصْلِهَا أَرْبَعَةُ أَنْهَارٍ نَهْرَانِ بَاطِنَانِ وَنَهْرَانِ ظَاهِرَانِ، فَسَأَلْتُ جِبْرِيلَ فَقَالَ أَمَّا الْبَاطِنَانِ فَفِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَمَّا الظَّاهِرَانِ النِّيلُ وَالْفُرَاتُ
problematic_excerpt.english: Then I was shown Sidrat-ul-Muntaha (i.e. a tree in the seventh heaven) and I saw its Nabk fruits which resembled the clay jugs of Hajr (i.e. a town in Arabia), and its leaves were like the ears of elephants, and four rivers originated at its root, two of them were apparent and two were hidden. I asked Gabriel about those rivers and he said, 'The two hidden rivers are in Paradise, and the apparent ones are the Nile and the Euphrates.'

bukhari:3207.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue, citing secondary figurative interpretations in Al-Nawawī's Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim and Ibn Ḥajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī, that placing the source of the Nile and Euphrates in the seventh heaven is merely a metaphor for their blessedness and sweet water, or a symbolic dream vision. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that four rivers originate directly at the physical root of the celestial Lote Tree (fī aṣlihā arbaʿatu anhārin) and contrasts the two hidden rivers of Paradise (al-bāṭināni) with the two visible, earthly rivers (al-ẓāhirāni al-Nīlu wa-al-Furātu). Furthermore, both Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ and Al-Nawawī affirm that the primary orthodox position takes the narration literally (ʿalā ẓāhirihi)—insisting that these waters physically spring from the tree in heaven before emerging from the earth—which simply codifies ancient Near Eastern cosmological myths as geographical fact.

muslim:5598.note: When the Christians of Najran question al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba about the Quranic recitation 'O sister of Aaron' ([Quran 19:28](quran://19/28)) regarding Mary despite Moses living long before Jesus, al-Mughira asks Muhammad, who replies that earlier peoples used to name their children after the prophets and pious individuals who preceded them.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: لَمَّا قَدِمْتُ نَجْرَانَ سَأَلُونِي فَقَالُوا إِنَّكُمْ تَقْرَءُونَ يَا أُخْتَ هَارُونَ وَمُوسَى قَبْلَ عِيسَى بِكَذَا وَكَذَا ‏.‏ فَلَمَّا قَدِمْتُ عَلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم سَأَلْتُهُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يُسَمُّونَ بِأَنْبِيَائِهِمْ وَالصَّالِحِينَ قَبْلَهُمْ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: When I came to Najran, they (the Christians of Najran) asked me: You read" O sister of Harun" (i. e. Hadrat Maryam) in the Qur'an, whereas Moses was born much before Jesus. When I came back to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) I asked him about that, whereupon he said: The (people of the old age) used to give names (to their persons) after the names of Apostles and pious persons who had gone before them

muslim:5598.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that calling Mary 'O sister of Aaron' (`يَا أُخْتَ هَارُونَ`) in [Quran 19:28](quran://19/28) is a figurative idiom for a pious descendant of Aaron, or that Muhammad's explanation resolves the chronology because Mary had a contemporary relative named after the earlier prophet. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that ancient people 'used to give names after their prophets and the pious persons before them' (`إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يُسَمُّونَ بِأَنْبِيَائِهِمْ وَالصَّالِحِينَ قَبْلَهُمْ`), which contradicts the 'figurative descendant' defense while failing to explain the family parallels in [Quran 3:35](quran://3/35) and [Quran 66:12](quran://66/12) that match the sister of Aaron and Moses in [Exodus 15:20](bible://ex/15/20) and [Numbers 26:59](bible://nm/26/59). Furthermore, al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba's inability to answer the Christians of Najran when they noted that Moses lived long before Jesus (`وَمُوسَى قَبْلَ عِيسَى بِكَذَا وَكَذَا`) until he returned to ask Muhammad (`فَلَمَّا قَدِمْتُ عَلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم سَأَلْتُهُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ`) shows that Muhammad's own companion knew of no such contemporary namesake ([Ibn Kathir 19:28](ibnkathir://19/28)).

muslim:4555.note: Muhammad narrates that a prior prophet exempted newlyweds, builders of unroofed houses, and owners of pregnant livestock from a campaign, asked Allah to halt the sun until victory, and exposed hidden plunder (ghulūl) when tribesmen's hands physically stuck to his hand during a pledge until they produced a gold cow's head for fire to consume (bukhari:3124). While combining elements parallel to [Deuteronomy 20:5](bible://dt/20/5), [Joshua 10:12](bible://jo/10/12), and [Joshua 7:1](bible://jo/7/1), Muhammad declares that war spoils were never lawful for anyone before Islam until Allah permitted them due to Muslims' weakness and incapacity ('ajzanā), contrary to explicit laws permitting Israelite war plunder in [Deuteronomy 20:14](bible://dt/20/14), [Joshua 8:2](bible://jo/8/2), and [Joshua 22:8](bible://jo/22/8).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَجَمَعُوا مَا غَنِمُوا فَأَقْبَلَتِ النَّارُ لِتَأْكُلَهُ فَأَبَتْ أَنْ تَطْعَمَهُ فَقَالَ فِيكُمْ غُلُولٌ فَلْيُبَايِعْنِي مِنْ كُلِّ قَبِيلَةٍ رَجُلٌ ‏.‏ فَبَايَعُوهُ فَلَصِقَتْ يَدُ رَجُلٍ بِيَدِهِ فَقَالَ فِيكُمُ الْغُلُولُ فَلْتُبَايِعْنِي قَبِيلَتُكَ ‏.‏ فَبَايَعَتْهُ - قَالَ - فَلَصِقَتْ بِيَدِ رَجُلَيْنِ أَوْ ثَلاَثَةٍ فَقَالَ فِيكُمُ الْغُلُولُ أَنْتُمْ غَلَلْتُمْ - قَالَ - فَأَخْرَجُوا لَهُ مِثْلَ رَأْسِ بَقَرَةٍ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ - قَالَ - فَوَضَعُوهُ فِي الْمَالِ وَهُوَ بِالصَّعِيدِ فَأَقْبَلَتِ النَّارُ فَأَكَلَتْهُ ‏.‏ فَلَمْ تَحِلَّ الْغَنَائِمُ لأَحَدٍ مِنْ قَبْلِنَا ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى رَأَى ضَعْفَنَا وَعَجْزَنَا فَطَيَّبَهَا لَنَا
problematic_excerpt.english: The people gathered the spoils of war (at one place). A fire approached the spoils to devour them, but it did not devour them. He (the Holy Prophet) said: Some of you have been guilty of misappropriation. So one man from each tribe should swear fealty to me. The did so (putting their hands into his). The hand of one man stuck to his hand and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: Your tribe is guilty of misappropriation. Let all the members of your tribe swear fealty to me one by one. They did so, when the hands of two or three persons got stuck with his hand. He said: You have misappropriated. So they took out gold equal in volume to the head of a cow. They-placed it among the spoils on the earth. Then the fire approached the spoils and devoured them. The spoils of war were not made lawful for any people before us, This is because Allah saw our weakness and humility and made them lawful for us

muslim:4555.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the prohibition of plunder in the account of Achan's theft ([Joshua 7:1](bible://jo/7/1)) confirms that war spoils were forbidden to previous nations, and claim that where this narration diverges from the Biblical record, the Hadith preserves the true history. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states an absolute universal rule—`فَلَمْ تَحِلَّ الْغَنَائِمُ لأَحَدٍ مِنْ قَبْلِنَا` ("spoils of war were not lawful for anyone before us")—rather than a single-battle restriction, directly contradicting the explicit Biblical laws permitting Israelites to take war plunder in [Deuteronomy 20:14](bible://dt/20/14), [Joshua 8:2](bible://jo/8/2), and [Joshua 22:8](bible://jo/22/8). Moreover, while relying on the military exemptions of [Deuteronomy 20:5](bible://dt/20/5) and the stopped sun of [Joshua 10:12](bible://jo/10/12), the Hadith conflates these episodes with thieves' hands physically sticking to the prophet (`فَلَصِقَتْ يَدُ رَجُلٍ بِيَدِهِ`) over gold shaped like a cow's head (`مِثْلَ رَأْسِ بَقَرَةٍ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ`), and concedes that spoils were made lawful only because Allah `رَأَى ضَعْفَنَا وَعَجْزَنَا` ("saw our weakness and our incapacity," which the English translator euphemizes as "humility").

muslim:7072.note: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud reports that while with Muhammad at Mina, the moon split into two pieces—one behind the mountain and the other on this side of it—and Muhammad commanded his companions to bear witness ([Quran 54:1](quran://54/1); bukhari:3869, bukhari:4864, muslim:7071).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: بَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ مَعَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِمِنًى إِذَا انْفَلَقَ الْقَمَرُ فِلْقَتَيْنِ فَكَانَتْ فِلْقَةٌ وَرَاءَ الْجَبَلِ وَفِلْقَةٌ دُونَهُ فَقَالَ لَنَا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ اشْهَدُوا ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: We were along with Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) at Mina, that moon was split up into two. One of its parts was behind the mountain and the other one was on this side of the mountain. Allah's Messenger (may peace be upbn him) said to us: Bear witness to this

muslim:7072.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1) refers solely to a future eschatological sign on the Day of Judgment or a figurative expression rather than a physical division of the moon during Muhammad's lifetime. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that while Abdullah ibn Mas'ud was with Muhammad at Mina (`بِمِنًى`), the moon split into two pieces (`انْفَلَقَ الْقَمَرُ فِلْقَتَيْنِ`)—with one piece behind the mountain and the other on this side of it (`فَكَانَتْ فِلْقَةٌ وَرَاءَ الْجَبَلِ وَفِلْقَةٌ دُونَهُ`)—whereupon Muhammad commanded his companions to bear witness (`اشْهَدُوا`) to this observable event (`bukhari:3869`, `bukhari:4864`, `muslim:7071`).

muslim:7073.note: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud reports that during Muhammad's lifetime the moon split into two pieces—with a mountain covering one piece while the other remained above it—whereupon Muhammad called upon Allah to bear witness ([Quran 54:1](quran://54/1)).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: انْشَقَّ الْقَمَرُ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فِلْقَتَيْنِ فَسَتَرَ الْجَبَلُ فِلْقَةً وَكَانَتْ فِلْقَةٌ فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ اللَّهُمَّ اشْهَدْ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Abdullah b. Mas'ud reported that the moon was split up in two parts during the lifetime of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ). The mountain covered one of its parts and one part of it was above the mountain and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said:Bear witness to this

muslim:7073.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the splitting of the moon in [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1) refers either to a future eschatological sign or to a non-literal vision rather than a physical division of the lunar body. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the moon split during the lifetime of Allah's Messenger (inshaqqa al-qamaru 'alā 'ahdi rasūli Allāhi) into two distinct pieces (filqatayni). Furthermore, Abdullah b. Mas'ud specifies the physical positions of the two halves—recording that the mountain covered one piece (fa-satara al-jabalu filqatan) while the other piece was above the mountain (wa-kānat filqatun fawqa al-jabali)—whereupon Muhammad called on Allah to bear witness (Allāhumma ishhad), as corroborated in bukhari:3869, bukhari:4864, and muslim:7072.

muslim:7076.note: Anas reports via Qatada that when the people of Mecca demanded a sign from Muhammad, he showed them the splitting of the moon twice (*marratayn*), whereas a parallel transmission from Qatada on the authority of Anas (muslim:7078) states that the moon split into two parts (*firqatayn*). This account of a physical sign granted upon Meccan demand ([Quran 54:1](quran://54/1)) stands in tension with [Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), which states that Allah refrained from sending miraculous signs.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ أَنَسٍ، أَنَّ أَهْلَ، مَكَّةَ سَأَلُوا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم أَنْ يُرِيَهُمْ آيَةً فَأَرَاهُمُ انْشِقَاقَ الْقَمَرِ مَرَّتَيْنِ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Anas reported that the people of Mecca demanded from Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) that he should show them (some) signs (miracles) and he showed twice the splitting of the moon.

muslim:7076.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that [Quran 54:1](quran://54/1) describes a future sign at the final judgment rather than a past event in Mecca, or that the narration's dual wording only means the moon divided into two halves once. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the people of Mecca asked Muhammad to show them a sign (`أَنْ يُرِيَهُمْ آيَةً`) and he showed them the splitting of the moon twice (`فَأَرَاهُمُ انْشِقَاقَ الْقَمَرِ مَرَّتَيْنِ`), using the explicit repetition marker `مَرَّتَيْنِ` (twice) to record a historical demonstration in Mecca (`bukhari:3637`, `bukhari:3868`). Moreover, this report of an on-demand sign given to the Meccans conflicts with [Quran 17:59](quran://17/59), which explains why miraculous signs were withheld when demanded.

bukhari:3320.note: Muhammad instructs that if a fly falls into someone's drink, they should submerge it and then remove it, stating that one of its wings contains a disease and the other contains a cure.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: إِذَا وَقَعَ الذُّبَابُ فِي شَرَابِ أَحَدِكُمْ فَلْيَغْمِسْهُ، ثُمَّ لِيَنْزِعْهُ، فَإِنَّ فِي إِحْدَى جَنَاحَيْهِ دَاءً وَالأُخْرَى شِفَاءً
problematic_excerpt.english: If a house fly falls in the drink of anyone of you, he should dip it (in the drink) and take it out, for one of its wings has a disease and the other has the cure for the disease

bukhari:3320.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that modern microbiology has vindicated this narration by identifying bacteriophages or antimicrobial microflora on houseflies, or cite Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* to claim the fly defensively dips its disease-bearing wing first so full immersion is required to release the antidote. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states as an anatomical rule that one wing holds the disease and the other holds its cure (فَإِنَّ فِي إِحْدَى جَنَاحَيْهِ دَاءً وَالأُخْرَى شِفَاءً) and commands the drinker to plunge the insect into the beverage (فَلْيَغْمِسْهُ). In reality, houseflies carry over a hundred pathogens—including *Salmonella*, *E. coli*, and *Shigella*—indiscriminately across their legs, gut, and mouthparts rather than segregated between asymmetric wings, and dunking a filthy vector into a drink only multiplies bacterial contamination rather than delivering a clinical cure.

muslim:5338.note: Muhammad declares that whoever eats seven dates from between the two lava plains in the morning will not be harmed by any poison until evening.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ مَنْ أَكَلَ سَبْعَ تَمَرَاتٍ مِمَّا بَيْنَ لاَبَتَيْهَا حِينَ يُصْبِحُ لَمْ يَضُرَّهُ سُمٌّ حَتَّى يُمْسِيَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Amir b. Sa'd b. Abu Waqqas, on the authority of his father, reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) having said:He who ate seven dates (of the land situated) between these two lava plains in the morning, no poison will harm him until it is evening

muslim:5338.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this statement is a figurative reference to the general nutritional benefits of Medina's dates or a spiritual protection that depends on the eater's personal faith. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states an unconditional physical rule: whoever eats seven dates from between the two lava plains in the morning (مَنْ أَكَلَ سَبْعَ تَمَرَاتٍ مِمَّا بَيْنَ لاَبَتَيْهَا حِينَ يُصْبِحُ), no poison will harm him until evening (لَمْ يَضُرَّهُ سُمٌّ حَتَّى يُمْسِيَ). In Classical Arabic grammar, the indefinite noun سُمٌّ (poison) following the negation لَمْ يَضُرَّهُ (will not harm him) denotes universality across all poisons, and the conditional pronoun مَنْ (he who) ties this immunity directly to eating the seven dates without qualification (bukhari:5445, bukhari:5768, muslim:5339).

muslim:5766.note: Muhammad declares that black seed (*al-ḥabbah al-sawdā'*, identified in the report as *al-shūnīz*, or nigella seed) contains a cure (*shifā'*) for every disease (*kull dā'*) except death (*illā al-sām*). By specifying death as the sole exception (cf. bukhari:5687, bukhari:5688, muslim:5768), the statement frames the seed's curative scope as universal across all illnesses rather than restricted to a subset of ailments.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ أَبَا هُرَيْرَةَ، أَخْبَرَهُمَا أَنَّهُ، سَمِعَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ ‏ "‏ إِنَّ فِي الْحَبَّةِ السَّوْدَاءِ شِفَاءً مِنْ كُلِّ دَاءٍ إِلاَّ السَّامَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ وَالسَّامُ الْمَوْتُ ‏.‏ وَالْحَبَّةُ السَّوْدَاءُ الشُّونِيزُ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Abu Huraira reported that he heard Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:Nigella seed is a remedy for every disease except death

muslim:5766.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the word *kull* ("every") is a general expression intended in a restricted sense (*ʿāmm urīda bihi al-khuṣūṣ*), meaning that black seed only treats certain categories of illness or merely supports general immunity. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *shifā'an min kulli dā'in illā al-sām* ("a remedy for every disease except death"), pairing the universal quantifier *kull* ("every") with the sole exception *illā al-sām* ("except death"). By explicitly excluding only death (*al-mawt*), the statement forecloses any restriction of the remedy to a narrower subset of diseases (`bukhari:5687`, `bukhari:5688`, `muslim:5768`).

muslim:5757.note: Asma' pours water into the shirt collar (*jaybihā*) of a feverish woman, citing Muhammad's command to cool fever with water because it originates from the boiling heat of Hell (*fayḥ Jahannam*).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ أَسْمَاءَ، أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تُؤْتَى بِالْمَرْأَةِ الْمَوْعُوكَةِ فَتَدْعُو بِالْمَاءِ فَتَصُبُّهُ فِي جَيْبِهَا وَتَقُولُ إِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏"‏ ابْرُدُوهَا بِالْمَاءِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ وَقَالَ ‏"‏ إِنَّهَا مِنْ فَيْحِ جَهَنَّمَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Asma' reported that a woman running high fever was brought to her. She asked water to be brought and then sprinkled it in the opening of a shirt at the uppermost part of the chest and said that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) had said:Cool (the fever) with water. for it is because of the vehemence of the beat of Hell

muslim:5757.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that describing fever as coming from Hell is a figurative metaphor for intense heat, and that cooling a feverish patient with water anticipates modern tepid sponging. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states `إِنَّهَا مِنْ فَيْحِ جَهَنَّمَ` ("it is from the vehemence of the heat of Hell"), using the partitive preposition *min* ("from") to assert a literal causal origin rather than a particle of comparison. Because Muhammad attributed the condition directly to the heat of Hellfire (as reinforced in `bukhari:3264`, `bukhari:5724`, and `muslim:5759`), Asma' treated the patient by pouring water into her shirt collar (`فَتَصُبُّهُ فِي جَيْبِهَا`) in obedience to the command `ابْرُدُوهَا بِالْمَاءِ` ("cool it with water").

bukhari:5707.note: Muhammad declares that there is no contagious disease transmission (*lā ʿadwā*), even while commanding in the same statement to flee from a leper as one flees from a lion. Parallel narrations confirm he denied physical host-to-host infection itself, dismissing a Bedouin's observation that a mangy camel infects healthy camels by asking, "Then who infected the first one?" (bukhari:5717, bukhari:5770).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ لاَ عَدْوَى وَلاَ طِيَرَةَ وَلاَ هَامَةَ وَلاَ صَفَرَ، وَفِرَّ مِنَ الْمَجْذُومِ كَمَا تَفِرُّ مِنَ الأَسَدِ ‏"
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said, "(There is) no 'Adwa (no contagious disease is conveyed without Allah's permission). nor is there any bad omen (from birds), nor is there any Hamah, nor is there any bad omen in the month of Safar, and one should run away from the leper as one runs away from a lion."

bukhari:5707.literal_translation: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: "There is no contagion, nor bad omens, nor owl-spirits, nor [the month of] Safar, and flee from the leper as one flees from a lion."

translation_issue.arabic_term: لاَ عَدْوَى
translation_issue.published_rendering: (There is) no 'Adwa (no contagious disease is conveyed without Allah's permission).
translation_issue.literal_meaning: There is no contagion
translation_issue.explanation: The translator inserted the theological caveat '(no contagious disease is conveyed without Allah's permission)' to soften Muhammad's categorical denial of disease transmission and harmonize it with medical reality.

bukhari:5707.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Ibn Ḥajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and Al-Nawawī—that Muhammad was merely refuting the pre-Islamic belief that diseases transmit autonomously apart from Allah's decree, claiming his command to 'flee from the leper' proves he affirmed physical contagion and quarantine. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states lā ʿadwā ('there is no contagion') using the exact same categorical negation applied alongside it to fictitious pagan myths like hāmah (owl-spirits) and ṭiyarah (bird omens), while the English qualifier ('without Allah's permission') is a pure translator interpolation absent from the Arabic manuscript. Moreover, when a Bedouin empirically challenged this claim in bukhari:5717 by noting that a single mangy camel infects an entire healthy herd, Muhammad did not reply that it spreads by Allah's permission, but instead denied host-to-host transmission altogether by asking, 'Then who infected the first one?' (fa-man aʿdā al-awwal?).

muslim:5800.note: Muhammad declares that there is no contagious disease (*lā ʿadwā*) and no evil omen (*wa-lā ṭiyarah*), while expressing approval of a good omen defined as a pleasant word. Although the published English text appends an editorial note stating that scholars interpret this to mean disease does not cause harm independently of Allah's control, the Arabic text itself states an unqualified negation of contagion.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ أَنَسٍ، أَنَّ نَبِيَّ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ لاَ عَدْوَى وَلاَ طِيَرَةَ وَيُعْجِبُنِي الْفَأْلُ الْكَلِمَةُ الْحَسَنَةُ الْكَلِمَةُ الطَّيِّبَةُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Anas reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:There is no transitive disease, no divination, but good omen pleases me, i. e. the good word or a good word. Note: The majority of scholars interpret this to mean that these things in and of themselves do not transmit or cause harm through supernatural or hidden means but that Allah is ultimately in control and any fearful superstition around these is false

muslim:5800.literal_translation: From Anas, that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no contagion and no evil omen, and I like the good omen—the good word, the pleasant word.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: لاَ عَدْوَى
translation_issue.published_rendering: There is no transitive disease
translation_issue.literal_meaning: There is no contagion
translation_issue.explanation: The published English text renders 'lā ʿadwā' with the obscure phrase 'no transitive disease' and appends an unattested apologetic note directly into the translation to qualify the categorical Arabic negation of contagion.

muslim:5800.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was not denying medical contagion itself, but rather teaching that diseases do not transmit or cause harm in and of themselves apart from Allah's control. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *lā ʿadwā* ('there is no contagion') as an unqualified categorical negation, grouping disease transmission directly alongside *wa lā ṭiyarah* ('and no evil omen') as a false superstition. The caveat that diseases do not transmit 'in and of themselves' is absent from the Arabic *matn* of `muslim:5800` (as well as `bukhari:5756`, `bukhari:5776`, and `muslim:5791`) and only appears as an editorial note appended to the English translation.

bukhari:3261.note: Citing Muhammad's declaration that human fever originates from the spreading heat of Hellfire (*fayḥ jahannam*), Ibn 'Abbas instructs a feverish companion to cool his illness with water or Zamzam water. Classical commentators such as Ibn Hajar and al-Nawawi affirm that the primary meaning (*ḥaqīqah*) of this prophetic etiology is a literal exhalation from Hellfire rather than a metaphor (*majāz*).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: كُنْتُ أُجَالِسُ ابْنَ عَبَّاسٍ بِمَكَّةَ، فَأَخَذَتْنِي الْحُمَّى، فَقَالَ أَبْرِدْهَا عَنْكَ بِمَاءِ زَمْزَمَ، فَإِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏"‏ الْحُمَّى مِنْ فَيْحِ جَهَنَّمَ فَأَبْرِدُوهَا بِالْمَاءِ ‏"‏‏.‏ أَوْ قَالَ ‏"‏ بِمَاءِ زَمْزَمَ ‏"‏‏.‏ شَكَّ هَمَّامٌ
problematic_excerpt.english: I used to sit with Ibn `Abbas in Mecca. Once I had a fever and he said (to me), "Cool your fever with Zamzam water, for Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'It, (the Fever) is from the heat of the (Hell) Fire; so, cool it with water (or Zamzam water)

bukhari:3261.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that describing fever as coming 'from the heat of Hell' (*min fayḥ jahannam*) is merely a figurative metaphor (*majāz*) for severe body heat meant to remind believers of the hereafter, while praising the water remedy as prescient medical advice. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states this as a literal causal etiology using the partitive preposition *min* ('from the spreading heat of Jahannam'), which is why both Ibn Ḥajar (*Fatḥ al-Bārī*) and Al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*) affirm that the authoritative Sunni position takes it strictly literally (*ʿalā ẓāhirihi*) as physical heat escaping from Hell—identical to adjacent Sahih narrations (bukhari:3260) claiming summer and winter weather are literally caused by Hellfire breathing twice a year. Attributing a hypothalamic immune response against pathogens to supernatural infernal radiation and prescribing water-dousing as a blanket cure completely misses the underlying infection and can dangerously trigger vasoconstriction and shivering.

bukhari:5445.note: Muhammad declares that anyone who eats seven 'Ajwa dates in the morning will not be harmed by poison (`summ`) or magic (`sihr`) throughout that day (bukhari:5768, bukhari:5769). Classical commentators such as Ibn Hajar and al-Nawawi affirm this as a literal prophetic prescription, debating only whether the immunity is restricted to 'Ajwa dates grown in Medina.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: مَنْ تَصَبَّحَ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ سَبْعَ تَمَرَاتٍ عَجْوَةً لَمْ يَضُرُّهُ فِي ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمِ سُمٌّ وَلاَ سِحْرٌ
problematic_excerpt.english: He who eats seven 'Ajwa dates every morning, will not be affected by poison or magic on the day he eats them

bukhari:5445.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* and Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī*—that this immunity is a miraculous blessing (*barakah*) exclusive to the 'Ajwa dates of Medina, or modernly claim that 'poison' (*summ*) merely refers to mild bodily toxins mitigated by antioxidants. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *lam yaḍurruhu fī dhālika al-yawmi summun wa-lā siḥrun* ('neither poison nor magic will harm him on that day'), using indefinite nouns in a negative clause (*nakirah fī siyāq al-nafy*) to assert categorical, universal immunity against any lethal poison or witchcraft whatsoever. Furthermore, this empirical claim is falsified by the Sahih corpus itself: despite residing in Medina with direct access to its 'Ajwa dates, Muhammad was both successfully bewitched (`bukhari:5763`) and ultimately killed by the lingering effects of the Khaybar poison (`bukhari:4428`).

muslim:5339.note: Muhammad declares that whoever eats seven 'Ajwa dates in the morning will not be harmed by poison or magic on that day.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: سَمِعْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ ‏ "‏ مَنْ تَصَبَّحَ بِسَبْعِ تَمَرَاتٍ عَجْوَةً لَمْ يَضُرَّهُ ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمَ سُمٌّ وَلاَ سِحْرٌ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Amir b. Sa'd b. Abu Waqqas reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:He who ate seven 'ajwa' dates in the morning, poison and magic will not harm him on that day

muslim:5339.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this statement refers merely to general nutritional support, spiritual protection, or a restricted local circumstance rather than literal immunity to lethal toxins. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states "مَنْ تَصَبَّحَ بِسَبْعِ تَمَرَاتٍ عَجْوَةً لَمْ يَضُرَّهُ ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمَ سُمٌّ وَلاَ سِحْرٌ" ("He who ate seven 'ajwa' dates in the morning, poison and magic will not harm him on that day"), using the universal conditional particle "مَنْ" (he who / whoever) to issue an unrestricted promise to anyone who eats seven 'ajwa' dates in the morning. Because the indefinite nouns "سُمٌّ" (poison) and "سِحْرٌ" (magic) fall under the negation "لَمْ يَضُرَّهُ" (will not harm him), the Arabic grammar establishes a categorical denial of physical or supernatural harm for that day ("ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمَ"), a literal guarantee repeated across parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:5445, bukhari:5769, muslim:5338).

muslim:5797.note: Muhammad declares that there is no contagious disease (*lā ʿadwā*), no *ṣafar*, and no *ghūl* (bukhari:5717, muslim:5791, muslim:5796). In the accompanying explanation, the narrator Jabir ibn Abdullah defines *ṣafar* as intestinal worms of the belly (*dawābb al-baṭn*), denying both infectious disease transmission and parasitic infection.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: سَمِعْتُ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ ‏"‏ لاَ عَدْوَى وَلاَ صَفَرَ وَلاَ غُولَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ وَسَمِعْتُ أَبَا الزُّبَيْرِ يَذْكُرُ أَنَّ جَابِرًا فَسَّرَ لَهُمْ قَوْلَهُ ‏"‏ وَلاَ صَفَرَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ أَبُو الزُّبَيْرِ الصَّفَرُ الْبَطْنُ ‏.‏ فَقِيلَ لِجَابِرٍ كَيْفَ قَالَ كَانَ يُقَالُ دَوَابُّ الْبَطْنِ ‏.‏ قَالَ وَلَمْ يُفَسِّرِ الْغُولَ ‏.‏ قَالَ أَبُو الزُّبَيْرِ هَذِهِ الْغُولُ الَّتِي تَغَوَّلُ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Jabir b. 'Abdullah reported Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) as saying:There is no transitive disease, no safar, no ghoul. He (the narrator) said: I heard Abu Zubair say: Jabir explained for them the word safar. Abu Zubair said: safar means belly. It was said to Jabir: Why is it so? He said that it was held that safar implied the worms of the belly, but he gave no explanation of ghoul. Abu Zubair said: Ghoul is that which kills the travellers

muslim:5797.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the negation of contagion (*lā ʿadwā*) only means diseases do not transmit independently of divine decree, and that *ṣafar* merely refers to superstitions surrounding the Islamic calendar month rather than a medical condition. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states the unqualified denial *lā ʿadwā wa lā ṣafar* ("There is no transitive disease, no *safar*"), and the narrator Jabir b. 'Abdullah directly explains *al-ṣafar* as *al-baṭn* ("the belly") and specifically *dawābb al-baṭn* ("the worms of the belly"). By grouping disease transmission (*ʿadwā*) and intestinal worms (*dawābb al-baṭn*) alongside mythical desert monsters (*wa lā ghūl*, "no ghoul"), the narration classifies real biological pathogens and parasites as non-existent superstitions.

muslim:5341.note: Muhammad states that the 'Ajwa dates of al-'Aliyah contain healing (*shifā'*) or serve as an antidote (*tiryāq*) in the early morning. In a companion narration in the same chapter (muslim:5339), he specifies that eating seven 'Ajwa dates in the morning prevents harm from both poison and magic that day.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَائِشَةَ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ إِنَّ فِي عَجْوَةِ الْعَالِيَةِ شِفَاءً أَوْ إِنَّهَا تِرْيَاقٌ أَوَّلَ الْبُكْرَةِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: A'isha reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:The 'ajwa' dates of 'Aliya' contain healing effects and these are antidote in the early morning

muslim:5341.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this narration merely describes the general nutritional value of dates or offers a metaphorical blessing restricted to the soil of al-'Aliyah rather than a literal pharmacological guarantee. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the 'Ajwa dates of al-'Aliyah contain healing (*shifā'*) and act as a literal medical antidote (*tiryāq*) when eaten first thing in the morning (*awwal al-bukrah*). Parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:5445, bukhari:5769, muslim:5339) confirm that this was taught as a concrete prophylactic remedy against poison, making a falsifiable medical claim that contradicts basic toxicology.

muslim:5768.note: Muhammad declares with the universal negation *mā min dā'in illā* that there is no disease for which black seed (*al-ḥabbah al-sawdā'*) does not provide a cure, except *al-sām* (defined in muslim:5766 as death, *al-mawt*). Although the English translation of muslim:5768 omits the final clause *illā al-sām* ('except death'), it is present in the primary Arabic text.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ مَا مِنْ دَاءٍ إِلاَّ فِي الْحَبَّةِ السَّوْدَاءِ مِنْهُ شِفَاءٌ إِلاَّ السَّامَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Abu Huraira reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:There is no disease for which Nigella seed does not provide remedy

muslim:5768.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this statement is a figure of speech referring only to select ailments or general immune support rather than a literal cure for every illness. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *"mā min dā'in illā fī al-ḥabbati al-sawdā'i minhu shifā'un illā al-sām"* ("there is no disease except that in the black seed there is a cure for it, except death"), pairing the universal negation *"mā min dā'in"* ("no disease whatsoever") with a single explicit exception. Because the statement and its parallels (`bukhari:5687`, `bukhari:5688`, `muslim:5766`) explicitly exclude only death (*al-sām*), the grammatical structure rules out restricting the claim to a limited subset of diseases.

muslim:5751.note: Via Ibn Umar, Muhammad declares that bodily fever comes from the raging heat of Hellfire (*fayḥi jahannam*) and commands that it be cooled with water. In a parallel report (bukhari:5723), Ibn Umar applies this statement literally by praying for relief from divine punishment when afflicted with a fever.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ، عَنِ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏ "‏ الْحُمَّى مِنْ فَيْحِ جَهَنَّمَ فَابْرُدُوهَا بِالْمَاءِ ‏"‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Ibn Umar reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:The fever from the vehement raging of the (heat of Hell), so cool it with the help of water

muslim:5751.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that describing fever as the raging of Hell is merely a metaphor for intense bodily heat and that cooling a patient with water is a practical first-aid measure. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *al-ḥummā min fayḥi jahannam* ('the fever is from the boiling heat of Hell'), using the partitive preposition *min* ('from') rather than a particle of simile, and directly links this origin to the command *fa-brudūhā bi-l-māʾi* ('so cool it with water'). As reinforced in parallel Sahih reports (`bukhari:3264`, `bukhari:5723`, `muslim:5752`), the instruction is predicated on the literal claim that bodily fever emanates from Hellfire rather than an immune response to illness.

muslim:5803.note: Muhammad declares that "there is no contagious disease" (*lā ʿadwā*), placing biological infection in the same categorical negation as pre-Islamic superstitions like the death-bird omen (*hāmah*) and evil-omen divination (*ṭiyarah*) while endorsing good omens (*al-faʾl al-ṣāliḥ*). Grouping contagion directly alongside non-existent superstitions under a single grammatical negation denies the reality of disease transmission itself rather than merely stating that infection requires divine permission.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ، قَالَ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ لاَ عَدْوَى وَلاَ هَامَةَ وَلاَ طِيَرَةَ وَأُحِبُّ الْفَأْلَ الصَّالِحَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Abu Huraira reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:There is no transitive disease, no hama, no divination, but I like good omen

muslim:5803.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was not denying the biological reality of contagious disease, but merely stating that illness does not transmit independently of divine decree. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *lā ʿadwā wa-lā hāmata wa-lā ṭiyarata* ('There is no transitive disease, no *hama*, no divination'), applying the exact same categorical negation (*lā*) to contagion as it does to non-existent pre-Islamic superstitions. By grouping transitive disease directly with imaginary omens like *hāmah* and *ṭiyarah* (see also bukhari:5757, muslim:5794, and muslim:5802), the text treats physical contagion itself as a false superstition rather than a real mechanism.

bukhari:5687.note: Ibn Abi 'Atiq treats an unspecified travel illness by dropping crushed black cumin (al-habbah al-sawda') mixed with oil into the patient's nostrils, citing Muhammad's declaration via Aisha that black cumin is a cure for every disease (kulli da') except death (al-sam). While classical commentators such as al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar attempt to restrict 'every disease' to cold or damp ailments, the primary text states an unqualified universal claim reinforced by the sole exception of death.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ لَنَا عَلَيْكُمْ بِهَذِهِ الْحُبَيْبَةِ السَّوْدَاءِ، فَخُذُوا مِنْهَا خَمْسًا أَوْ سَبْعًا فَاسْحَقُوهَا، ثُمَّ اقْطُرُوهَا فِي أَنْفِهِ بِقَطَرَاتِ زَيْتٍ فِي هَذَا الْجَانِبِ وَفِي هَذَا الْجَانِبِ، فَإِنَّ عَائِشَةَ حَدَّثَتْنِي أَنَّهَا سَمِعَتِ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ ‏ "‏ إِنَّ هَذِهِ الْحَبَّةَ السَّوْدَاءَ شِفَاءٌ مِنْ كُلِّ دَاءٍ إِلاَّ مِنَ السَّامِ ‏"‏‏.‏ قُلْتُ وَمَا السَّامُ قَالَ الْمَوْتُ
problematic_excerpt.english: Treat him with black cumin. Take five or seven seeds and crush them (mix the powder with oil) and drop the resulting mixture into both nostrils, for `Aisha has narrated to me that she heard the Prophet (ﷺ) saying, 'This black cumin is healing for all diseases except As-Sam.' Aisha said, 'What is As-Sam?' He said, 'Death

bukhari:5687.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Ibn Ḥajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and al-Nawawī—that the phrase 'every disease' (kulli dāʾin) is a general expression intended only for specific 'cold-natured' ailments (ʿāmm urīda bihi al-khuṣūṣ), or that black cumin merely supports general immunity. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states 'shifāʾun min kulli dāʾin illā mina s-sāmi' ('a cure for every disease except death'), where Muhammad's own explicit exception (istithnāʾ) of death alone grammatically locks in the literal universality of 'every disease' and rules out any unstated medical limitations. Furthermore, the Hadith itself records the early Muslims applying this claim with literal universality, as Ibn Abī ʿAtīq immediately prescribes snorting five or seven crushed seeds in oil for an undiagnosed travel illness.

bukhari:4610.note: When a group of people complained that the climate of the land did not suit them, Muhammad instructed them to go out to pasture with his camels and drink their milk and urine, after which they recovered. Classical commentators affirm this as a literal medicinal prescription, debating only whether it establishes the ritual purity of camel urine or a dispensation for medical necessity.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَدِمَ قَوْمٌ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَكَلَّمُوهُ فَقَالُوا قَدِ اسْتَوْخَمْنَا هَذِهِ الأَرْضَ‏.‏ فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ هَذِهِ نَعَمٌ لَنَا تَخْرُجُ، فَاخْرُجُوا فِيهَا، فَاشْرَبُوا مِنْ أَلْبَانِهَا وَأَبْوَالِهَا ‏"‏‏.‏ فَخَرَجُوا فِيهَا فَشَرِبُوا مِنْ أَبْوَالِهَا وَأَلْبَانِهَا وَاسْتَصَحُّوا
problematic_excerpt.english: some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and they spoke to him saying, 'The climate of this land does not suit us.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'These are camels belonging to us, and they are to be taken out to the pasture. So take them out and drink of their milk and urine.' So they took them and set out and drank of their urine and milk, and having recovered

bukhari:4610.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that this prescription was merely a temporary concession (*ḍarūrah*) tailored to the desert customs of the 'Uraynah tribesmen rather than universal Prophetic revelation, or they claim modern science validates camel urine's medicinal value. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad issued a direct imperative—`فَاشْرَبُوا مِنْ أَلْبَانِهَا وَأَبْوَالِهَا` ('so drink of their milk and their urine')—which Imam al-Bukhārī codified as universal normative practice under the *Book of Medicine* (`bukhari:5686`, 'Chapter on Medication with Camel Urine') and which Ibn Ḥajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* defends as a divinely inspired cure. Far from being scientifically sound, excretory waste contains toxic metabolic urea, and the World Health Organization explicitly warns against drinking camel urine as a lethal vector for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS-CoV).

muslim:5791.note: Muhammad declares that there is no contagious disease transmission ('There is no transitive disease'), while also instructing that the sick (or sick camels) should not be brought to the healthy. Abu Salama reports that Abu Huraira initially narrated both statements from Muhammad before later falling silent on the denial of contagion, leaving Abu Salama uncertain whether Abu Huraira forgot it or considered one statement to have abrogated the other.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ أَبَا سَلَمَةَ بْنَ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنِ عَوْفٍ، حَدَّثَهُ أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏"‏ لاَ عَدْوَى ‏"‏ ‏.‏ وَيُحَدِّثُ أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ ‏"‏ لاَ يُورِدُ مُمْرِضٌ عَلَى مُصِحٍّ ‏"‏ ‏.
problematic_excerpt.english: Abu Salama h. 'Abd al-Rahman b. 'Auf reported Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying:There is no transitive disease, but he is also reported to have said: A sick person should not be taken to one who is healthy.

muslim:5791.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the statement 'There is no transitive disease' merely means illness does not spread independently of divine decree, making it harmonious with the command not to bring the sick to the healthy. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Abu Huraira himself abandoned narrating 'لاَ عَدْوَى' ('There is no transitive disease') while retaining 'لاَ يُورِدُ مُمْرِضٌ عَلَى مُصِحٍّ' ('A sick person should not be taken to one who is healthy'), and even denied knowing the first statement when confronted by Harith b. Abu Dhubab. Furthermore, the narrator Abu Salama concludes with 'فَلاَ أَدْرِي أَنَسِيَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ أَوْ نَسَخَ أَحَدُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ الآخَرَ' ('I do not know whether Abu Huraira has forgotten it or he deemed it an abrogated statement in the light of the other one'), demonstrating that the earliest transmitters viewed the two claims as mutually conflicting rather than complementary.

muslim:5791.note: Abu Huraira initially narrated two statements from Muhammad—that there is no transitive disease and that the sick should not be brought to the healthy—before ceasing to narrate the first statement and denying knowledge of it in the Abyssinian language when confronted by his cousin Harith b. Abu Dhubab. Confirming by oath that Abu Huraira had previously transmitted the omitted report, Abu Salama states that he does not know whether Abu Huraira forgot it or deemed one of the two statements to have abrogated the other.
