Umar's explicit desire to inscribe the verse into the codex proves he did not believe Allah had abrogated its wording, exposing naskh al-tilāwah as a post-hoc theological invention to explain away lost Quranic text.

bukhari:5499.note: Before receiving revelation, Muhammad presented a dish of meat to Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl at Baldah, which Zayd refused to eat, stating that he did not eat what was slaughtered on pagan stone altars or without Allah's name mentioned over it. Although transmitted via the same narrator (Musa ibn 'Uqbah) regarding the same encounter, this report inverts (bukhari:3826)—where the dish is instead presented to Muhammad—while the English translation adds parenthetical interpolations attributing the meat offering and Zayd's refusal to the pagans.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّهُ لَقِيَ زَيْدَ بْنَ عَمْرِو بْنِ نُفَيْلٍ بِأَسْفَلِ بَلْدَحٍ، وَذَاكَ قَبْلَ أَنْ يُنْزَلَ عَلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم الْوَحْىُ، فَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم سُفْرَةً فِيهَا لَحْمٌ، فَأَبَى أَنْ يَأْكُلَ مِنْهَا، ثُمَّ قَالَ إِنِّي لاَ آكُلُ مِمَّا تَذْبَحُونَ عَلَى أَنْصَابِكُمْ، وَلاَ آكُلُ إِلاَّ مِمَّا ذُكِرَ اسْمُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said that he met Zaid bin `Amr Nufail at a place near Baldah and this had happened before Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) received the Divine Inspiration. Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) presented a dish of meat (that had been offered to him by the pagans) to Zaid bin `Amr, but Zaid refused to eat of it and then said (to the pagans), "I do not eat of what you slaughter on your stonealtars (Ansabs) nor do I eat except that on which Allah's Name has been mentioned on slaughtering

bukhari:5499.literal_translation: That he met Zaid bin 'Amr bin Nufail at the lower part of Baldah, and that was before revelation was sent down upon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ). So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) presented to him a dining-mat containing meat, but he refused to eat from it, then said: "I do not eat from what you [plural] slaughter on your stone altars, nor do I eat except from that on which Allah's Name has been mentioned."

translation_issue.arabic_term: فَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم سُفْرَةً فِيهَا لَحْمٌ، فَأَبَى أَنْ يَأْكُلَ مِنْهَا، ثُمَّ قَالَ إِنِّي لاَ آكُلُ مِمَّا تَذْبَحُونَ عَلَى أَنْصَابِكُمْ
translation_issue.published_rendering: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) presented a dish of meat (that had been offered to him by the pagans) to Zaid bin `Amr, but Zaid refused to eat of it and then said (to the pagans), "I do not eat of what you slaughter on your stonealtars
translation_issue.literal_meaning: So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) presented to him a dining-mat containing meat, but he refused to eat from it, then said: "I do not eat from what you [plural] slaughter on your stone altars
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates two unattested parenthetical phrases—'(that had been offered to him by the pagans)' and '(to the pagans)'—neither of which exists in the Arabic text, in order to harmonize this report with Bukhari 3826 and obscure that Muhammad himself presented the dish of meat to Zaid and that Zaid spoke his refusal (using the plural tadhbaḥūna, 'what you people slaughter') in direct response to Muhammad's offer.

bukhari:5499.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue, following Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* and Muhsin Khan's bracketed interpolations, that Qurayshi pagans first offered the meat to Muhammad, who merely passed the dish to Zayd ibn 'Amr without eating it, and that Zayd's rebuke was directed at the pagans rather than the Prophet. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states in the active voice that Muhammad himself presented the meat dish to Zayd (*fa-qaddama ilayhi Rasūlu Allāhi ... sufratan fīhā laḥmun*) with zero mention of third-party pagans in the narration, exposing Muhsin Khan's parenthetical additions—"(that had been offered to him by the pagans)" and "(to the pagans)"—as apologetic fabrications absent from the Arabic. Furthermore, the direct contradiction between Mūsā ibn 'Uqbah's active phrasing here and Sufyān's passive phrasing in bukhari:3826 (*fa-quddimat ilā al-Nabī*, "it was presented to the Prophet") demonstrates how early transmitters altered the text to retroactively shield Muhammad from offering idol-sacrificed meat and being rebuked by a pre-Islamic monotheist.

muslim:4233.note: Weeping as he recalls 'Thursday,' Ibn Abbas recounts that Muhammad asked for a shoulder blade (or tablet) and an inkpot to write a document after which his followers would 'never go astray.' Those present responded with the emphatic declaration (`إِنَّ`), 'Verily, the Messenger of Allah is talking delirious nonsense' (`إِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَهْجُرُ`), which the English translation softens to 'is in the state of unconsciousness.'

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ ائْتُونِي بِالْكَتِفِ وَالدَّوَاةِ - أَوِ اللَّوْحِ وَالدَّوَاةِ - أَكْتُبْ لَكُمْ كِتَابًا لَنْ تَضِلُّوا بَعْدَهُ أَبَدًا ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالُوا إِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَهْجُرُ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: He (the narrator) said that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: Bring me a shoulder blade and ink-pot (or tablet and inkpot), so that I write for you a document (by following which) you would never go astray. They said: Allah's Messenger (may peace upon him) is in the state of unconsciousness

muslim:4233.literal_translation: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Bring me a shoulder blade and an inkpot—or a tablet and an inkpot—so that I may write for you a document after which you will never go astray.' They said: 'Verily, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is talking delirious nonsense (yahjuru).'

translation_issue.arabic_term: فَقَالُوا إِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَهْجُرُ
translation_issue.published_rendering: They said: Allah's Messenger (may peace upon him) is in the state of unconsciousness
translation_issue.literal_meaning: They said: Verily, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is talking delirious nonsense / raving (yahjuru)
translation_issue.explanation: The translator renders 'yahjuru' (from hajr, talking delirious nonsense or raving in fever) as 'is in the state of unconsciousness' to sanitize the companions' blunt accusation that Muhammad was speaking incoherently.

muslim:4233.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the companions were merely expressing compassionate concern that Muhammad was overcome by illness or unconsciousness, and that no further written guidance was needed because Islamic revelation was already complete. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states `إِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَهْجُرُ` (inna Rasūla Allāhi yahjuru), an emphatic assertion using `إِنَّ` ('verily') and the verb `يَهْجُرُ` ('talking delirious nonsense' or 'raving') to refuse his direct command (`ائْتُونِي بِالْكَتِفِ وَالدَّوَاةِ`). Furthermore, Muhammad himself stated that this prevented document was intended so that his followers 'would never go astray after it forever' (`لَنْ تَضِلُّوا بَعْدَهُ أَبَدًا`), a loss over which Ibn Abbas wept until his tears flowed like strings of pearls (`كَأَنَّهَا نِظَامُ اللُّؤْلُؤِ`).

muslim:5705.note: After eating poisoned mutton brought by a Jewish woman who admits she intended to kill him, Muhammad declares without temporal qualification that Allah would not give her power to do so (مَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُسَلِّطَكِ عَلَى ذَاكِ) and forbids his companions from killing her (bukhari:2617). Anas nonetheless testifies that he continued to recognize the effects of the poison on Muhammad's uvula, and in bukhari:4428 Muhammad states during his fatal illness that the poisoned food severed his aorta.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ امْرَأَةً، يَهُودِيَّةً أَتَتْ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِشَاةٍ مَسْمُومَةٍ فَأَكَلَ مِنْهَا فَجِيءَ بِهَا إِلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَسَأَلَهَا عَنْ ذَلِكَ فَقَالَتْ أَرَدْتُ لأَقْتُلَكَ ‏.‏ قَالَ ‏"‏ مَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُسَلِّطَكِ عَلَى ذَاكِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ أَوْ قَالَ ‏"‏ عَلَىَّ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ قَالُوا أَلاَ نَقْتُلُهَا قَالَ ‏"‏ لاَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ فَمَا زِلْتُ أَعْرِفُهَا فِي لَهَوَاتِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Anas reported that a Jewess came to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) with poisoned mutton and he took of that what had been brought to him (Allah's Messenger). (When the effect of this poison were felt by him) he called for her and asked her about that, whereupon she said:I had determined to kill you. Thereupon he said: Allah will never give you the power to do it. He (the narrator) said that they (the Companion's of the Holy Prophet) said: Should we not kill her? Thereupon he said: No. He (Anas) said: I felt (the affects of this poison) on the uvula of Allah's Messenger

muslim:5705.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad only meant Allah would not allow the woman to kill him immediately on the spot, claiming the delayed effect of the poison later granted him martyrdom. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states مَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُسَلِّطَكِ عَلَى ذَاكِ ("Allah will never give you the power to do it") as an unqualified denial of her stated intent to kill him (أَرَدْتُ لأَقْتُلَكَ), while Anas records that the poison's effects remained continually visible on Muhammad's uvula (فَمَا زِلْتُ أَعْرِفُهَا فِي لَهَوَاتِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ). Furthermore, Muhammad confesses on his deathbed in bukhari:4428 that the Khaybar poison ultimately severed his aorta ([Quran 69:44](quran://69/44)), confirming that her poison did in fact cause his death.

muslim:6479.note: Near the end of his life, Muhammad declared that at the end of one hundred years not a single person on the surface of the earth would remain—a statement made under oath when asked about the Last Hour (muslim:6481). Ibn Umar reports that people became confused over these one-hundred-year traditions and re-states the saying with the added word 'today' (*al-yawma*) to mean that generation would pass away, while the English translation further interpolates '(from amongst my Companions)' without basis in the Arabic text.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَامَ فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ أَرَأَيْتَكُمْ لَيْلَتَكُمْ هَذِهِ فَإِنَّ عَلَى رَأْسِ مِائَةِ سَنَةٍ مِنْهَا لاَ يَبْقَى مِمَّنْ هُوَ عَلَى ظَهْرِ الأَرْضِ أَحَدٌ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ ابْنُ عُمَرَ فَوَهَلَ النَّاسُ فِي مَقَالَةِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم تِلْكَ فِيمَا يَتَحَدَّثُونَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الأَحَادِيثِ عَنْ مِائَةِ سَنَةٍ وَإِنَّمَا قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم لاَ يَبْقَى مِمَّنْ هُوَ الْيَوْمَ عَلَى ظَهْرِ الأَرْضِ ‏.‏ أَحَدٌ يُرِيدُ بِذَلِكَ أَنْ يَنْخَرِمَ ذَلِكَ الْقَرْنُ
problematic_excerpt.english: he stood up and said:Have you seen this night of yours? At the end of one hundred years after this none would survive on the surface of the earth (from amount my Companions). Ibn Umar said: People were (not understanding) these words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) which had been uttered pertaining to one hundred years. Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) in fact meant (by these words) that on that day none from amongst those who had been living upon the earth (from amongst his Companions) would survive (after one hundred years) and that would be the end of this generation

muslim:6479.literal_translation: He stood up and said: 'Do you see this night of yours? Indeed, at the end of one hundred years from it, not a single one of those who are on the surface of the earth will remain.' Ibn Umar said: 'People became confused regarding that statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what they narrate of these traditions about one hundred years; rather, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only said: Not a single one of those who are today on the surface of the earth will remain—meaning by that that this generation would pass away.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: لاَ يَبْقَى مِمَّنْ هُوَ عَلَى ظَهْرِ الأَرْضِ أَحَدٌ
translation_issue.published_rendering: none would survive on the surface of the earth (from amount my Companions)
translation_issue.literal_meaning: not a single one of those who are on the surface of the earth will remain
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates '(from amount my Companions)' and '(from amongst his Companions)' to restrict a universal statement about everyone on Earth so the prophecy is not falsified by centenarians.

muslim:6479.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was not predicting the end of the world within a century, relying on Ibn Umar's explanation that he only meant the passing of that generation (*al-qarn*) and on the English translator's interpolation limiting the scope to his Companions. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that 'not a single one of those who are on the surface of the earth will remain' (*lā yabqā mimman huwa ʿalā ẓahri al-arḍi aḥadun*), containing no restriction to the Companions. Even with Ibn Umar's addition of 'today' (*al-yawm*) to resolve the people's confusion (*fa-wahala al-nās*), the universal claim that no human alive anywhere on Earth in AD 632 would survive one hundred years is falsified by anyone born that day who lived to age one hundred (cf. bukhari:116, bukhari:564, muslim:6481).

bukhari:5771.note: Abu Huraira narrates Muhammad's command not to bring diseased livestock near healthy ones, and—in a concluding section omitted from the published English translation—denies his own earlier narration declaring that there is no contagion (bukhari:5770). When listeners ask whether he had not previously narrated that there is no contagion, Abu Huraira speaks in Abyssinian, and Abu Salama remarks that he never saw him forget any other narration.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ لاَ يُورِدَنَّ مُمْرِضٌ عَلَى مُصِحٍّ ‏"‏‏.‏ وَأَنْكَرَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ حَدِيثَ الأَوَّلِ قُلْنَا أَلَمْ تُحَدِّثْ أَنَّهُ لاَ عَدْوَى فَرَطَنَ بِالْحَبَشِيَّةِ‏.‏ قَالَ أَبُو سَلَمَةَ فَمَا رَأَيْتُهُ نَسِيَ حَدِيثًا غَيْرَهُ
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: The cattle (sheep, cows, camels, etc.) suffering from a disease should not be mixed up with healthy cattle, (or said: "Do not put a patient with a healthy person ). " (as a precaution)

bukhari:5771.literal_translation: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'An owner of diseased livestock must not bring them to watering with the healthy livestock of another.' And Abu Huraira denied the first hadith. We said: 'Did you not narrate that there is no contagion?' So he spoke in Abyssinian. Abu Salama said: 'I never saw him forget a hadith other than it.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: وَأَنْكَرَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ حَدِيثَ الأَوَّلِ قُلْنَا أَلَمْ تُحَدِّثْ أَنَّهُ لاَ عَدْوَى فَرَطَنَ بِالْحَبَشِيَّةِ. قَالَ أَبُو سَلَمَةَ فَمَا رَأَيْتُهُ نَسِيَ حَدِيثًا غَيْرَهُ
translation_issue.published_rendering: (as a precaution)
translation_issue.literal_meaning: And Abu Huraira denied the first hadith. We said: 'Did you not narrate that there is no contagion?' So he spoke in Abyssinian. Abu Salama said: 'I never saw him forget a hadith other than it.'
translation_issue.explanation: The translator completely omitted the second half of the Arabic text—in which Abu Huraira denies his earlier report ('there is no contagion'), is confronted by his listeners over the contradiction, and speaks incomprehensibly in Abyssinian (raṭana bi-l-ḥabashiyyah)—and instead appended the unattested parenthetical gloss '(as a precaution)' to harmonize the two conflicting sayings.

bukhari:5771.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue, citing Ibn Hajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī and Al-Nawawī, that there is no contradiction because 'there is no contagion' (لَا عَدْوَى) merely negates the pre-Islamic belief that disease spreads independently of Allah's decree, while 'do not bring diseased livestock to the healthy' (لَا يُورِدَنَّ مُمْرِضٌ عَلَى مُصِحٍّ) establishes practical quarantine. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states—in a second half completely omitted from the published English translation—that when Abu Huraira's own disciples confronted him with this exact contradiction (أَلَمْ تُحَدِّثْ أَنَّهُ لاَ عَدْوَى), he knew of no such harmonization, instead flatly denying his first narration (وَأَنْكَرَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ حَدِيثَ الأَوَّلِ) and babbling in Ethiopian (فَرَطَنَ بِالْحَبَشِيَّةِ). Furthermore, the sub-narrator Abu Salama explicitly concludes that Islam's most prolific Hadith transmitter forgot his own report (فَمَا رَأَيْتُهُ نَسِيَ حَدِيثًا غَيْرَهُ), proving that the earliest generation recognized the two statements as irreconcilable.

muslim:7409.note: When desert Arabs ask Muhammad when the Last Hour (al-sāʿah) will arrive, he looks at the youngest person among them and declares that if he lives, old age will not overtake him before 'your Hour is established upon you' (qāmat ʿalaykum sāʿatukum). Although the English translation adds the parenthetical gloss '(he would see you dying)'—which is absent from the Arabic text—the immediate chapter parallels (muslim:7410, muslim:7411) record this prediction unconditionally as 'until the Hour is established' (ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: كَانَ الأَعْرَابُ إِذَا قَدِمُوا عَلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم سَأَلُوهُ عَنِ السَّاعَةِ مَتَى السَّاعَةُ فَنَظَرَ إِلَى أَحْدَثِ إِنْسَانٍ مِنْهُمْ فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ إِنْ يَعِشْ هَذَا لَمْ يُدْرِكْهُ الْهَرَمُ قَامَتْ عَلَيْكُمْ سَاعَتُكُمْ ‏"‏
problematic_excerpt.english: A'isha reported that when the desert Arabs came to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) they asked about the Last Hour as to when that would come. And he looked towards the youngest amongst them and said:If he lives he would not grow very old that he would find your Last Hour coming to you (he would see you dying)

muslim:7409.literal_translation: A'isha reported that when the desert Arabs came to Allah's Messenger (ﷺ), they asked him about the Hour: 'When is the Hour?' So he looked at the youngest person among them and said: 'If this one lives, old age will not overtake him before your Hour is established upon you.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: إِنْ يَعِشْ هَذَا لَمْ يُدْرِكْهُ الْهَرَمُ قَامَتْ عَلَيْكُمْ سَاعَتُكُمْ
translation_issue.published_rendering: If he lives he would not grow very old that he would find your Last Hour coming to you (he would see you dying)
translation_issue.literal_meaning: If this one lives, old age will not overtake him before your Hour is established upon you
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates the parenthetical gloss '(he would see you dying)'—which has no corresponding words in the Arabic clause qāmat ʿalaykum sāʿatukum ('your Hour is established upon you')—to force a metaphorical reading of 'your Hour' as the questioners' personal deaths.

muslim:7409.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that by saying 'your Hour' (sāʿatukum), Muhammad only predicted the natural death of that generation of questioners rather than the cosmic Day of Judgment, as reflected in the English translator's parenthetical addition '(he would see you dying)'. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that the desert Arabs asked about 'the Hour' (al-sāʿah—the Last Hour), and the explanatory gloss '(he would see you dying)' is completely absent from the Arabic wording of muslim:7409. Furthermore, parallel Sahih narrations (bukhari:6511, muslim:7410, muslim:7411) record Muhammad stating unconditionally that the cosmic Hour itself (al-sāʿah) would be established before a young boy grew old, exposing this phrasing as a harmonization of a failed prophecy ([Deuteronomy 18:22](bible://dt/18/22)).

muslim:3433.note: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib reports that Muhammad prohibited temporary marriage (*nikāḥ al-mutʿah*) and the meat of domestic donkeys on the Day of Khaybar in AD 628, into which the English translator interpolates the phrase "for ever" despite its absence from the Arabic text. This report conflicts with canonical traditions stating that Muhammad authorized *mutʿah* two years later at Mecca and Awtas in AD 630 (muslim:3418, muslim:3420) and that Companions practiced it until 'Umar banned it (muslim:3415, muslim:3416, muslim:3434)—a discrepancy Sunni commentators harmonize by positing repeated abrogation (*naskh*) in which *mutʿah* was prohibited at Khaybar, re-authorized, and prohibited a second time.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَلِيٍّ، أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم نَهَى عَنْ نِكَاحِ الْمُتْعَةِ يَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ وَعَنْ لُحُومِ الْحُمُرِ الأَهْلِيَّةِ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Muhammad b. 'Ali narrated on the authority of his father 'Ali that Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) on the Day of Khaibar prohibited for ever the contracting of temporary marriage and eating of the flesh of the domestic asses

muslim:3433.literal_translation: From Ali, that the Prophet (ﷺ) prohibited mut'ah [temporary pleasure] marriage on the Day of Khaybar, and the meat of domestic donkeys.

translation_issue.arabic_term: نَهَى عَنْ نِكَاحِ الْمُتْعَةِ يَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ
translation_issue.published_rendering: on the Day of Khaibar prohibited for ever the contracting of temporary marriage
translation_issue.literal_meaning: prohibited mut'ah marriage on the Day of Khaybar
translation_issue.explanation: The English translation interpolates the words 'for ever' without brackets, despite there being no equivalent term (such as abadan or ilā yawm al-qiyāmah) in the Arabic text, in order to dogmatically project a single permanent prohibition onto the Day of Khaybar (AD 628) despite canonical narrations showing Muhammad permitted mut'ah again two years later at Mecca and Awtas (muslim:3418, muslim:3420).

muslim:3433.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that, as proposed by Al-Shāfiʿī and Al-Nawawī (*Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*), temporary marriage (*nikāḥ al-mutʿah*) underwent repeated abrogation (*naskh*)—being banned at Khaybar in AD 628, briefly re-authorized at Mecca and Awṭās in AD 630, and then permanently outlawed—or claim via syntactic inversion (*taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr*) that 'the Day of Khaybar' applies only to the ban on donkey meat. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *nahā ʿan nikāḥi l-mutʿati yawma Khaybara* ('he prohibited *mutʿah* marriage on the Day of Khaybar'), directly binding the date to the marriage ban while containing no Arabic words whatsoever for the English translator's fabricated interpolation 'for ever.' Furthermore, parallel *Ṣaḥīḥ* testimonies from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh (muslim:3415, muslim:3416) and ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn (bukhari:4518, muslim:3023) collapse the repeated-abrogation excuse by confirming that no Qur'ānic verse or prophetic command ever revoked *mutʿah* and that Muslims practiced it throughout Muhammad's lifetime and Abū Bakr's caliphate until ʿUmar prohibited it by his own decree.

muslim:7278.note: Muhammad declares that the Last Hour will not arrive until an army from Medina fights the Romans at al-A'maq or Dabiq, after which the victorious third of that army will conquer Constantinople (فَيَفْتَتِحُونَ قُسْطُنْطِينِيَّةَ). The prophecy binds the conquest of Roman Constantinople directly to the arrival of the Dajjal and the descent of Jesus son of Mary in a single contiguous sequence, stating that the alarm and subsequent march to Syria occur while those same conquerors are still dividing the city's spoils with their swords hung on olive trees (فَبَيْنَمَا هُمْ يَقْتَسِمُونَ الْغَنَائِمَ قَدْ عَلَّقُوا سُيُوفَهُمْ بِالزَّيْتُونِ).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: لاَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى يَنْزِلَ الرُّومُ بِالأَعْمَاقِ أَوْ بِدَابِقَ فَيَخْرُجُ إِلَيْهِمْ جَيْشٌ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ مِنْ خِيَارِ أَهْلِ الأَرْضِ يَوْمَئِذٍ فَإِذَا تَصَافُّوا قَالَتِ الرُّومُ خَلُّوا بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَ الَّذِينَ سَبَوْا مِنَّا نُقَاتِلْهُمْ ‏.‏ فَيَقُولُ الْمُسْلِمُونَ لاَ وَاللَّهِ لاَ نُخَلِّي بَيْنَكُمْ وَبَيْنَ إِخْوَانِنَا ‏.‏ فَيُقَاتِلُونَهُمْ فَيَنْهَزِمُ ثُلُثٌ لاَ يَتُوبُ اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِمْ أَبَدًا وَيُقْتَلُ ثُلُثُهُمْ أَفْضَلُ الشُّهَدَاءِ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ وَيَفْتَتِحُ الثُّلُثُ لاَ يُفْتَنُونَ أَبَدًا فَيَفْتَتِحُونَ قُسْطُنْطِينِيَّةَ فَبَيْنَمَا هُمْ يَقْتَسِمُونَ الْغَنَائِمَ قَدْ عَلَّقُوا سُيُوفَهُمْ بِالزَّيْتُونِ إِذْ صَاحَ فِيهِمُ الشَّيْطَانُ إِنَّ الْمَسِيحَ قَدْ خَلَفَكُمْ فِي أَهْلِيكُمْ ‏.‏ فَيَخْرُجُونَ وَذَلِكَ بَاطِلٌ فَإِذَا جَاءُوا الشَّأْمَ خَرَجَ فَبَيْنَمَا هُمْ يُعِدُّونَ لِلْقِتَالِ يُسَوُّونَ الصُّفُوفَ إِذْ أُقِيمَتِ الصَّلاَةُ فَيَنْزِلُ عِيسَى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ فَأَمَّهُمْ
problematic_excerpt.english: The Last Hour would not come until the Romans would land at al-A'maq or in Dabiq. An army consisting of the best (soldiers) of the people of the earth at that time will come from Medina (to counteract them). When they will arrange themselves in ranks, the Romans would say: Do not stand between us and those (Muslims) who took prisoners from amongst us. Let us fight with them; and the Muslims would say: Nay, by Allah, we would never get aside from you and from our brethren that you may fight them. They will then fight and a third (part) of the army would run away, whom Allah will never forgive. A third (part of the army) which would be constituted of excellent martyrs in Allah's eye, would be killed and the third who would never be put to trial would win and they would be conquerors of Constantinople. And as they would be busy in distributing the spoils of war (amongst themselves) after hanging their swords by the olive trees, the Satan would cry: The Dajjal has taken your place among your family. They would then come out, but it would be of no avail. And when they would come to Syria, he would come out while they would be still preparing themselves for battle drawing up the ranks. Certainly, the time of prayer shall come and then Jesus (peace be upon him) son of Mary would descend and would lead them.

muslim:7278.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the AD 1453 fall of Constantinople was only a preliminary event and that this narration describes a second, future end-times conquest in which references to swords and lances are metaphorical for modern weaponry. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that an army from Medina (jaysh min al-Madīnah) will fight the Romans (al-Rūm) at al-A'maq or Dabiq over captured prisoners, conquer Constantinople (fayaftaḥūna Qusṭanṭīniyyah), and while dividing the spoils after hanging their swords on olive trees (fa-baynamā hum yaqtasimūna al-ghanāʾim qad ʿallaqū suyūfahum bi-al-zaytūn), march directly to Syria (al-Shām) where the Dajjal emerges and Jesus descends to kill him with his lance (ḥarbatihi). Because the temporal clause fa-baynamā ("and as they would be busy") locks the defeat of the Romans, the conquest of Constantinople, the hanging of physical swords on olive trees, and the appearance of the Dajjal into a single continuous campaign by the same soldiers, the text excludes both a multi-century gap after AD 1453 and any metaphorical reinterpretation of its weapons.

muslim:7354.note: Muhammad tests the adolescent Ibn Sayyad by challenging him to guess something he has concealed—to which the boy replies, 'It is al-Dukh [the smoke]'—and tells Umar not to behead him because 'if he is he [the Dajjal], you will never be able to overpower him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him' (bukhari:1354, bukhari:3055). Muhammad then hides behind palm-tree trunks to listen to Ibn Sayyad murmuring under a blanket so that the boy 'would have made things clear,' remaining uncertain whether the Medinan youth is the Dajjal even though Umar swears in Muhammad's presence without objection that he is (muslim:7353, bukhari:3056).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ مَاذَا تَرَى ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ يَأْتِينِي صَادِقٌ وَكَاذِبٌ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ خُلِّطَ عَلَيْكَ الأَمْرُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ إِنِّي قَدْ خَبَأْتُ لَكَ خَبِيئًا ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ ‏"‏ هُوَ الدُّخُّ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ اخْسَأْ فَلَنْ تَعْدُوَ قَدْرَكَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ ذَرْنِي يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أَضْرِبْ عُنُقَهُ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ إِنْ يَكُنْهُ فَلَنْ تُسَلَّطَ عَلَيْهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْهُ فَلاَ خَيْرَ لَكَ فِي قَتْلِهِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ وَقَالَ سَالِمُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ سَمِعْتُ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ عُمَرَ، يَقُولُ انْطَلَقَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَأُبَىُّ بْنُ كَعْبٍ الأَنْصَارِيُّ إِلَى النَّخْلِ الَّتِي فِيهَا ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ حَتَّى إِذَا دَخَلَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم النَّخْلَ طَفِقَ يَتَّقِي بِجُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ وَهُوَ يَخْتِلُ أَنْ يَسْمَعَ مِنِ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ شَيْئًا قَبْلَ أَنْ يَرَاهُ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ فَرَآهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهُوَ مُضْطَجِعٌ عَلَى فِرَاشٍ فِي قَطِيفَةٍ لَهُ فِيهَا زَمْزَمَةٌ فَرَأَتْ أُمُّ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهُوَ يَتَّقِي بِجُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ فَقَالَتْ لاِبْنِ صَيَّادٍ يَا صَافِ - وَهُوَ اسْمُ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ - هَذَا مُحَمَّدٌ ‏.‏ فَثَارَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ لَوْ تَرَكَتْهُ بَيَّنَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: What do you see? Ibn Sayyad said: It is a Dukh. Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: May you be disgraced and dishonoured, you would not not be able to go beyond your rank. 'Umar b. Khattab said: Allah's Messenger, permit me that I should strike his neck. Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: If he is the same (Dajjal) who would appear near the Last Hour, you would not be able to overpower him, and if he is not that there is no good for you to kill him. 'Abdullah b. 'Umar further narrated that after some time Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and Ubayy b. Ka'b went towards the palm trees where Ibn Sayyad was. When Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) went near the tree he hid himself behind a tree with the intention of hearing something from Ibn sayyad before Ibn Sayyad could see him, but Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) saw him on a bed with a blanket around him from which a murmuring sound was being heard and Ibn Sayyad's mother saw Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) behind the trunk of the palm tree. She said to Ibn Sayyad: Saf (that being his name), here is Muhammad. Thereupon Ibn Sayyad jumped up murmuring and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: If she had left him alone he would have made things clear.

muslim:7354.literal_translation: Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'What do you see?' Ibn Sayyad said: 'A truthful one and a liar come to me.' So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'The matter has been confounded for you.' Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'I have concealed something for you [to guess].' Ibn Sayyad said: 'It is al-Dukh [the smoke].' Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'Be off with you! You will never exceed your rank.' Umar b. al-Khattab said: 'Leave me, O Messenger of Allah, to strike his neck!' Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'If he is he [the Dajjal], you will never be able to overpower him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him.' ... After that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and Ubayy b. Ka'b al-Ansari went to the palm grove in which Ibn Sayyad was, until when Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) entered the palm grove he began hiding behind the trunks of the palm trees, stalking to hear something from Ibn Sayyad before Ibn Sayyad could see him, and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) saw him lying on a bed in a velvet sheet from which a murmuring sound was heard. Ibn Sayyad's mother saw Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) hiding behind the trunks of the palm trees and said to Ibn Sayyad: 'O Saf—which is Ibn Sayyad's name—here is Muhammad!' So Ibn Sayyad jumped up, and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'Had she left him alone, he would have made things clear.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: قَالَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ يَأْتِينِي صَادِقٌ وَكَاذِبٌ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم " خُلِّطَ عَلَيْكَ الأَمْرُ " . ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم " إِنِّي قَدْ خَبَأْتُ لَكَ خَبِيئًا " .
translation_issue.published_rendering: [omitted]
translation_issue.literal_meaning: Ibn Sayyad said: 'A truthful one and a liar come to me.' So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'The matter has been confounded for you.' Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'I have concealed something for you [to guess].'
translation_issue.explanation: The published English translation completely omits two sentences in which Ibn Sayyad states that a truthful one and a liar come to him and Muhammad tests him by concealing something for him to guess ('إِنِّي قَدْ خَبَأْتُ لَكَ خَبِيئًا'), jumping directly from 'What do you see?' to Ibn Sayyad's answer 'It is a Dukh.'

muslim:7354.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was merely exposing Ibn Sayyad as an ordinary soothsayer rather than genuinely doubting whether the youth was the Antichrist (Dajjal). However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that after testing him with a concealed word (إِنِّي قَدْ خَبَأْتُ لَكَ خَبِيئًا) from [Quran 44:10](quran://44/10) omitted by the English translator, Muhammad told Umar, 'If he is he [the Dajjal], you will never be able to overpower him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him' (إِنْ يَكُنْهُ فَلَنْ تُسَلَّطَ عَلَيْهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْهُ فَلاَ خَيْرَ لَكَ فِي قَتْلِهِ). Furthermore, the narration records that Muhammad later hid behind palm-tree trunks stalking to overhear Ibn Sayyad (يَتَّقِي بِجُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ وَهُوَ يَخْتِلُ أَنْ يَسْمَعَ مِنِ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ شَيْئًا) and remarked after being spotted, 'Had she left him alone, he would have made things clear' (لَوْ تَرَكَتْهُ بَيَّنَ), confirming alongside bukhari:1354 and bukhari:3055 that he remained uncertain whether the boy was the Dajjal.

muslim:6481.note: When asked about the Last Hour one month before his death, Muhammad swears by Allah that there is no breathing soul (`nafs manfusah`) upon the earth over whom one hundred years will pass. While the Arabic text of `muslim:6481` states this unconditionally, the English translation interpolates `(from amongst my Companions)` and parallel transmissions (`muslim:6479`, `muslim:6483`) add the qualifier 'today' (`al-yawma`) or reinterpret the oath as diminishing lifespans.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: سَمِعْتُ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَقُولُ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَمُوتَ بِشَهْرٍ ‏ "‏ تَسْأَلُونِي عَنِ السَّاعَةِ وَإِنَّمَا عِلْمُهَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ وَأُقْسِمُ بِاللَّهِ مَا عَلَى الأَرْضِ مِنْ نَفْسٍ مَنْفُوسَةٍ تَأْتِي عَلَيْهَا مِائَةُ سَنَةٍ ‏"‏
problematic_excerpt.english: I heard Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as saying this one month before his death: You asked me about the Last Hour whereas its knowledge is with Allah. I, however, take an oath and say that none upon the earth, the created beings (from amongst my Companions), would survive at the end of one hundred years

muslim:6481.literal_translation: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) saying one month before he died: 'You ask me about the Hour, whereas its knowledge is only with Allah; and I swear by Allah, there is not upon the earth any breathing soul upon whom one hundred years will come.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: مَا عَلَى الأَرْضِ مِنْ نَفْسٍ مَنْفُوسَةٍ تَأْتِي عَلَيْهَا مِائَةُ سَنَةٍ
translation_issue.published_rendering: none upon the earth, the created beings (from amongst my Companions), would survive at the end of one hundred years
translation_issue.literal_meaning: there is not upon the earth any breathing/created soul upon whom one hundred years will come
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates '(from amongst my Companions)'—which is absent from the Arabic text—to salvage an unconditional 100-year pronouncement made in response to a question about the Last Hour.

muslim:6481.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was not predicting the timing of the Last Hour, but merely stating that the generation of Companions alive at that moment would pass away within a century, as reflected in the English translator's parenthetical gloss '(from amongst my Companions)'. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states mā ʿalā al-arḍ min nafsin manfūsatin taʾtī ʿalayhā miʾatu sanah ('there is not upon the earth any breathing soul upon whom one hundred years will come') as a sworn answer to a question about the Hour (tasʾalūnī ʿani al-sāʿah), containing no restriction to his Companions. Furthermore, while this narration dates the oath to one month before Muhammad's death (AD 632), it conflicts with muslim:6485, which places the same exchange upon his return from Tabuk in AD 630.

muslim:6486.note: In response to the Companions asking about the Last Hour after returning from Tabuk (muslim:6485), Muhammad declared that 'there is no created soul that reaches one hundred years.' To account for the unfulfilled prediction, the narrator Jabir ibn Abdullah restricted the statement to every soul created on that day, and the English translator further interpolated '(from my Companions)' despite no such limitation in the Arabic text.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: قَالَ قَالَ نَبِيُّ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ مَا مِنْ نَفْسٍ مَنْفُوسَةٍ تَبْلُغُ مِائَةَ سَنَةٍ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ سَالِمٌ تَذَاكَرْنَا ذَلِكَ عِنْدَهُ إِنَّمَا هِيَ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ مَخْلُوقَةٍ يَوْمَئِذٍ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Jabir b. 'Abdullah reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said:None amongst the created beings (from my Companions) would survive after one hundred years. Salim said: We made a mention of it to him (Jabir), whereupon he said: It means those who had been living on that day

muslim:6486.literal_translation: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'There is no created soul that reaches one hundred years.' Salim said: 'We discussed that in his presence, [and he said]: It is only every soul created on that day.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: مَا مِنْ نَفْسٍ مَنْفُوسَةٍ تَبْلُغُ مِائَةَ سَنَةٍ
translation_issue.published_rendering: None amongst the created beings (from my Companions) would survive after one hundred years
translation_issue.literal_meaning: There is no created (or born) soul that reaches one hundred years
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates '(from my Companions)' and renders 'reaches one hundred years' as 'would survive after one hundred years' to restrict a universal statement about all living souls so the prophecy is not falsified.

muslim:6486.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was not predicting the end of the world within a century, but merely stating that the specific generation of Companions alive on that day would pass away within one hundred years. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states مَا مِنْ نَفْسٍ مَنْفُوسَةٍ تَبْلُغُ مِائَةَ سَنَةٍ ('there is no created soul that reaches one hundred years'), a universal declaration containing no restriction to the Companions—which the English translator had to interpolate parenthetically. Furthermore, Salim's report that they had to discuss the saying before Jabir added the qualification إِنَّمَا هِيَ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ مَخْلُوقَةٍ يَوْمَئِذٍ ('it is only every soul created on that day') demonstrates how an unqualified answer regarding the Last Hour (muslim:6481) was retroactively narrowed after the prophecy failed ([Deuteronomy 18:22](bible://dt/18/22)).

muslim:7410.note: When asked when the Last Hour will be established, Muhammad points to a young Ansari boy named Muhammad in his presence and declares that if the boy lives, old age will likely not overtake him until the Hour is established (ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah). Unlike muslim:7409, which uses the possessive phrase 'your Hour' (sāʿatukum), the Arabic text here and in parallel narrations (bukhari:6167, muslim:7411) uses the absolute eschatological term 'the Hour' without any second-person pronoun, which the published English rendering obscures by interpolating '(he would see)' and 'coming to you.'

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً، سَأَلَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم مَتَى تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ وَعِنْدَهُ غُلاَمٌ مِنَ الأَنْصَارِ يُقَالُ لَهُ مُحَمَّدٌ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ إِنْ يَعِشْ هَذَا الْغُلاَمُ فَعَسَى أَنْ لاَ يُدْرِكَهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ ‏"‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Anas reported that a person asked Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) as to when the Last Hour would come. He had in his presence a young boy of the Ansar who was called Muhammad. Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said:If this young boy lives, he may not grow very old till (he would see) the Last Hour coming to you

muslim:7410.literal_translation: That a man asked Allah's Messenger (ﷺ): 'When will the Hour be established?' And with him was a boy from the Ansar called Muhammad. So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'If this boy lives, perhaps old age will not overtake him until the Hour is established.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: إِنْ يَعِشْ هَذَا الْغُلاَمُ فَعَسَى أَنْ لاَ يُدْرِكَهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ
translation_issue.published_rendering: If this young boy lives, he may not grow very old till (he would see) the Last Hour coming to you
translation_issue.literal_meaning: If this boy lives, perhaps old age will not overtake him until the Hour is established
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates '(he would see)' and 'coming to you'—words absent from the Arabic clause 'ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah' ('until the Hour is established')—restricting the universal Hour to the addressees' lifetimes to soften the failed apocalyptic prophecy.

muslim:7410.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that 'the Hour' refers merely to the death of the immediate audience—a reading propped up by the English translator's interpolation of 'coming to you'—or that the conditional phrasing ('if this boy lives, perhaps...') means the boy simply died before reaching old age. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah* ('until the Hour is established'), repeating the exact apocalyptic term from the questioner's inquiry (*matā taqūmu al-sāʿah*, 'When will the Hour be established?') without any Arabic words corresponding to '(he would see)' or 'coming to you.' Furthermore, deflecting the failed prophecy ([Deuteronomy 18:22](bible://dt/18/22)) onto the death of that generation cannot explain why parallel narrations (`bukhari:6167`, `muslim:7409`, `muslim:7411`) contradict one another over the boy's identity, variously describing him as an Ansari named Muhammad, a desert Arab, a youth from Azd Shanu'a, or a slave of al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.

muslim:7411.note: When asked when the Hour (*al-sāʿah*) will be established, Muhammad points to a young boy from Azd Shanu'a of Anas's age and declares that if the boy lives long, decrepit old age will not overtake him until the Hour is established (*ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah*). Unlike variant reports such as muslim:7409 and bukhari:6511 that attach a second-person pronoun ('your Hour') to reinterpret the prediction as the generation's death, the Arabic text here and in muslim:7410 and muslim:7412 uses the unqualified definite noun *al-sāʿah*—which the English translation obscures by inserting 'to you' without brackets—recording an unfulfilled apocalyptic prediction that also contradicts [Quran 7:187](quran://7/187).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّ رَجُلاً، سَأَلَ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ مَتَى تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ قَالَ فَسَكَتَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم هُنَيْهَةً ثُمَّ نَظَرَ إِلَى غُلاَمٍ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنْ أَزْدِ شَنُوءَةَ فَقَالَ ‏ "‏ إِنْ عُمِّرَ هَذَا لَمْ يُدْرِكْهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ قَالَ أَنَسٌ ذَاكَ الْغُلاَمُ مِنْ أَتْرَابِي يَوْمَئِذٍ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Anas b. Malik reported that a person asked Allah's Apostle (ﷺ):When would the Last Hour come? Thereupon Allah's Messenger (way peace be upon him) kept quiet for a while. Then looked at a young boy in his presence belonging to the tribe of Azd Shanu'a and he said: If this boy lives he would not grow very old till the Last Hour would come to you. Anas said that this young boy was of our age during those days

muslim:7411.literal_translation: Anas b. Malik reported that a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ): 'When will the Hour be established?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept silent for a little while, then looked at a young boy in front of him from Azd Shanu'a and said: 'If this boy is granted a long life, decrepitude will not overtake him until the Hour is established.' Anas said: 'That boy was of my age at that time.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ
translation_issue.published_rendering: till the Last Hour would come to you
translation_issue.literal_meaning: until the Hour is established
translation_issue.explanation: The translator inserts the words 'to you' (which do not exist in the Arabic phrase 'ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah') without brackets to reframe Muhammad's failed prophecy of the universal Last Hour as merely the death of his audience.

muslim:7411.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that 'the Hour' (*al-sāʿah*) in Muhammad's reply refers only to the passing away of the questioner's generation rather than the universal Last Hour—an excuse the English translation reinforces by inserting the words 'to you' without brackets. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah* ('until the Hour is established') with the definite article (*al-*) and no pronoun for 'you,' repeating the exact apocalyptic phrasing of the man's question, *matā taqūmu al-sāʿah* ('When will the Hour be established?'). Because Muhammad's answer uses the identical unmodified term for the Last Hour that the questioner asked about, his prediction that the young boy from Azd Shanu'a would not reach decrepit old age (*al-haram*) before the Hour arrived failed when that boy grew old and died.

muslim:7412.note: When a young boy belonging to al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba—a peer of Anas in age—passes by, Muhammad declares that if the boy's life is prolonged, decrepitude will not overtake him until the Hour is established (*ḥattā taqūma al-sāʿah*; cf. muslim:7410, muslim:7411). This unqualified Arabic phrasing of the cosmic Last Hour contrasts with both the English translator's parenthetical addition ('to the old people of this generation') and the variant wording 'your Hour' paired with the narrator Hisham's gloss ('meaning their death') in bukhari:6511.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ أَنَسٍ، قَالَ مَرَّ غُلاَمٌ لِلْمُغِيرَةِ بْنِ شُعْبَةَ وَكَانَ مِنْ أَقْرَانِي فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏ "‏ إِنْ يُؤَخَّرْ هَذَا فَلَنْ يُدْرِكَهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Anas reported:A young boy of Mughira b. Shu'ba happened to pass by (the Holy Prophet) and he was of my age. Thereupon Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) said: If he lives long he would not grow very old till the Last Hour would come (to the old people of this generation)

muslim:7412.literal_translation: Anas reported: A young boy belonging to al-Mughira b. Shu'ba passed by, and he was of my age, whereupon the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'If this one's life is prolonged, decrepitude will never overtake him until the Hour is established.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ
translation_issue.published_rendering: till the Last Hour would come (to the old people of this generation)
translation_issue.literal_meaning: until the Hour is established
translation_issue.explanation: The translator appends the parenthetical gloss '(to the old people of this generation)'—which has no basis in the Arabic text—to disguise Muhammad's failed apocalyptic prophecy that the final Hour would arrive within that boy's lifetime.

muslim:7412.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that "the Hour" (*al-sāʿah*) in this narration refers metaphorically to the death of the people of that generation rather than the final Day of Judgment, as reflected in the English translator's parenthetical addition "(to the old people of this generation)." However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *إِنْ يُؤَخَّرْ هَذَا فَلَنْ يُدْرِكَهُ الْهَرَمُ حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ* ("If this one's life is prolonged, decrepitude will never overtake him until the Hour is established"), using the unqualified definite expression *taqūma al-sāʿah* without any possessive pronoun or generational qualifier, which exposes the translator's parenthetical gloss as an ungrounded interpolation.

muslim:3434.note: Ali cautions Ibn 'Abbas against showing leniency regarding temporary marriage (*mutʿat al-nisāʾ*), declaring that Muhammad prohibited it alongside domestic donkey meat on the Day of Khaybar in AD 628—a statement into which the published English translation interpolates the word 'forever' despite its absence from the Arabic text. This dating conflicts with Ibn 'Abbas's continued legal verdicts permitting *mutʿah* (bukhari:5116, muslim:3429) and with *Sahih* reports stating that Muhammad permitted it two years later at Awtas and the Conquest of Mecca in AD 630 (muslim:3418, muslim:3420) or that Companions practiced it until 'Umar banned it (muslim:3415, muslim:3416), prompting classical Sunni commentators to posit repeated cycles of abrogation and re-permission.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَلِيٍّ، أَنَّهُ سَمِعَ ابْنَ عَبَّاسٍ، يُلَيِّنُ فِي مُتْعَةِ النِّسَاءِ فَقَالَ مَهْلاً يَا ابْنَ عَبَّاسٍ فَإِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم نَهَى عَنْهَا يَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ وَعَنْ لُحُومِ الْحُمُرِ الإِنْسِيَّةِ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Ali (Allah be pleased with him) heard that Ibn Abbas (Allah be pleased with them) gave some relaxation in connection with the contracting of temporary marriage, whereupon he said:Don't be hasty (in your religious verdict), Ibn 'Abbas, for Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) on the Day of Khaibar prohibited that forever - along with the eating of flesh of domestic asses

muslim:3434.literal_translation: From Ali, that he heard Ibn 'Abbas showing leniency regarding the mut'ah [temporary pleasure-marriage] of women, so he said: 'Hold on, O Ibn 'Abbas, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prohibited it on the Day of Khaybar, along with the meat of domestic donkeys.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: نَهَى عَنْهَا يَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ
translation_issue.published_rendering: on the Day of Khaibar prohibited that forever
translation_issue.literal_meaning: prohibited it on the Day of Khaybar
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates the word 'forever' (entirely absent from the Arabic text) without brackets to make Ali's citation of the Khaybar prohibition (AD 628) read as an explicit, permanent abrogation, whereas the Arabic simply states that he forbade it on the Day of Khaybar—a timeline that clashes with rival Sahih Muslim reports in which Muhammad permitted mut'ah again in AD 630.

muslim:3434.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that *mutʿah* underwent double abrogation—citing Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* and Ibn Hajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī* to claim it was banned at Khaybar (AD 628), briefly re-permitted at the Conquest of Mecca (AD 630), and permanently outlawed thereafter—and that Ibn 'Abbas retracted his permissive verdict once 'Alī corrected him. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that 'Alī anchored the prohibition solely to the Day of Khaybar (*nahā ʿanhā yawma Khaybar*, exposing the English translator's addition of 'forever' as a harmonization fabrication), while parallel *Ṣaḥīḥ* traditions prove that Ibn 'Abbas continued defending *mutʿah* (bukhari:5116) and that Companions practiced it throughout Muhammad's lifetime and Abu Bakr's reign until 'Umar unilaterally forbade it (muslim:3415, muslim:3416).

muslim:3435.note: Ali ibn Abi Talib tells Ibn 'Abbas that Muhammad prohibited temporary marriage (*mutʿat al-nisāʾ*) and the meat of domestic donkeys on the Day of Khaybar in AD 628, conflicting with canonical reports in the same chapter where Muhammad permitted *mutʿah* two years later at the Conquest of Mecca and Awtas in AD 630 (muslim:3418, muslim:3420) and where companions practiced it until 'Umar's caliphate (muslim:3415, muslim:3416). Although Sunni commentators like al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar harmonize these reports by claiming *mutʿah* was repeatedly abrogated and re-permitted, that fails to explain why Ali cited the AD 628 Khaybar ban to Ibn 'Abbas as decisive—a chronological tension the published English translation obscures by inserting the word 'forever' without basis in the Arabic text.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: أَنَّهُ سَمِعَ عَلِيَّ بْنَ أَبِي طَالِبٍ، يَقُولُ لاِبْنِ عَبَّاسٍ نَهَى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم عَنْ مُتْعَةِ النِّسَاءِ يَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ وَعَنْ أَكْلِ لُحُومِ الْحُمُرِ الإِنْسِيَّةِ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Ali (Allah be pleased with him) said to Ibn 'Abbas (Allah be pleased with them) that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) on the Day of Khaibar forbade forever the contracting of temporary marriage and the eating of the flesh of domestic asses

muslim:3435.literal_translation: That he heard Ali ibn Abi Talib saying to Ibn 'Abbas: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prohibited the mut'ah [temporary pleasure-marriage] of women on the Day of Khaybar, and the eating of the meat of domestic donkeys.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: نَهَى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم عَنْ مُتْعَةِ النِّسَاءِ يَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ
translation_issue.published_rendering: Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) on the Day of Khaibar forbade forever the contracting of temporary marriage
translation_issue.literal_meaning: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prohibited the mut'ah [temporary pleasure-marriage] of women on the Day of Khaybar
translation_issue.explanation: The translator interpolates the word 'forever' without brackets, even though no word for 'forever' (such as abadan) appears in the Arabic text (which simply reads nahā, 'forbade/prohibited'), smoothing over the chronological contradiction that mut'ah was permitted again two years later in AD 630.

muslim:3435.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue—citing Al-Nawawī's *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* and Ibn Ḥajar's *Fatḥ al-Bārī*—either that temporary marriage (*mutʿah*) underwent repeated abrogation (*naskh*), being banned at Khaybar in AD 628 before being re-permitted and banned again in AD 630, or that the phrase 'on the Day of Khaybar' (*yawma Khaybar*) grammatically applies only to domestic donkey meat. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states *nahā Rasūlu Allāhi (ﷺ) ʿan mutʿati al-nisāʾi yawma Khaybar* ('The Messenger of Allah prohibited the *mutʿah* of women on the Day of Khaybar'), directly binding the date of Khaybar to *mutʿah* before donkey meat is even mentioned, while containing no equivalent for the word 'forever' fabricated by the English translator. Furthermore, the excuse of a final prophetic abrogation collapses against parallel Sahih narrations in the very same chapter (muslim:3415, muslim:3416), where Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh testifies that the Companions continued practicing *mutʿah* throughout Muhammad's lifetime, the reign of Abū Bakr, and into the caliphate of ʿUmar.

muslim:4234.note: On his deathbed, Muhammad offers to write a document so that his followers will not go astray after him, but Umar ibn al-Khattab objects that pain has overpowered him and declares, 'You have the Quran with you; the Book of Allah is sufficient for us.' After those in the house quarrel and raise a clamor over whether to bring writing materials or repeat Umar's words, Muhammad orders them to leave, prompting Ibn Abbas to lament that it was 'a heavy loss, indeed a heavy loss' that their dispute and noise prevented the Messenger of Allah from writing that document (cf. bukhari:114, muslim:4232).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ هَلُمَّ أَكْتُبْ لَكُمْ كِتَابًا لاَ تَضِلُّونَ بَعْدَهُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ عُمَرُ إِنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَدْ غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ الْوَجَعُ وَعِنْدَكُمُ الْقُرْآنُ حَسْبُنَا كِتَابُ اللَّهِ ‏.‏ فَاخْتَلَفَ أَهْلُ الْبَيْتِ فَاخْتَصَمُوا فَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ قَرِّبُوا يَكْتُبْ لَكُمْ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم كِتَابًا لَنْ تَضِلُّوا بَعْدَهُ ‏.‏ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ مَا قَالَ عُمَرُ ‏.‏ فَلَمَّا أَكْثَرُوا اللَّغْوَ وَالاِخْتِلاَفَ عِنْدَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ قُومُوا ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ عُبَيْدُ اللَّهِ فَكَانَ ابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ يَقُولُ إِنَّ الرَّزِيَّةَ كُلَّ الرَّزِيَّةِ مَا حَالَ بَيْنَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَبَيْنَ أَنْ يَكْتُبَ لَهُمْ ذَلِكَ الْكِتَابَ مِنِ اخْتِلاَفِهِمْ وَلَغَطِهِمْ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Allah's Apostle (ﷺ) said: Come, I may write for you a document; you would not go astray after that. Thereupon Umar said: Verily Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) is deeply afflicted with pain. You have the Qur'an with you. The Book of Allah is sufficient for us. Those who were present in the house differed. Some of them said: Bring him (the writing material) so that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) may write a document for you and you would never go astray after him And some among them said what 'Umar had (already) said. When they indulged in nonsense and began to dispute in the presence of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ), he said: Get up (and go away) 'Ubaidullah said: Ibn Abbas used to say: There was a heavy loss, indeed a heavy loss, that, due to their dispute and noise. Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) could not write (or dictate) the document for them

muslim:4234.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Umar ibn al-Khattab intervened out of compassion to spare the ailing Muhammad unnecessary hardship, and that the unwritten document was non-essential because the Quran was already sufficient. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad offered to write a document by which his followers 'would not go astray after it' (كِتَابًا لاَ تَضِلُّونَ بَعْدَهُ), directly tying the prevented dictation to the community's protection from error. Far from approving Umar's assertion that 'pain has overpowered him' (قَدْ غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ الْوَجَعُ) and 'the Book of Allah is sufficient for us' (حَسْبُنَا كِتَابُ اللَّهِ), Muhammad expelled the companions (قُومُوا) over their nonsense and dispute (اللَّغْوَ وَالاِخْتِلاَفَ), and Ibn Abbas lamented their obstruction of the document as 'the heavy loss, indeed the heavy loss' (إِنَّ الرَّزِيَّةَ كُلَّ الرَّزِيَّةِ).

muslim:3430.note: Al-Rabi' b. Sabra reports from his father that Muhammad prohibited temporary marriage (*mutʿah*), declaring it forbidden 'from this very day of yours to the Day of Resurrection' and ordering that any dower already given not be taken back. While Sabra's parallel chains variously date this perpetual ban to the Conquest of Mecca in AD 630 (muslim:3425, muslim:3428) or the Farewell Pilgrimage in AD 632 (muslim:3426), other *Sahih* traditions place the prohibition at Khaybar in AD 628 (bukhari:4216, muslim:3431), report permission at Awtas (muslim:3418), or state that Companions practiced *mutʿah* throughout Muhammad's lifetime and Abu Bakr's caliphate until 'Umar banned it (muslim:3416, muslim:3417)—a chronological conflict classical commentators attempt to harmonize by positing multiple cycles of abrogation and re-permission.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: حَدَّثَنَا الرَّبِيعُ بْنُ سَبْرَةَ الْجُهَنِيُّ، عَنْ أَبِيهِ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم نَهَى عَنِ الْمُتْعَةِ وَقَالَ ‏ "‏ أَلاَ إِنَّهَا حَرَامٌ مِنْ يَوْمِكُمْ هَذَا إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ وَمَنْ كَانَ أَعْطَى شَيْئًا فَلاَ يَأْخُذْهُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Sabra al-Juhanni reported on the authority of his father:Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) prohibited the contracting of temporary marriage and said: Behold, it is forbidden from this very day of yours to the Day of Resurrection, and he who has given something (as a dower) should not take it back

muslim:3430.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that temporary marriage (*mutʿah*) underwent repeated abrogation (*naskh*)—as claimed by Al-Nawawī and Ibn Ḥajar—being banned at Khaybar (AD 628) and briefly re-permitted before its final abolition, while Companions who practiced it under Abū Bakr were simply unaware of the prophetic decree. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states "أَلاَ إِنَّهَا حَرَامٌ مِنْ يَوْمِكُمْ هَذَا إِلَى يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ" ("Behold, it is forbidden from this very day of yours to the Day of Resurrection") at the Conquest of Mecca (AD 630, muslim:3422), which directly collides both with muslim:3418 permitting it afterward at Awṭās and with Sabra's own conflicting variant placing this exact eternal ban two years later at the Farewell Pilgrimage (muslim:3428). Moreover, Jābir's explicit testimony in muslim:3417 that the Companions openly practiced *mutʿah* throughout Muhammad's lifetime and Abū Bakr's entire caliphate "حَتَّى نَهَى عَنْهُ عُمَرُ" ("until 'Umar forbade it") renders an earlier public, eternal prophetic prohibition historically impossible.

muslim:7355.note: After the adolescent Ibn Sayyad says that both a truthful one and a liar come to him, Muhammad tests him by stating, 'I have concealed something for you'—a challenge omitted from the published English translation—to which the boy replies, 'It is al-Dukh.' When Umar asks to behead him, Muhammad replies regarding the Dajjal, 'If he is he, you will never be able to overpower him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him,' and later hides behind palm-tree trunks to hear Ibn Sayyad murmuring under a sheet before being seen, stating that had the boy's mother left him alone, 'he would have made things clear' (bukhari:1354, bukhari:3055).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ مَاذَا تَرَى ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ يَأْتِينِي صَادِقٌ وَكَاذِبٌ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ خُلِّطَ عَلَيْكَ الأَمْرُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ إِنِّي قَدْ خَبَأْتُ لَكَ خَبِيئًا ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ ‏"‏ هُوَ الدُّخُّ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ اخْسَأْ فَلَنْ تَعْدُوَ قَدْرَكَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ ذَرْنِي يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أَضْرِبْ عُنُقَهُ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ إِنْ يَكُنْهُ فَلَنْ تُسَلَّطَ عَلَيْهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْهُ فَلاَ خَيْرَ لَكَ فِي قَتْلِهِ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ وَقَالَ سَالِمُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ سَمِعْتُ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ عُمَرَ، يَقُولُ انْطَلَقَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَأُبَىُّ بْنُ كَعْبٍ الأَنْصَارِيُّ إِلَى النَّخْلِ الَّتِي فِيهَا ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ حَتَّى إِذَا دَخَلَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم النَّخْلَ طَفِقَ يَتَّقِي بِجُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ وَهُوَ يَخْتِلُ أَنْ يَسْمَعَ مِنِ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ شَيْئًا قَبْلَ أَنْ يَرَاهُ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ فَرَآهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهُوَ مُضْطَجِعٌ عَلَى فِرَاشٍ فِي قَطِيفَةٍ لَهُ فِيهَا زَمْزَمَةٌ فَرَأَتْ أُمُّ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهُوَ يَتَّقِي بِجُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ فَقَالَتْ لاِبْنِ صَيَّادٍ يَا صَافِ - وَهُوَ اسْمُ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ - هَذَا مُحَمَّدٌ ‏.‏ فَثَارَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ ‏.‏ فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ لَوْ تَرَكَتْهُ بَيَّنَ ‏"‏ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: What do you see? Ibn Sayyad said: It is a Dukh. Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: May you be disgraced and dishonoured, you would not not be able to go beyond your rank. 'Umar b. Khattab said: Allah's Messenger, permit me that I should strike his neck. Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: If he is the same (Dajjal) who would appear near the Last Hour, you would not be able to overpower him, and if he is not that there is no good for you to kill him. 'Abdullah b. 'Umar further narrated that after some time Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and Ubayy b. Ka'b went towards the palm trees where Ibn Sayyad was. When Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) went near the tree he hid himself behind a tree with the intention of hearing something from Ibn sayyad before Ibn Sayyad could see him, but Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) saw him on a bed with a blanket around him from which a murmuring sound was being heard and Ibn Sayyad's mother saw Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) behind the trunk of the palm tree. She said to Ibn Sayyad: Saf (that being his name), here is Muhammad. Thereupon Ibn Sayyad jumped up murmuring and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: If she had left him alone he would have made things clear.

muslim:7355.literal_translation: Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'What do you see?' Ibn Sayyad said: 'A truthful one and a liar come to me.' So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'The matter has been confounded for you.' Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'I have concealed something for you [to guess].' Ibn Sayyad said: 'It is al-Dukh [the smoke].' Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'Be off with you! You will never exceed your rank.' Umar b. al-Khattab said: 'Leave me, O Messenger of Allah, to strike his neck!' Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'If he is he [the Dajjal], you will never be able to overpower him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him.' ... After that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and Ubayy b. Ka'b al-Ansari went to the palm grove in which Ibn Sayyad was, until when Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) entered the palm grove he began hiding behind the trunks of the palm trees, stalking to hear something from Ibn Sayyad before Ibn Sayyad could see him, and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) saw him lying on a bed in a velvet sheet from which a murmuring sound was heard. Ibn Sayyad's mother saw Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) hiding behind the trunks of the palm trees and said to Ibn Sayyad: 'O Saf—which is Ibn Sayyad's name—here is Muhammad!' So Ibn Sayyad jumped up, and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'Had she left him alone, he would have made things clear.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: قَالَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ يَأْتِينِي صَادِقٌ وَكَاذِبٌ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم " خُلِّطَ عَلَيْكَ الأَمْرُ " . ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم " إِنِّي قَدْ خَبَأْتُ لَكَ خَبِيئًا " .
translation_issue.published_rendering: [omitted]
translation_issue.literal_meaning: Ibn Sayyad said: 'A truthful one and a liar come to me.' So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'The matter has been confounded for you.' Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'Indeed, I have concealed something hidden for you.'
translation_issue.explanation: The published English translation omits two full sentences in which Ibn Sayyad claims both a truthful one and a liar come to him and Muhammad tests him by concealing something hidden for him to guess before Ibn Sayyad replies 'It is al-Dukh.'

muslim:7355.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad knew Ibn Sayyad was merely a local soothsayer rather than the apocalyptic Antichrist (Dajjal), and only tested him with a concealed word from [Quran 44:10](quran://44/10) (*al-Dukh*) to expose the limits of his divination to the Companions. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad told Umar, 'If he is he [the Dajjal], you will never be able to overpower him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him' (*in yakunhu fa-lan tusallaṭa ʿalayhi wa-in lam yakunhu fa-lā khayra laka fī qatlihi*), demonstrating that Muhammad himself remained uncertain whether the youth was the Dajjal. Moreover, the narration records that Muhammad later hid behind palm-tree trunks stalking (*yakhtilu*) to eavesdrop on Ibn Sayyad murmuring under a sheet and lamented after the boy's mother warned him, 'Had she left him alone, he would have made things clear' (*law tarakathu bayyana*).

muslim:7356.note: In the Arabic text, Muhammad tests the adolescent Ibn Sayyad by declaring, 'I have concealed something for you'—a challenge omitted from the English translation along with Ibn Sayyad's statement that both a truthful one and a liar come to him—before Ibn Sayyad replies 'al-Dukh' and Muhammad tells Umar that if the boy is the Dajjal, Umar cannot overpower him (bukhari:1354, bukhari:3055, muslim:7354). Muhammad subsequently hides behind palm-tree trunks to overhear Ibn Sayyad murmuring under a sheet before being seen, remarking after Ibn Sayyad's mother alerts her son that 'had she left him alone, he would have made things clear.'

When Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) went near the tree he hid himself behind a tree with the intention of hearing something from Ibn sayyad before Ibn Sayyad could see him, but Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) saw him on a bed with a blanket around him from which a murmuring sound was being heard and Ibn Sayyad's mother saw Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) behind the trunk of the palm tree. She said to Ibn Sayyad: Saf (that being his name), here is Muhammad. Thereupon Ibn Sayyad jumped up murmuring and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: If she had left him alone he would have made things clear.

muslim:7356.literal_translation: Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'What do you see?' Ibn Sayyad said: 'A truthful one and a liar come to me.' So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'The matter has been confounded for you.' Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'Indeed, I have concealed something for you.' So Ibn Sayyad said: 'It is al-Dukh.' Thereupon Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'Be off with you, for you will never exceed your rank!' Umar b. al-Khattab said: 'Leave me, O Messenger of Allah, that I may strike his neck!' Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'If he is he, you will never be given power over him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him.' And Salim b. Abdullah said: I heard Abdullah b. Umar say: After that, Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and Ubayy b. Ka'b al-Ansari went to the palm trees in which Ibn Sayyad was, until when Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) entered the palm trees he began shielding himself behind the trunks of the palm trees, stalking to hear something from Ibn Sayyad before Ibn Sayyad could see him, and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) saw him lying on a bed in a velvet sheet of his in which there was a murmuring sound. Ibn Sayyad's mother saw Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) shielding himself behind the trunks of the palm trees and said to Ibn Sayyad: 'O Saf—which is the name of Ibn Sayyad—here is Muhammad!' So Ibn Sayyad jumped up, and Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said: 'Had she left him alone, he would have made things clear.'

translation_issue.arabic_term: قَالَ ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ يَأْتِينِي صَادِقٌ وَكَاذِبٌ فَقَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم " خُلِّطَ عَلَيْكَ الأَمْرُ " . ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم " إِنِّي قَدْ خَبَأْتُ لَكَ خَبِيئًا " .
translation_issue.published_rendering: [omitted]
translation_issue.literal_meaning: Ibn Sayyad said: 'A truthful one and a liar come to me.' So Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'The matter has been confounded for you.' Then Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'Indeed, I have concealed something for you.'
translation_issue.explanation: The published English translation omits two entire sentences in which Ibn Sayyad claims both a truthful one and a liar come to him and Muhammad challenges him to guess a secret he has concealed for him, making Ibn Sayyad's reply ('It is al-Dukh') appear to answer 'What do you see?' rather than Muhammad's divination test.

muslim:7356.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that Muhammad was merely exposing Ibn Sayyad as an ordinary soothsayer for the benefit of his Companions rather than genuinely doubting whether the Medinan youth was the Dajjal. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad told Umar, "If he is he, you will never be able to overpower him, and if he is not he, there is no good for you in killing him" (in yakunhu fa-lan tusallaṭa 'alayhi wa-in lam yakunhu fa-lā khayra laka fī qatlihi), and subsequently crept behind palm-tree trunks stalking to overhear the boy (yattaqī bi-judhū'i al-nakhli wa-huwa yakhtilu an yasma'a min Ibni Ṣayyādin shay'an) before lamenting, "Had she left him alone, he would have made things clear" (law tarakathu bayyana). Furthermore, the English translation omits the Arabic sentences in which Muhammad tested Ibn Sayyad with a mental guessing game—"I have concealed something for you" (innī qad khaba'tu laka khabī'an, referencing [Quran 44:10](quran://44/10), as preserved in bukhari:1354, bukhari:3055, and muslim:7354)—demonstrating that Muhammad relied on a divination test and physical eavesdropping in Medina to ascertain whether the youth was the Dajjal.

muslim:5005.note: Ali ibn Abi Talib reports that Muhammad forbade temporary marriage (*mutʿat al-nisāʾ*) and the flesh of domestic donkeys on the Day of Khaybar (bukhari:4216, muslim:3431), conflicting with Jabir's testimony that companions practiced temporary marriage throughout the lifetimes of Muhammad and Abu Bakr until 'Umar banned it (muslim:3416). Sunni jurisprudence regards temporary marriage as permanently abrogated (*mansūkh*), reconciling these competing timelines through claims of repeated prophetic prohibition and re-permission or widespread companion ignorance of the ban.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: عَنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ، أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم نَهَى عَنْ مُتْعَةِ النِّسَاءِ يَوْمَ خَيْبَرَ وَعَنْ لُحُومِ الْحُمُرِ الإِنْسِيَّةِ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: Ali b. Abi Talib reported that Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) forbade on the Day of Khaibar temporary marriage (Muta') with women and the eating of the flesh of domestic asses

muslim:5005.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the conflicting timelines reflect repeated cycles of abrogation in which Muhammad banned temporary marriage (*mutʿat al-nisāʾ*) on the Day of Khaybar in AD 628, temporarily re-permitted it during the Conquest of Mecca and at Awtas in AD 630, and then banned it again. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Muhammad forbade *mutʿat al-nisāʾ* on the Day of Khaybar alongside the meat of domestic donkeys (*nahā ʿan mutʿat al-nisāʾ yawma Khaybar wa-ʿan luḥūm al-ḥumur al-insiyyah*), while rival *Sahih* narrations (muslim:3415, muslim:3416) state that Muslims practiced it throughout Muhammad's lifetime and Abu Bakr's caliphate until 'Umar banned it.

muslim:7284.note: Addressing his Companions directly in the second-person plural (*taghzuna*, 'you will attack'), Muhammad declares a four-stage sequence joined by *thumma* ('then'): they will attack and Allah will enable them to conquer the Arabian Peninsula, then Persia, then Rome (*al-Rum*), and then the Dajjal. The narrator Nafi' b. 'Utba concludes by telling Jabir b. Samura that because of this sequence, they do not expect the Dajjal to emerge until Rome is conquered (*la nara al-Dajjal yakhruju hatta tuftaha al-Rum*, rendered in the English translation as thinking he would appear after Roman Syrian territory was conquered).

problematic_excerpt.arabic: فَحَفِظْتُ مِنْهُ أَرْبَعَ كَلِمَاتٍ أَعُدُّهُنَّ فِي يَدِي قَالَ ‏ "‏ تَغْزُونَ جَزِيرَةَ الْعَرَبِ فَيَفْتَحُهَا اللَّهُ ثُمَّ فَارِسَ فَيَفْتَحُهَا اللَّهُ ثُمَّ تَغْزُونَ الرُّومَ فَيَفْتَحُهَا اللَّهُ ثُمَّ تَغْزُونَ الدَّجَّالَ فَيَفْتَحُهُ اللَّهُ ‏"‏ ‏.‏ قَالَ فَقَالَ نَافِعٌ يَا جَابِرُ لاَ نَرَى الدَّجَّالَ يَخْرُجُ حَتَّى تُفْتَحَ الرُّومُ ‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: I remember four of the words (on that occasion) which I repeat (on the fingers of my hand) that he (Allah's Messenger) said: You will attack Arabia and Allah will enable you to conquer it, then you would attack Persia and He would make you to conquer it. Then you would attack Rome and Allah will enable you to conquer it, then you would attack the Dajjal and Allah will enable you to conquer him. Nafi' said: Jabir, we thought that the Dajjal would appear after Rome (Syrian territory) would be conquered

muslim:7284.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue that the conquest of Rome (*al-Rūm*) refers to a distant end-times victory rather than the AD 630s–650s conquest of Roman Syria, claiming the conjunction *thumma* ("then") permits a gap of centuries before the Dajjal appears. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states all four campaigns in a single continuous sequence addressed to the living Companions in the second-person plural (*taghzūna*, "you will attack"), grouping the conquest of Rome (*al-Rūm*) directly with the conquests of Arabia (*Jazīrat al-ʿArab*) and Persia (*Fāris*). Moreover, the eyewitness narrator Nafi' b. Utba confirms in his closing statement (*lā narā al-Dajjāla yakhruju ḥattā tuftaḥa al-Rūm*) that the Companions themselves understood the prophecy to mean the Dajjal would appear as soon as Roman Syrian territory was conquered.

bukhari:7355.note: Jabir ibn Abdullah swears by Allah that the Medinan contemporary Ibn Sayyad is the apocalyptic Antichrist (Dajjal) on the grounds that Muhammad did not disapprove when Umar swore the same oath in his presence. This tacit prophetic approval conflicts both with Ibn Sayyad's subsequent conversion to Islam and ordinary death in Medina and with the Tamim al-Dari narration placing the Dajjal chained on a distant island.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: إِنِّي سَمِعْتُ عُمَرَ يَحْلِفُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ عِنْدَ النَّبِيِّ صلى الله عليه وسلم فَلَمْ يُنْكِرْهُ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم
problematic_excerpt.english: I have heard `Umar swearing by Allah regarding this matter in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not disapprove of it

bukhari:7355.anticipated_defense: Muslim apologists typically argue, citing Al-Nawawi and Ibn Hajar's *Fath al-Bari*, that Muhammad's silence occurred before he received definitive revelation about the Dajjal (such as Tamim al-Dari's account in muslim:7386), or that Umar only meant Ibn Sayyad was a lesser impostor rather than the apocalyptic Antichrist. However, the primary Arabic text explicitly states that Umar and Jabir swore by Allah that he was *the* Dajjal (*al-Dajjal*) while the Prophet did not disapprove (*falam yunkirhu al-nabiyyu*), violating the foundational Sunni principle of *taqrir* (prophetic tacit approval), which forbids a prophet from silently ratifying a false oath made in Allah's name. Furthermore, Jabir continued swearing this oath long after Muhammad's death—even as Ibn Sayyad professed Islam, performed Hajj, and died in Medina (muslim:7348)—proving that Muhammad's prophetic silence actively misled his senior companions into a false eschatological belief.

bukhari:6173.note: Uncertain whether the Medinan youth Ibn Sayyad was the Dajjal, Muhammad told Umar not to kill him and later hid behind date-palm trunks hoping to overhear his murmuring so his identity might become clear. This account stands in tension with the Tamim al-Dari narration (muslim:7386), which depicts the Dajjal as an adult man already chained on a remote island.

problematic_excerpt.arabic: طَفِقَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم يَتَّقِي بِجُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ، وَهْوَ يَخْتِلُ أَنْ يَسْمَعَ مِنِ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ شَيْئًا قَبْلَ أَنْ يَرَاهُ، وَابْنُ صَيَّادٍ مُضْطَجِعٌ عَلَى فِرَاشِهِ فِي قَطِيفَةٍ لَهُ فِيهَا رَمْرَمَةٌ أَوْ زَمْزَمَةٌ، فَرَأَتْ أُمُّ ابْنِ صَيَّادٍ النَّبِيَّ صلى الله عليه وسلم وَهْوَ يَتَّقِي بِجُذُوعِ النَّخْلِ، فَقَالَتْ لاِبْنِ صَيَّادٍ أَىْ صَافِ ـ وَهْوَ اسْمُهُ ـ هَذَا مُحَمَّدٌ‏.‏ فَتَنَاهَى ابْنُ صَيَّادٍ‏.‏ قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم ‏"‏ لَوْ تَرَكَتْهُ بَيَّنَ ‏"‏‏.‏
problematic_excerpt.english: When Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) entered the garden, he started hiding behind the trunks of the date-palms intending to hear something from Ibn Saiyad before the latter could see him. Ibn Saiyad was Lying on his bed, covered with a velvet sheet from where his mumur were heard. Ibn Saiyad's mother saw the Prophet and said, "O Saf (the nickname of Ibn Saiyad)! Here is Muhammad!"
